mark_bands.1-Mark Questions: Short answer — one crisp definition or single fact.
mark_bands.3-Marks Questions: Three developed points, or a compact structured paragraph.
mark_bands.4-Marks & Above Questions: Full-length answers — definition, explanation, examples and, where the question asks for it, a defended point of view.

meta.source: PYQ-Combined.html (2021-2026) answered from the S1.x course notes

papers.title: CHILDHOOD, CHILD PROTECTION AND THE DEVELOPMENT OF CHILDREN

questions.question: What is cognitive development?
questions.answer: Cognitive development is the sequential and orderly change in a child's mental processes — perception, attention, memory, thinking, reasoning, problem solving, understanding and symbolisation — by which the child acquires and organises knowledge.

questions.question: Write one advantage of maintaining anecdotal records.
questions.answer: An anecdotal record captures a single significant incident while it is still fresh, and over a term these little entries become the raw material from which patterns in a child's behaviour begin to emerge.

questions.question: Write full form: ICPS, BBBP.
questions.answer:
ICPS — Integrated Child Protection Services.
BBBP — Beti Bachao Beti Padhao.
BBBP was launched in 2015 for the girl child; ICPS is the scheme through which a child's case reaches the Child Welfare Committee.

questions.question: What is emotional development?
questions.answer: Emotional development is the progressive process by which a child learns to experience, recognise, express and control emotions, becomes attached to people and shares the feelings of others, so that a self-aware and socially responsive person gradually forms.

questions.question: What is developmental delay?
questions.answer: Developmental delay is the persistent failure of a child to attain, within the expected period, a milestone that most children reach by that age, in one or more of the physical-motor, cognitive, language, social, emotional or adaptive areas.

questions.question: Write the name of an Act related to child right.
questions.answer: The Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2000, amended in 2015. It governs the care, protection and rehabilitation of all children below eighteen and establishes the Child Welfare Committee.

questions.question: Define Fine Motor Skill.
questions.answer: Fine motor skill is the ability to use the small muscles of the hands, wrists and fingers together with hand-eye coordination — grasping, pincer grip, holding a pencil, colouring, cutting, threading beads and buttoning.

questions.question: What is maturation?
questions.answer: Maturation is the genetically determined, largely self-unfolding process by which the physical and neurological systems become capable of allowing new behaviours to appear, independent of and prior to any training.

questions.question: Write one example of cognitive development.
questions.answer: A four-year-old who sorts a heap of pencils by length and colour, and counts to ten with one object in hand, is showing cognitive development — the gain is not more knowledge but better organisation of what is already known.

questions.question: Write one advantage of maintaining reflective journal for gathering data about development of children.
questions.answer: A reflective journal makes the observer's own thinking visible and therefore examinable, so it exposes the commonest error in child study — believing we have seen a child objectively when we have seen the child through our own expectations.

questions.question: What is emotion?
questions.answer: Emotion is a feeling arising in response to a situation, carrying both bodily arousal and an urge to act. For the child it is the first language — hunger, fear, anger and distress are all communicated through the face and the cry.

questions.question: Write one example of developmental hazards during infancy period.
questions.answer: Prematurity and low birth weight are the classic hazards of infancy. Others include failure to breastfeed, untreated diarrhoea and measles, absence of immunisation, and sudden separation from the mother.

questions.question: When was "Mission Vatsalya" introduced in India?
questions.answer: Mission Vatsalya was adopted in 2021. It is the national scheme for the protection, care and rehabilitation of children in need of care and protection, and it consolidates the child protection framework on a continuum of care.

questions.question: Write one symptom of developmental delays during childhood period.
questions.answer: Loss of skills already acquired is the most serious symptom — a child who could speak and has stopped speaking, or could walk and has stopped walking. It needs immediate referral; it is not shyness.

questions.question: Write full form of POCSO.
questions.answer: POCSO — Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012. It defines a child as one below eighteen, is gender-neutral, and creates a Special Court and a Special Public Prosecutor. Any offence under it is reportable.

questions.question: Mention one principle of development.
questions.answer: Cephalocaudal development — control appears first in the muscles of the head and neck, then the trunk and shoulders, then the arms, and last the legs and feet. An infant controls the head before the hands, and the hands before the feet.

questions.question: Write one demerit of naturalistic observation.
questions.answer: The observer cannot control or repeat the situation, and may interpret what is seen through personal expectation. Behaviour that is rare or unusual is easily missed, since it may simply not occur while the observer is watching.

questions.question: Write one factor that influence on child's social development.
questions.answer: The home is the first and most enduring social environment. It sets the child's basic attitude to other people — whether the world is a place to be trusted or one to be defended against.

questions.question: Write one function of emotion.
questions.answer: Emotion signals to others what a child needs and how they are. The distress that brings a caregiver running is the child's first communication, and the whole system of attachment is built on it.

questions.question: Mention one social skill of children.
questions.answer: Taking turns — waiting for a classmate's turn to speak, to use the slide or to finish first at the game. It is the simplest social skill and one of the hardest for a four-year-old to learn.

questions.question: Write the name of an Act related to child right.
questions.answer: The Protection of Children from Sexual Offences (POCSO) Act, 2012. It is the single most important Act for a teacher's duty: on a disclosure of sexual abuse, do not delay, do not investigate, report.

questions.question: Name any one tool used for collecting data about Child development.
questions.answer: Naturalistic observation — systematic, unobtrusive watching of a child in a natural setting such as the playground or classroom. It becomes a tool only when the watching is planned, focused, timed and written down.

questions.question: Define Fine Motor Skill.
questions.answer: Fine motor skill is the controlled movement of the small muscles of the fingers, hands and wrists together with the eye — grasping, pincer grip, drawing, colouring, cutting, threading beads, buttoning and writing.

questions.question: What is Positive emotion?
questions.answer: A positive emotion is a feeling of pleasantness and well-being — joy, interest, pleasure, pride, hope or gratitude. It widens attention, keeps the child engaged and makes the child more open to others.

questions.question: Write one factor which influences on language development of children.
questions.answer: The quantity and quality of talk in the home is the strongest single factor. Children who hear many words in varied, responsive conversation learn more words — it is adult talk directed at the child, not television, that matters.

questions.question: Write one primary agent of Socialization.
questions.answer: The family. Socialisation begins in the home with the parents, who supply attachment, the model of communication, the treatment of feelings and the child's earliest experience of conflict and its resolution.

questions.question: Mention the name of one Act on protection of Child Rights implemented in India.
questions.answer: The Prohibition of Child Marriage Act, 2006. It forbids marriage below eighteen for a girl and below twenty-one for a boy — the two numbers a teacher and a whole community must know.

questions.question: What is development?
questions.answer: Development is the progressive series of orderly, coherent changes, qualitative as well as quantitative, by which the child comes to function at progressively higher levels of physical, mental, social and emotional organisation.

questions.question: Write name of one child-rights protection Act.
questions.answer: The Child Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act, 1986, amended in 2016. It bans employment below fourteen in any occupation and below eighteen in hazardous work, and requires a child found working to be rescued and educated.

questions.question: Which age is known as 'the age of questioning'?
questions.answer: Early childhood, roughly two to six years, and especially around four — the age when a child begins asking 'why' about everything. This falls in Piaget's pre-operational stage, so the questions are intuitive rather than logical.

questions.question: Write a mental characteristic of childhood?
questions.answer: Curiosity is the great mental characteristic of childhood. The child asks 'why' about everything, wants to know how things work, and learns best through activity, discovery and play rather than through verbal instruction.

questions.question: Write full form: ICPS, CCI.
questions.answer:
ICPS — Integrated Child Protection Services.
CCI — Child Care Institution, the institution where children who have no family or who need long-term care are kept, supported by Mission Vatsalya.

questions.question: Give one example of child's social development.
questions.answer: A five-year-old organising a game with three friends — common goal, shared plot, each taking a role — is showing social development, because this is cooperative play, the transition from playing beside others to playing with them.

questions.question: Give an example of play based on motor development.
questions.answer: Skipping with a rope, or hopping on one foot and then clapping the hands overhead, is play based on motor development — it exercises the large muscles of the trunk and legs and builds balance, strength and coordination.

questions.question: Define Social development.
questions.answer: Social development is the progressive process by which a child acquires the knowledge, skills, attitudes and values needed to interact effectively with others, beginning with the family and extending to the wider community.

questions.question: What is positive feedback?
questions.answer: Positive feedback is a response that approves and reinforces what has been done — a nod of approval, a word of praise or a mark awarded for correct work — so that the behaviour is more likely to be repeated.

questions.question: Mention one social skill of children.
questions.answer: Sharing and cooperating — playing a joint game with a common goal and a division of roles. It is the single most important social development the early childhood period produces, and structured group games in the classroom make it happen.

questions.question: Name two primary emotions.
questions.answer: Any two of interest, distress, disgust, anger, fear and pleasure — these are the emotions of infancy, and the child's cry, gesture and facial expression carry all of them long before language does.

questions.question: Write one demerit of naturalistic observation.
questions.answer: It consumes a great deal of time, and the results depend heavily on the observer's skill and honesty. Because the situation cannot be controlled or repeated, a rare behaviour may simply not occur during the period of watching.

questions.question: Write the name of one Act related to Child Right.
questions.answer: The Commissions for Protection of Child Rights Act, 2005. It provides for the NCPCR at the national level and the SCPCR at the State level — Assam has one — which inquire into violations of children's rights.

questions.question: Mention one principle of child protection.
questions.answer: The best interests of the child. It guides the JJ Act and the UNCRC, and it means the child's welfare comes first in every decision taken by an adult or an institution.

questions.question: Compose a slogan to prevent children from 'Substance abuse'.
questions.answer:
"Say no to gutka and kharra — let the child grow, not the habit."

The point of the slogan is to name the actual danger in an Assamese context — gutka and kharra sold openly near schools, and inhalant sniffing among street and working children. As a teacher I would put up such a poster along with the honest message that a child exposed to adults who use substances is harmed too, even if the child never touches one.

questions.question: Write one merit and one demerit of Interview as a tool for gathering data about development of children.
questions.answer:
Merit: an interview reaches information no observation can. The parent tells us the language used at home, feeding, health, discipline and early worries — the years the child cannot report himself — and the child interview is the only way to hear the child's own account of school, fears and likes.

Demerit: what we get is a report, not a fact. Parents may forget, exaggerate or say what they think we want, and the child's own memory and language may be limited. Answered well it gives depth, but it must never stand alone.

questions.question: Write two principles of growth and development.
questions.answer:
1. Cephalocaudal — development proceeds from head to toe, so control comes first in the muscles of the head and neck, then the trunk, then the arms, and last the legs. An infant holds the head before sitting.

2. Proximodistal — development proceeds from centre outward, so control moves from the trunk to the shoulder, elbow, wrist and finally the fingers.

questions.question: Mention four factors that influences motor development in children.
questions.answer:
Four influences worth naming:

- Opportunity and practice — movement must be practised to exist, so a child kept constantly carried or seated gets far less of it.
- Nutrition and health, which supply the muscle and bone the movement is made of.
- Space and safety — a courtyard, a field, a protected play period.
- Emotional security, because a child who expects to be shouted at will not risk a difficult movement.

questions.question: Mention two functions of emotion.
questions.answer:
Any two of these:

- Signal — emotion tells others what a child needs and how they are.
- Motivating — it energises and directs behaviour; interest and joy hold attention, fear and anger produce avoidance or aggression.

Emotion is not a nuisance to be suppressed. It also communicates, protects, bonds, evaluates situations as good or bad, and carries the child's sense of self-worth.

questions.question: Write differences: Growth and Maturation.
questions.answer:
Growth is the quantitative increase in size, weight, length or girth, measurable in objective units. Maturation is the genetically determined unfolding of physical and neurological potential that makes new behaviour possible.

Growth depends on genes plus nutrition, health and endocrinology; maturation depends chiefly on biological programming and is almost independent of practice. Growth gives a bigger body; maturation gives a body capable of new performance — which is why grouping strictly by birth date repeatedly disadvantages the youngest-maturing child.

questions.question: Write differences: Fine motor movement and gross motor movement.
questions.answer:
Gross motor movement uses the large muscles of the trunk, shoulders, thighs and arms — walking, running, jumping, skipping, climbing, throwing, catching, swimming. Fine motor movement uses the small muscles of the fingers, hands and wrists — grasping, pincer grip, drawing, colouring, writing, cutting, threading, buttoning.

Gross motor is acquired earlier and follows the cephalocaudal direction; fine motor comes later, follows the proximodistal direction, and directly determines school readiness in writing and drawing.

questions.question: Write differences: Physical abuse and emotional abuse.
questions.answer:
Physical abuse is deliberate injury to the body — beating, burning, twisting limbs, boxing the ears, withholding food, made to stand in the sun — and it is usually disguised as discipline.

Emotional abuse is persistent psychological harm done through words, silences and the withdrawal of affection — rejection, humiliation, constant comparison, ridicule, threats. It is often the more hidden of the two, because it leaves no wound, and so it is rarely reported. Neglect and bullying belong here too.

questions.question: Write differences: Child Protection and Child Rights.
questions.answer:
Child rights are the entitlements — protection, care, development, participation, equality and freedom — that belong to every child simply by being a child, whatever their gender, caste, religion, disability or income. They are claims the child holds.

Child protection is the machinery that makes those claims real: the laws, services and institutions, governmental and non-governmental, that ensure every child's survival and well-being. Protection is universal but targeted, and preventive as well as remedial. Rights are the goal; protection is the working.

questions.question: Write short note (any two): (a) Factors that influence emotional development of children, (b) The Juvenile Justice Act, (c) The Prohibition of Child Marriage Act. [2 Marks each]
questions.answer:
(a) Factors that influence emotional development

The inborn temperament — the easy, the difficult, the slow-to-warm — sets the initial intensity and regularity of emotional response. Then the quality of attachment in infancy becomes the child's working model of every later close relationship. Warm, responsive, reasonably firm parenting supports healthy emotional growth; a harsh or rejecting style produces insecurity and, later, aggression or withdrawal. Family stability matters too, since separation, loss and chronic conflict are powerfully corrosive to a child's emotional life.

(b) The Juvenile Justice Act

The Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act was passed in 2000 and amended in 2015. It governs the care, protection, rehabilitation and justice of all children below eighteen. The 2015 amendment aligned it with the UNCRC, strengthened the best-interests-of-the-child principle, and reoriented the system towards children in need of care and protection. For a teacher it matters because it establishes the Child Welfare Committee, the statutory body to which a neglected, abused or at-risk child is reported.

(c) The Prohibition of Child Marriage Act

Passed in 2006, this Act prohibits the marriage of a girl below eighteen and a boy below twenty-one. It makes the offence cognizable with stringent punishment and brings in the District Magistrate and the Child Protection Committee. Child marriage is abuse because it denies the child childhood, education, health and free consent, and exposes her to early pregnancy and lifelong economic dependence. For a teacher the two numbers — 18 for the girl, 21 for the boy — are the ones to remember and to speak about to parents.

questions.question: Write any two factors influencing child development.
questions.answer:
Any two of the following:

1. Heredity — genes set the growth curve and its timing, temperament and rate of maturation; prenatal conditions such as maternal nutrition, illness, prematurity and low birth weight can damage a developmental process before it has begun.

2. Environment — nutrition, family and parenting, school and teacher, socio-economic status, culture and language, and the peer group. Of these the teacher most directly controls the school environment and the peer climate.

questions.question: How home influences on child's social development.
questions.answer:
The home is the first and most enduring social environment, and it sets the child's basic attitude to other people — whether the world is a place to be trusted or one to be defended against. From it come secure attachment, the model of communication, the treatment of feelings, and the earliest experience of conflict and how it is resolved.

Temperament also counts: an infant who is difficult to soothe may be handled less patiently and so socialised less richly.

questions.question: Write any two differences between gross and fine motor development.
questions.answer:
1. Muscles involved — gross motor uses the large muscles of the trunk, shoulders, thighs and arms; fine motor uses the small muscles of the fingers, hands and wrists.

2. Order and skills — gross motor skills (running, jumping, skipping, climbing, throwing) are acquired earlier and follow the cephalocaudal direction. Fine motor skills (grasping, drawing, colouring, writing, cutting) come later, follow the proximodistal direction, and directly determine school readiness in writing and drawing.

questions.question: Write briefly about cognitive development in children.
questions.answer:
Cognitive development is the orderly change in perception, attention, memory, thinking, reasoning, problem solving and understanding. Three features matter: it is qualitative as well as quantitative — the child reorganises, not merely accumulates; it is constructive — the child actively selects, organises and tests; and it is stage-like in Piaget's account.

For a Class III child the practical point is simple: build on concrete material, let the child do the conservation experiment before you name the rule, and let a wrong answer be argued about rather than simply marked wrong.

questions.question: Write briefly about the Prohibition of Child Marriage Act (2006).
questions.answer:
The Prohibition of Child Marriage Act, 2006, prohibits marriage below eighteen for a girl and below twenty-one for a boy. The offence is cognizable and carries stringent punishment, and the District Magistrate and the Child Protection Committee are involved.

It matters because child marriage denies the child childhood, schooling, health and free consent, and exposes a girl to early pregnancy, childbirth complications, domestic violence and lifelong economic dependence. Beti Bachao Beti Padhao, launched in 2015, is the principal programme working against it.

questions.question: Write one merit and one demerit of case-study method.
questions.answer:
Merit: it gives a comprehensive, multi-source, longitudinal picture of the whole person rather than one fragment, combining school records, observation, interviews with child, parents and teacher, medical history and the child's own drawings over time.

Demerit: it is very costly in time and effort, and because it studies one individual only, its findings cannot be generalised to a wider population. Handled badly it also becomes gossip — it must be kept as a confidential professional document.

questions.question: How does play help in child's motor development?
questions.answer:
Play is how most children actually get their motor practice, so it does two things. It supplies the opportunity, space and repetition that movement needs — running, jumping, climbing, throwing and catching cannot be learned from a book. And it builds the foundation in the right order: a child who cannot control the shoulder, elbow and wrist will grip a pencil weakly and painfully.

So removing play from the timetable is not saving time for study; it is removing the practice the writing will later depend on.

questions.question: Write two factors that influence on language development.
questions.answer:
1. The quantity and quality of talk in the home — the strongest predictor. Children who hear many words in varied, responsive conversation learn more words, and it is adult talk directed at the child, not television, that counts.

2. Responsiveness — language grows through turn-taking. When an adult answers a child's sound or word, the child learns that language produces results; when the child is ignored or spoken over, the incentive to speak weakens.

Reading aloud daily, using the mother tongue and hearing clearly all matter as much.

questions.question: What are the stages of social development of the child.
questions.answer:
The stages follow the sequence of play forms:

- Reflexive or solitary (0–2 years) — plays alone; the social smile and stranger anxiety appear.
- Parallel play (2–3) — plays beside other children with separate toys.
- Associative play (3–4) — plays with similar toys in a group, exchanging materials but playing their own game.
- Cooperative play (4–6) — a joint game with common goals and divided roles.
- Games and group activities (7–12) — formal games with rules, teams and competition; the peer group dominates.
- Adolescence (12–18) — peer-group identification and sub-culture.

questions.question: Write two principles of growth and development.
questions.answer:
1. Development is a continuous process — there is no sudden jump from stage to stage, and a skill acquired today rests on what was built yesterday. Gaps in the foundation cannot be repaired cheaply later.

2. The rate of development is uneven — physical growth is rapid in infancy, slows in early childhood and surges again at puberty. Development follows a general sequence, not a uniform timetable.

questions.question: Write one merit and one demerit of Naturalistic observation.
questions.answer:
Merit: it records behaviour as it really happens, without the child knowing he is being watched, so the data is free of the distortion that a test or a formal interview produces. It is also cheap, needs no equipment, and every teacher already does it informally.

Demerit: the observer cannot control or repeat the situation, so rare behaviour may simply not occur, and the recording is coloured by the observer's own expectations. Interpretation must therefore be kept strictly separate from description.

questions.question: Explain gross motor skills with examples.
questions.answer:
Gross motor skills are the movements made with the large muscles of the trunk, shoulders, arms and thighs. They are acquired earlier, practised spontaneously, and depend chiefly on opportunity, space and safety.

Examples: sitting, crawling, standing, walking, running, jumping, skipping, hopping, climbing, throwing, catching, kicking, balancing and swimming. A two-brick balance beam, a hoop to jump through and a ball thrown at a target are all cheap classroom versions of the same practice. Deprivation shows up as weakness, poor balance and low stamina.

questions.question: Mention two functions of emotion.
questions.answer:
Any two of the seven functions:

- Communicating — even before language, emotion is a message, and the tone and emphasis of speech are read correctly long before the words are.
- Adaptive and protective — fear and anxiety have evolved to keep the child out of danger, so removing the capacity for fear is not a developmental achievement.

The others are signalling, motivating, social bonding, evaluating situations, and carrying self-worth.

questions.question: Suggest two measures to stop child labour in India.
questions.answer:
1. Rescue and rehabilitate rather than simply punish the employer. Under the Child Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act, 1986 as amended in 2016, a child found working is to be rescued, educated and rehabilitated — and the fourteen-year general minimum and eighteen-year hazardous-work limit enforced through inspections of tea gardens, brick kilns and workshops.

2. Attack the root through schooling and income support — mid-day meals, scholarships and hostels, and linking families to MGNREGA, so that a child is not a wage-earner because the household has no other option.

questions.question: What is Constructive play? Give an example.
questions.answer:
Constructive play is play in which the child builds, arranges or makes something out of materials, using fine motor skill, imagination and planning together. The product matters less than the designing.

Example: a group of children given wooden blocks, empty matchboxes and a sheet of chart paper, asked to build a bridge strong enough to hold a book. They plan, measure, lay the base, test it and rebuild it when it topples — which is at once construction, problem solving, cooperation and real practice of the pincer grip and wrist control that writing needs.

questions.question: Compose a slogan to prevent children from "Substance abuse".
questions.answer:
"Our child is not a habit — say no to gutka, kharra and inhalants."

The slogan is meant to be said out loud in the community, because in Assam the substance nearest the school gate is often gutka or kharra containing tobacco and areca nut, and inhalant sniffing among street and working children is a recognised problem. A slogan alone changes nothing; but paired with a clear rule about what is sold near a school, and with adults who do not use substances in front of children, it starts a conversation.

questions.question: Mention four factors that influences motor development in children.
questions.answer:
Four factors:

- Opportunity and practice, since movement must be practised to exist.
- Nutrition and general health, which supply the muscle and bone the movement is made of.
- Space, time and safety — a protected play period, a courtyard, simple equipment like balls, ropes and hoops.
- Emotional security, because a child who expects to be shouted at for spilling will not try to hold a cup steadily.

questions.question: Write two strategies for developing social skills in children at school.
questions.answer:
1. Structured group games that push the child from parallel to cooperative play — common goal, divided roles, rules, turn-taking. This is the transition the early childhood period must make, and a teacher can actually make it happen.

2. Give every child a real part in class life — pairs or small groups for tasks, taking turns at the board, looking after the class plants. Social learning is not only peer learning; the teacher's own conduct is part of the social curriculum.

questions.question: Write differences (any three, 2 marks each): (a) Growth and Development, (b) Child Protection and Child Rights, (c) Growth and Maturation, (d) Fine motor movement and Gross motor movement.
questions.answer:
(a) Growth and Development

Growth is quantitative and measurable — height, weight, girth, vocabulary count — and it stops when physical growth ceases around the end of adolescence. Development is qualitative and quantitative change in function and behaviour; it continues well into adulthood and is measured by rating scales, observation and teacher judgement. Growth is chiefly biological; development is biological and environmental. The child who grows 11 cm in a year has grown; the child who learns to hold a pencil has developed.

(b) Child Protection and Child Rights

Child rights are the guarantees of protection, care, development, participation, equality and freedom that belong to every child irrespective of gender, caste, religion or income — entitlements, not favours. Child protection is the set of laws, services, institutions and activities that ensure those entitlements are actually enjoyed, especially by the most vulnerable. Protection is universal but targeted, and preventive as well as remedial; it is also a continuum of care from community support to alternative care.

(c) Growth and Maturation

Growth is a quantitative increase in size, weight and length, measured in objective units. Maturation is the genetically determined unfolding of inherited physical and neurological potential that allows new behaviours to appear without practice. Growth depends on genes plus nutrition and endocrinology; maturation is almost entirely biological programming. The result of growth is a bigger body; the result of maturation is a body capable of new performance — so grouping by birth date alone disadvantages the youngest-maturing child in the class.

(d) Fine motor movement and Gross motor movement

Fine motor movement uses the small muscles of the fingers, hands and wrists, with hand-eye coordination: grasping, pincer grip, drawing, colouring, writing, cutting, threading and buttoning. Gross motor movement uses the large muscles of the trunk, shoulders, arms and thighs: sitting, walking, running, jumping, skipping, climbing, throwing, catching and swimming.

Fine motor is acquired later and follows the proximodistal direction; gross motor is acquired earlier and follows the cephalocaudal direction. Fine motor is easily delayed by opportunity deprivation and directly affects school readiness in writing and drawing.

questions.question: Write short notes (any two, 2 marks each): (a) Parenting, (b) Fear for stranger, (c) Child trafficking.
questions.answer:
(a) Parenting

Parenting is the whole set of care a parent gives a child — feeding, clothing, health, protection, affection, discipline, conversation, and the transmission of values. It is the first and largest influence on every domain of development. What matters is not money but responsiveness: a warm, reasonably firm style supports healthy development, while harsh, rejecting or anxious styles produce insecurity and, later, the aggressive or withdrawn patterns we see in schools.

(b) Fear of strangers

Also called stranger anxiety, it is the distress an infant shows when approached by an unfamiliar adult. It commonly appears around six to eight months and is a normal stage, not a sign of fearfulness. It shows the child now holds a mental picture of the familiar person and can compare the two — so it is one of our earliest pieces of evidence of memory and of an emerging internal sense of self.

(c) Child trafficking

It is the recruitment, transportation, harbouring, transfer or receipt of a child by any means for exploitation — sexual exploitation, forced labour, criminal activity, organ removal, forced marriage or use in armed conflict. The recruitment itself is an abuse, even if the child is never moved. Assam is a source, a transit and a destination in the regional circuit, and floods and seasonal displacement make tracing harder. The teacher must notice, record and refer, and never investigate.

questions.question: Discuss about the type of role that should be played by the parents for ensuring physical-motor development of children.
questions.answer:
A child develops motorically only through practice, and practice needs opportunity, material, time and safety. All four come from the parent, because for the young child the home is the entire motor world — the floor, the stair, the courtyard, the road.

- Allow movement instead of restricting it. Give an infant floor time rather than continuous carrying; let a toddler walk up the steps instead of being carried; keep an open outdoor space where messy active play is possible even in bad weather.
- Supply the material of growth — food, sleep, health care and immunisation. A child who is underfed has no strength left to practise with.
- Protect from injury. A hazardous staircase, an unguarded well, an open road and a stored pesticide are all motor hazards, and one fall can undo months of practice.
- Give emotional security. A child who expects to be shouted at for spilling will not try to hold a cup steadily.

I have watched parents who consider sport unfashionable or unsafe for girls transmit that view silently and very effectively. Active parents model an active life, and that is the cheapest motor provision there is.

questions.question: Analyse the factors influencing cognitive development in children.
questions.answer:
Cognitive development is the orderly change in perception, attention, memory, thinking, reasoning and understanding. Like all development it is the outcome of heredity and environment interacting, but the cognitive domain is especially sensitive to one thing — the quantity and quality of language the child hears.

- Genetic and biological endowment. Genes set the size and structure of the brain, its efficiency and the timing of neural development. Prenatal nutrition, maternal illness, birth complications and later health affect it directly, and damage in the prenatal period and the first two years is the hardest to compensate for.
- Language and communication. Vocabulary, memory and reasoning all grow on talk. The gap in vocabulary at school entry is one of the best-known predictors of later attainment.
- Stimulation, experience and opportunity. Books and materials, guided play, contact with adults and older children, and encouragement to ask, guess, try, fail and try again.
- Family, school and socio-economic conditions — parental expectations, class size, quality of instruction, and the quiet place and the books the household can actually provide.

The child's own motivation, effort, attention and self-concept form a fifth group, interacting with all the others.

questions.question: Write any three factors influencing cognitive development among children.
questions.answer:
Any three of the following will earn the marks.

1. Genetic and biological endowment. Genes determine the size and structure of the brain, its efficiency and the timing of neural development, and thus each child's individual pattern of intelligence. Damage done in the prenatal period and the first two years — maternal malnutrition, illness, alcohol or tobacco, difficult delivery, prematurity — is the hardest of all damage to repair later.

2. Language and communication environment. Cognitive development rides on language. How much talk a child hears, whether adults ask questions and wait for the answer, whether the child is read to, and whether the talk is in a language the child understands well — all of these shape vocabulary, memory, reasoning and the ability to think in words. The vocabulary gap at school entry is among the best-known predictors of later attainment.

3. Stimulation, experience and opportunity. Books and learning materials, guided rather than merely permitted play, interaction with adults and older children, varied situations, and a child who is encouraged to ask why, to guess, to try, to fail and to try again.

A fourth, if you prefer it, is family, school and socio-economic influence — parental expectations, home stability, class size, quality of instruction, and the material conditions reflected in nutrition and health.

questions.question: Write briefly about Integrated Child Development Services (ICDS).
questions.answer:
ICDS — Integrated Child Development Services — is one of the earliest and largest Central Government programmes in India, launched in 1975-76 in rural and backward areas. It delivers a package of services through the Anganwadi centre, which works as the hub for early child care.

Who it serves. Children below six years, pregnant and lactating mothers, and adolescent girls.

What it provides. Supplementary nutrition, health check-ups, immunisation, nutrition and health education, and pre-school play and care for children aged three to six.

Why it matters to a teacher. ICDS reaches the child before the school does — before birth, through the mother, and through the first two years of life. It is the first contact point where developmental delay can be spotted early, and it is where an Anganwadi worker and a school teacher can support the same child instead of working at arm's length. Read it as the opening move in the sequence: ICDS reaches earliest, Beti Bachao Beti Padao addresses the girl child, ICPS is the statutory protection response, and Mission Vatsalya (2021) is the rehabilitation pathway.

questions.question: Write differences (3 marks each): (a) Growth and Development, (b) Child protection and child rights, (c) Nature and Nurture.
questions.answer:
(a) Growth and Development

Growth is a measurable, quantitative increase in the size, proportion and number of the body's parts — height, weight, girth, head circumference — and also in vocabulary. It can be expressed in objective units. Development is the progressive series of orderly, coherent changes, qualitative as well as quantitative, by which the child comes to function at progressively higher levels of physical, mental, social and emotional organisation. Growth is chiefly biological, caused by heredity, nutrition and endocrine functioning; development is biological and environmental, built on opportunity, practice and relationships. Growth in the body stops around the end of adolescence, while development continues well into adulthood. Growth is measured with instruments and scales; development is assessed through observation, rating scales and teacher judgement. In short, growth supplies the raw material on which development builds — a child with healthy limbs may never learn to write because nobody taught them, and development cannot proceed normally without adequate growth.

(b) Child protection and child rights

A right is an entitlement that belongs to the child simply in being a child — not a privilege, favour or property of adults. Child rights are the guarantees of protection, care, development, participation, equality and freedom recognised by international and national law irrespective of gender, caste, religion, race, disability or economic status. Child protection, on the other hand, is the set of activities, laws, services and institutions, governmental and non-governmental, that ensure the survival, development, protection and well-being of every child, especially the most vulnerable. So rights are the entitlements, which exist before any service is delivered, whereas protection is the machinery that secures those entitlements. Protection is also universal but targeted, preventive as well as remedial, and a continuum of care. Rights are usually grouped into three generations — civil-political, economic-social-cultural, and collective — while protection is carried forward by the JJ Act 2000 (amended 2015), the Child Marriage Act 2006, POCSO Act 2012, the Child Labour Act 1986 (amended 2016) and schemes like ICPS and Mission Vatsalya.

(c) Nature and Nurture

Nature is the heredity factor — the genes that set the pattern and timing of the growth curve, the temperament, the individual genetic endowment that explains why two children of the same age mature at different rates. Nurture is the environmental factor — nutrition, family and parenting, school and teacher, socio-economic status, culture, language and media, and the peer group and the shocks life brings. Development is the outcome of the two constantly interacting. Heredity supplies the potential, the timetable and the limits; environment supplies the stimulation that makes the most of that potential. Neither can be substituted for the other: a child with delayed growth may still show normal intellectual development in a responsive environment, and a child with average heredity given rich stimulation will go further than a better-endowed child denied opportunity. This is the point of the whole paper — the teacher does not change the genes, but decides how much of the child's potential is ever actually used.

questions.question: Write short note (any two, 3 marks each): (a) Child rights protection, (b) POCSO Act 2012, (c) Child trafficking.
questions.answer:
(a) Child rights protection

Child rights protection is the practical work of ensuring that the entitlements a child holds by virtue of being a child — protection, care, development, participation, equality and freedom — are actually respected. In India these rights rest on three pillars: the Constitution, the international conventions and the special Acts and schemes. Article 21A, inserted by the 86th Amendment Act of 2002, made free and compulsory education for the six-to-fourteen age group a fundamental right; Article 51A(k) makes it a fundamental duty of the State that the tender age of childhood is not abused; Article 29(2) bars employment of any child under fourteen in a factory or mine or other hazardous work; and Article 23(3) prohibits trafficking and exploitation for economic purposes. The UNCRC, adopted on 20 November 1989 and acceded to by India on 11 December 1992, supplies the wider framework, built on non-discrimination, the best interests of the child and respect for the child's views. Protection is universal but targeted, preventive as well as remedial, and a continuum of care.

(b) POCSO Act 2012

The Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, passed in 2012, is the single most important Act for a teacher's duty. It deals specifically with offences against children, is gender-neutral in its protection, and defines a child as one below eighteen years. It prescribes stringent punishment, including where the offender is a police officer, a public servant or a person in a position of trust, and provides for a Special Court and a Special Public Prosecutor, for the rescue of the child and for protection of the child's identity. For the classroom teacher the practical content is short and sharp: on receiving a disclosure of sexual abuse, do not delay, do not investigate, and report. The offence is reportable by whoever knows of it — the teacher has a legal duty, not merely an ethical one.

(c) Child trafficking

Child trafficking is the recruitment, transportation, harbouring, transfer or receipt of a child by any means for exploitation — sexual exploitation, forced labour, criminal activity, organ removal, forced marriage or use in armed conflict. The recruitment itself is an abuse even where the child is never moved. Assam is a source, a transit and a destination state in the regional circuit linking the plains to the neighbouring North-Eastern states and beyond, for sexual exploitation, domestic and bonded labour and early marriage of girls; floods and seasonal displacement increase vulnerability, and riverine and border geography makes tracing very difficult. It is aggravated by child marriage and child labour, which are the routes by which most children are made available. The POCSO Act 2012 and the Juvenile Justice Act protect the child; the teacher detects, records and refers.

questions.question: Identify the main differences between the concept of Growth and Development.
questions.answer:
Growth and development are often used as if they mean the same thing. They do not, and the distinction is the first thing a teacher has to be clear about.

Growth is a measurable, quantitative increase in the size, proportion and number of the body's parts — height, weight, girth, head circumference — and of vocabulary. It is expressed in objective units, and it is chiefly biological, arising from heredity, nutrition and endocrine functioning.

Development is the progressive series of orderly, coherent changes, qualitative as well as quantitative, by which the child comes to function at progressively higher levels of physical, mental, social and emotional organisation. It depends on opportunity, practice, relationships and culture.

The practical differences are four. Growth stops around the end of adolescence, development continues into adulthood. Growth is measured with instruments; development is assessed through observation and teacher judgement. Growth is an increase in quantity, development an increase in organisation and competence. And the two are bound together: development cannot proceed normally without adequate growth, but growth alone does not guarantee it — a child with healthy limbs may never learn to write because nobody taught them.

questions.question: Mention the merits and demerits of Case-Study method in collecting data about child development.
questions.answer:
A case study is a detailed, comprehensive, longitudinal study of a single individual, family, group or community, combining many sources of data over time in order to understand the whole rather than one part. It is the tool the School Internship Programme requires.

Merits.
- It gives the whole picture of a child — physical-motor, cognitive, language, social, emotional — which no single observation or interview can give.
- It draws on many sources: school records, observation, interviews with child, parent and teacher, medical history, the child's own drawings, and the reflective journal.
- Being longitudinal, it shows change over time rather than a single slice.
- It is the only tool that captures the child's own account of their own life.

Demerits.
- Time-consuming and demanding, needing skill in interviewing and record-keeping.
- The observer's own expectations colour what is noticed — the classic error of believing one has seen a child objectively.
- Findings cannot be generalised, since the sample is one case.
- It carries an ethical risk and must be handled as a confidential professional document, not as gossip.

questions.question: Explain the importance of Gross and Fine motor development in child.
questions.answer:
Motor development is the acquisition of the capacity to move the body and its parts with increasing control, strength, accuracy and coordination. It is the domain in which the environment has the clearest and most immediate effect, because movement must be practised to exist.

Gross motor development uses the large muscles of trunk and limbs — sitting, crawling, walking, running, jumping, skipping, climbing, throwing and catching. It is acquired earlier, practised spontaneously, and depends chiefly on opportunity, space, safety and freedom. Its importance is fitness, balance, stamina and the confidence that lets a child join in; deprived of it, a child grows weak and poorly balanced.

Fine motor development uses the smaller muscles of hands, wrists and fingers and the coordination of hand and eye — grasping, pincer grip, holding a pencil, colouring within the lines, writing, cutting, buttoning and tying. It is slower, more easily delayed by opportunity deprivation, and it directly determines school readiness in writing and drawing. When it is delayed we see a poor pencil grip, painful writing and trouble with buttons and zips.

The two are linked: fine motor is built on the gross motor foundation, so hurrying a child to write before the shoulder, elbow and wrist are controlled produces weak grip and a lifelong dislike of writing. Free play is not a break from physical education — it is the main occasion on which most children get their gross motor practice.

questions.question: Explain about peer influence in Socialization process.
questions.answer:
Socialisation is the process by which a child learns to take a place in a group, to form relationships, to cooperate and compete, and to see the self as others see it. It begins in the family, but from about six, and certainly from about ten, the peer group becomes a powerful agent.

The peer group is the child's first chosen social group, the one where they are evaluated by people who have nothing to offer except friendship. Peer groups sort themselves into friendships, gender groups, cliques and outcasts, and membership confers status. A child's peer reputation may predict their school life better than their home circumstances.

The influence works both ways. Peer groups can teach cooperation, courage, generosity, the rules of a game and how to lose well. They can equally teach exclusion, teasing, pressure to smoke or gamble, risk-taking and open defiance of adults.

For the teacher this creates the practical problem of the school-age shift from adult to peer orientation. A teacher unaware of it will find that the standards the child cares about are not the standards the teacher has set. So I would structure the class so that every child belongs to some working group — the child left at the edge is the one most easily drawn into a group that does neither of these things well.

questions.question: Write about different types of Child abuse.
questions.answer:
Child abuse is any act, or any failure to act, by a parent, caregiver, relative, institution or stranger that causes, or is likely to cause, harm to a child — physically, sexually, emotionally or psychologically — or places the child at risk. Two features of that definition matter: it includes failure to act, so neglect is abuse; and it includes harm that is only likely, so a threat or an evident risk counts before anything has happened.

The main types recognised are:

- Child marriage — below eighteen for a girl and twenty-one for a boy under the 2006 Act.
- Child labour — work below fourteen, or hazardous work below eighteen.
- Child trafficking — recruitment or movement of a child for exploitation.
- Corporal punishment — force used as discipline, prohibited in schools by section 17 of the RTE Act 2009.
- Sexual abuse — governed by the POCSO Act 2012.
- Emotional abuse — harm through rejection, humiliation, comparison, ridicule and isolation; the most hidden form, because it leaves no mark.
- Physical abuse — deliberate injury, usually disguised as discipline.
- Substance abuse — use of or exposure to alcohol, tobacco, gutka and inhalants.
- Stress and the risk of suicide — the pathway through which most other forms do their damage.

A teacher's duty in every case is the same: notice, record the same day in neutral language, refer to the child protection functionary or the Child Welfare Committee or helpline 1098 — never investigate, never promise secrecy, never return the child to the risk.

questions.question: What is child abuse? Mention any four types of child abuse?
questions.answer:
Child abuse is any act, or any failure to act, by a parent, caregiver, relative, institution or stranger that causes, or is likely to cause, harm to a child — physically, sexually, emotionally or psychologically — or that places the child at risk, whether that harm is actual or potential. Two features of this definition must not be forgotten. It includes failure to act, so neglect — not providing food, care, medical attention, education or protection — is abuse. And it includes harm that is only likely, so a threat, a sexual proposition to a child, or an evident situation of risk counts even when nothing has yet happened. Protectionists often use the acronym ASI, for child abuse and sexual exploitation; that is a classification, not a word.

Any four of the following types:

- Physical abuse — beating, burning, twisting limbs, boxing the ears, throwing, poisoning, withholding food, made to stand in the sun.
- Sexual abuse — rape, attempted rape, molestation, incest, inappropriate touching, use of a child in pornography. A child cannot give free consent.
- Emotional abuse — rejection, humiliation, constant comparison, ridicule, isolation, threats and deliberate denial of love; no mark is left, which is why it goes unreported.
- Neglect — chronic undernutrition, poor hygiene, untreated illness, consistently late or absent, no caregiver at meetings.

Corporal punishment, child labour, child marriage, trafficking, substance abuse and stress leading to self-harm are the remaining types in the full list.

questions.question: How does language development occur in early childhood?
questions.answer:
Language develops in a remarkably consistent sequence that runs right through the early childhood period. It begins with the cry, which differentiates by about two to three weeks so that a mother can tell hunger from pain or tiredness. From six weeks to six months comes cooing, and the infant turns towards a familiar voice by about four months. Between six and twelve months there is babbling, with first comprehension around nine to twelve months. The first word falls within a normal range of roughly nine to fifteen months, followed by two-word combinations such as "my cup" at twelve to eighteen months.

The great burst comes between two and five years, the most dramatic language growth of the whole developmental period. The child moves into short sentences with plurals, prepositions, questions and past tense, produces a simple narrative, and goes from roughly fifty words at two to well over a thousand by five.

What makes this happen is the adults around the child. Language develops through turn-taking, so a child whose word is answered learns that language produces results, while a child who is spoken over or ignored loses the incentive to speak. Reading aloud and story-telling are the most economical intervention a teacher has. Grammar errors should be accepted as signs of development, and the most damaging practice is public correction of every error, which teaches a child that speaking is dangerous.

questions.question: Describe the role of competition in social development.
questions.answer:
Social development is the process by which a child learns to become a member of a group, to cooperate and compete, to resolve conflict, and to see the self as others see it. Competition is one of the two ways children learn this, the other being cooperation, and a child needs both.

Constructive competition teaches a great deal. Between seven and twelve years, formal games with rules and teams dominate play, and this is exactly where the peer group holds real power, because a child's status among peers is settled in these games. A rule-governed game is where a child learns to wait for a turn, accept a decision, lose without crying, follow an agreed procedure and work towards a shared goal with other people. The child who is never picked, however, learns early that being left out is normal — and that is a heavy lesson to unlearn later.

But competition can turn destructive. When the adult running the activity compares children publicly, ranks them and rewards only the winner, competition becomes a fixed hierarchy in which the loser withdraws. The shy child stops trying, the aggressive child dominates, and the group learns that some people are not worth competing with at all.

So I would keep competition inside the rules of a game — mixed-ability teams, rotated roles — so that every child is on a winning side sometimes and the purpose stays the learning, not the ranking.

questions.question: What is emotional development? Discuss about the emotional development in different stages?
questions.answer:
Emotional development is the progressive process by which a child acquires the capacity to experience, recognise, express and control emotions, to form an increasingly differentiated emotional repertoire, to become attached to people, and to share and understand the emotional states of others, so that a regulated, socially responsive and self-aware person is gradually formed. Emotion is the child's first language and the fastest means of communication — an infant who cannot speak communicates hunger, fear, anger, joy and distress entirely through face, body and cry.

Across the stages two things happen at once: the repertoire grows, and control improves.

- Infancy (0-2). Interest, distress, disgust, anger, fear, pleasure, with crying and gesture as the main language. Self-soothing appears and improves, attachment forms, and stranger and separation anxiety appear — the first evidence of an inner self.
- Early childhood (2-6). Fantasy, pride, shame, guilt, jealousy and embarrassment join the list. Feeling becomes more language-expressed, dramatic play becomes the child's way of working things out, and self-control appears first in play and much later outside it.
- Late childhood (6-12). A wide and well-differentiated repertoire — disappointment, relief, gratitude, resentment, loyalty, fear of failure. Good impulse control develops, the child can wait and postpone, and self-talk begins to regulate feeling. Pride and shame now depend on achievement and comparison.
- Adolescence (12-18). Intense and rapidly shifting, with the full adult range of ambivalence, longing, resentment and idealism. Control is temporarily reduced by strong feeling and self-consciousness; mood swings and sensitivity to criticism are an ordinary stage, not defiance.

Self-control, note, is learned and not inherited, in small repeated ordinary situations. And children read an adult's face and tone with an accuracy adults underestimate — a volatile teacher models volatility to the whole class.

questions.question: Write in short (any three, 3 marks each): (i) Case study, (ii) Functions of emotion, (iii) School culture, (iv) Child rights protection.
questions.answer:
(i) Case study

A case study is a detailed, comprehensive, longitudinal study of a single individual, family, group or community, combining many sources of data over time in order to understand the whole rather than one part. It is the opposite of the controlled experiment: where an experiment isolates one variable by controlling everything else, the case study deliberately gathers everything. In use, the case is built from multiple sources — school records, observation, interviews with the child, parents and teacher, medical history, the child's own drawings, and the reflective journal — and organised chronologically, with three strands kept visible: what happened, how the child responded, and what the child's own account was. Because this is the tool the School Internship Programme requires, the essential discipline is not to report only the difficulties. Handle it as a professional confidential document, not gossip.

(ii) Functions of emotion

Emotions are not nuisances to be suppressed. They serve at least seven identifiable functions. Signal — emotion tells others what the child needs and how they are; the distress that brings a caregiver running is the child's first communication, and attachment is built on it. Motivating — emotion energises and directs behaviour; interest and joy sustain attention, fear and anger produce avoidance or aggression. Communicating — even before language, emotion is a message, and the emotional content of speech is read correctly before the words are. Adaptive and protective — fear has evolved to protect the child from danger, and losing the capacity for fear is not a developmental achievement. Social bonding — shared emotion is the basis of attachment, sympathy, empathy and love; friends are held together by common feeling rather than shared tasks. Evaluating — emotion is part of the basis on which a person judges a situation as safe or threatening, fair or unjust, and guilt and pride are the emotional forms of moral self-assessment. Self-knowledge and stress — emotion carries the child's sense of self-worth, and sustained strain shows in sleep disturbance, stomach aches, withdrawal or school refusal. The body of a distressed child often speaks before the child does.

(iii) School culture

School culture is the shared set of values, beliefs, norms and practices a school develops over time and that shapes how every member behaves — the ordinary atmosphere of a classroom rather than the written rules. It is built in small repeated ways: how a teacher responds when a child makes a mistake, whether waiting and turn-taking are actually practised, whether the teacher's own conduct is calm and fair, whether a child with no books at home is treated differently from one who has them. A healthy culture is one in which every child has a place, mistakes are treated as information, effort is noticed aloud, and no child's standing depends on family income, caste, language or disability. An unhealthy one is competitive, shaming and indifferent — and it is learned by the children far more thoroughly than anything on the notice board.

(iv) Child rights protection

Child rights protection is the practical work of ensuring that the entitlements a child holds by virtue of being a child — protection, care, development, participation, equality and freedom — are actually respected in daily life. In India these rights rest on three pillars: the Constitution, the international conventions, and the special Acts and schemes. Article 21A, inserted by the 86th Amendment Act of 2002, made free and compulsory education for the six-to-fourteen age group a fundamental right; Article 51A(k) makes it a fundamental duty of the State that the tender age of childhood is not abused; Article 29(2) bars employment of any child under fourteen in hazardous work; Article 23(3) prohibits trafficking and exploitation for economic purposes. The UNCRC, adopted on 20 November 1989 and acceded to by India on 11 December 1992, supplies the wider framework, built on non-discrimination, the best interests of the child and respect for the child's views. Protection is universal but targeted, preventive as well as remedial, and a continuum of care.

questions.question: Principles of growth and development.
questions.answer:
The principles of development are the working rules that let us predict what a normally developing child should be doing at a given age. The four most commonly listed are attributed to Edgar Arnold Hurlock.

1. Cephalocaudal — head to toe. Control appears first in the muscles of the head and neck, then the trunk and shoulders, then the arms, then the legs and feet. An infant controls the head before the hands, and the hands before the feet.

2. Proximodistal — centre outward. Control moves outwards from the central nervous system and trunk to the extremities: shoulders, then elbow, then wrist, then fingers. The whole arm moves before the digits can be moved separately.

3. Development is a continuous process. There is no sudden jump from stage to stage; a skill acquired today rests on what was built yesterday. This is why gaps in the foundation cannot be repaired cheaply later.

4. The rate of development is uneven. Physical growth is rapid in infancy, slows in early childhood and surges again at puberty; language is explosive between two and five; abstract reasoning is a late bloomer.

Two further principles are widely used. Integration — development in one domain supports the others, since secure language lets a child join in with peers, and accepted peers give the confidence to attempt harder cognitive tasks. Individual difference — the sequence is broadly common to all children, but the rate, the intensity and the final pattern vary. Development follows a general sequence, not a uniform timetable.

questions.question: Importance of sports in social development.
questions.answer:
Sports are not a break from real education in an elementary classroom; they are one of the main places where social development is actually practised.

- Learning the group. Team games are the clearest route from solitary and parallel play to cooperative play. A child who has organised a joint game with a common goal, a shared plot and divided roles has already learned group loyalty, rule-making and team feeling. The years of seven to twelve are exactly the years when formal games with rules and teams dominate play.
- Learning fair dealing. Waiting for a turn, accepting a decision, losing without sulking and winning without gloating are learned nowhere else so cheaply. They are the small repeated situations in which self-control is actually built.
- Learning the self. Sport gives a child a position — fast, strong, clever, persistent — that has nothing to do with family income, caste or marks. For many children that is the first experience of mattering for something they can succeed at, and it carries into classroom confidence.
- Learning to include. Mixed-ability teams and rotated roles teach that everyone has a place, which is the practical answer to exclusion and teasing.

There is a real caution. If the teacher announces winners publicly and ranks children, competition turns into a fixed hierarchy and the losers withdraw. Sport builds social development when the game is the point, not the ranking.

questions.question: Child labour and its impact on the society.
questions.answer:
Child labour is the employment of a child below fourteen in any work, or below eighteen in a hazardous occupation, that interferes with schooling, denies play and education, or is harmful to health, safety or development. The Child Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act 1986, amended in 2016, bars employment below fourteen in any occupation and below eighteen in hazardous ones. Two ages to remember: fourteen as the general minimum, eighteen for hazardous work.

Its impact on society is severe and lasting.

- On the child. The years in which language, cognition and the foundations of learning are laid down are lost, and that loss is very hard to make up. Reported forms in Assam include work in tea gardens, brick kilns, domestic service, rag picking, roadside work and small workshops, with children from poor, riverine, marginalised, Scheduled Caste and Scheduled Tribe households over-represented, frequently as "brought" children.
- On the family. Poverty is the root cause, but child labour traps families in it, because the child's earnings are counted on and the child cannot get the education that would break the cycle.
- On society. It produces an unskilled, underemployed adult generation, keeps wages low, and costs the nation the human capital it will need. The denial of play harms every other developmental domain at once, not only schooling.

The Act's answer is rescue, education and rehabilitation, not merely telling the child to stop. The teacher's part is to notice, record and refer — never to assume that a working child simply prefers to work.

questions.question: Discuss in detail about the developmental hazards in different stages of childhood. [4 Marks]
questions.answer:
A developmental hazard is any condition, exposure or event lying in the path of a child's normal development with the potential to delay or distort it. The word hazard is used deliberately in preference to trauma, because a hazard need not already have done damage — it is a risk, and it becomes damage only when it operates. Hazards work through three routes: direct injury to the developing brain or body; deprivation of what development requires, such as nutrition, medical care, stimulation and safety; and psychological or social disruption of attachment and daily life.

The syllabus follows four stages, and what changes across them is not only the nature of the hazard but who controls it.

- Prenatal (conception to birth). Maternal malnutrition and anaemia, maternal illness, alcohol, tobacco or drugs, no antenatal care, untreated infection, physical and emotional stress, domestic violence, early and closely spaced pregnancy, early marriage. The consequences are low birth weight, prematurity and impaired brain development — the child is born already disadvantaged. The teacher's part is awareness alone.
- Infancy (birth to 2 years). Prematurity, failure to breastfeed, malnutrition and infection, untreated diarrhoea, pneumonia and measles, unsafe water, falls, burns, poisoning, drowning, no immunisation, sudden separation from the mother, absence of responsive care and conversation. The result is failure to thrive, delayed motor, language and cognitive development, and disturbed attachment. This is the single most vulnerable period of life.
- Early childhood (2 to 6 years). Child marriage and early pregnancy, child labour, malnutrition, no play space, road and drowning accidents, physical, sexual and emotional abuse, neglect, domestic violence witnessed at home, family substance use, a heavy domestic and sibling care load, migration or displacement. Denying a child play damages every other domain at once.
- Late childhood (6 to 12 years). Child labour in its persistent forms — agriculture, tea gardens, brick kilns, domestic work, rag picking — child marriage in some communities, continuing abuse and neglect, sexual exploitation, school violence and bullying, and family crisis or death. What is lost is schooling in the very years in which the foundations are laid.

Two things stay in a teacher's power at all four stages: the register and the notice, meaning knowing which children work, which are often absent and which are never collected by a parent; and making the school a warm, predictable, non-violent place with a meal, a chair, and one adult who notices distress.

questions.question: Analyse the factors that influence language development of children. [5 Marks]
questions.answer:
Language is the child's first tool and the most reliable index of development a teacher has. What makes it develop is remarkably ordinary, so the list of factors is mostly a list of things adults do, or fail to do.

- Quantity and quality of talk in the home. This is the strongest predictor of all. Children who hear many words, in varied and responsive conversation, learn many words. What counts is adult talk directed at the child, not the noise of a television in the corner.
- Responsiveness. Language grows through turn-taking. When an adult answers a child's sound or word, the child learns that speech produces results; when it is ignored, or the child is spoken over, the incentive to speak quietly dies.
- Reading aloud and story-telling. The most economical intervention a teacher has — fifteen minutes a day gives vocabulary, the structure of a narrative, the knowledge that print carries meaning, and shared pleasure.
- Mother tongue and the language of the classroom. A child thinks and forms concepts in the language of the home. In many Assamese schools a child may speak Bodo, Mising, Karbi, Tiwa or Assamese at home and be taught in Assamese or English, and the gap between the two has to be bridged deliberately through songs, stories, rhymes and play. A child who speaks no standard language at home but talks freely with friends in the mother tongue is not delayed.
- Physical and health factors. Hearing is the foundation of spoken language, and a child with an unrecognised hearing loss is called slow in talking, or stupid, and the damage runs on for years. Nutrition and general health matter too.
- Stimulation and print exposure. Books in the home, printed matter lying about, the child's own scribbles and drawings, and a wall on which children's own writing is displayed and treated as real writing.
- Peer and cultural factors. The language of play with friends, the songs and games a community gives its children, and what a culture values. In many families talk is treated as a nuisance and silence as virtue, so a teacher who reads a quiet child as deficient is often reading the culture instead of the child.
- The school and the teacher. The teacher's own speech, the time given for talk, whether a child is ever actually answered, and the decision to teach in a language the child understands.

The most damaging practice of all is the public correction of every error, which teaches a child very efficiently that speaking in class is dangerous.

questions.question: What are the characteristics of social development? Explain the role of discipline in social development of a child. [5 Marks]
questions.answer:
Social development is the process by which a child learns to become a member of a group — to understand its expectations, to form relationships, to cooperate and compete, to resolve conflict, and to see the self as others see it. It moves the child over some fifteen years from a wholly self-contained organism to a person who can take a place in a family, a friendship, a classroom and a community.

Characteristics of social development:

- It is learned, not inherited. Nothing about sharing, waiting or apologising is in the blood; the first and largest lessons come from the family.
- It is reciprocal. It is accomplished between people, not done to the child. There is no such thing as a child socialised entirely by adults while the child contributes nothing.
- It has two interlocking aspects. Social performance is the observable behaviour — sharing, leading, following, negotiating, excluding, teasing. Social understanding is the growing capacity to read another person's feelings and intentions and to know the rules. A child can be perfectly well behaved and understand nobody, which is why the two must be judged separately.
- It is inseparable from emotion. Social experience is the main source of emotional learning: a child rejected by friends learns helplessness, and a child who feels anxious cannot concentrate, falls behind, and is rejected further.
- It is staged — solitary, parallel, associative and cooperative play, then rule-governed games and teams, then the intense small friendship groups of adolescence.
- It has a decisive turning point at school age, when the centre of gravity shifts from the adult to the peer group.

The role of discipline:

Discipline is the professional management of behaviour by appropriate means. It is not regulation by force, and the difference is the whole point — corporal punishment may silence a child for a minute; discipline teaches something that lasts.

Used well, discipline is one of the main engines of social development. Self-control does not arrive on its own; it is built in small, repeated, ordinary situations — waiting for a turn, putting away a toy, finishing a task before starting another, sitting through a lesson that is not interesting. Discipline is how a child learns that other people's needs are real, that rules exist before they are enforced, and that frustration can be survived. A classroom that never frustrates the child in order to stay pleasant produces an adult who cannot tolerate frustration.

It works best when it is warm and firm together. A teacher who only punishes produces fear and teaches nothing; a teacher who never holds a line produces a child who expects the world to rearrange itself.

Two cautions. Discipline must never be physical — section 17 of the RTE Act 2009 prohibits corporal punishment in educational institutions, and apart from the law, a child who is beaten learns that power settles arguments. And a teacher cannot discipline a child out of a condition: a child who is beaten at home or works fourteen hours needs protection, not punishment.

questions.question: Write about the various stages of development and their characteristics. [5 Marks]
questions.answer:
Development is not a smooth ramp but a series of qualitatively distinct periods, each with its own characteristic rate, style and dominant task. For elementary teacher education the childhood years are arranged in four periods.

- Infancy (birth to 2 years). Physical growth is rapid and almost uninterrupted; sensory and motor control advances; speech begins. The dominant task is trust and secure attachment, first autonomy, and the laying of language foundations. Growth in these three years is so fast that the child roughly doubles its birth weight in four to six months and triples it by the end of the first year, which is why infant nutrition is a matter of urgency rather than refinement.
- Early childhood (2 to 6 years). Physical growth slows noticeably while language, cognition and imagination develop dramatically. Attention span is short, learning is by play, and social play moves from parallel towards cooperative. The dominant task is initiative, the mastery of language, and pre-operational thinking.
- Late childhood (6 to 12 years). Growth is steady and slow, fine motor skills are refined, reasoning becomes logical and concrete, and the peer group grows more important than the adult. The dominant task is industry and achievement — the child wants to be competent at something. This is the elementary school, and everything a D.El.Ed teacher does is aimed at it.
