- Adolescence (12 to 18 years). The pubertal growth spurt arrives, emotion becomes intense and rapidly shifting, abstract reasoning begins, and identity is in question. The dominant task is identity and self-definition, with formal operational thinking emerging unevenly.

Three characteristics of development as a whole belong with these stages. Growth is not linear but sporadic and roughly sigmoid — slow at first, rapid in infancy, a pause in middle childhood, and a second surge at puberty; the most dramatic phase of all is prenatal and the first two years. Development is continuous, with no sudden jumps, so every skill acquired today rests on what was built yesterday, which is why a gap in the foundation cannot be repaired cheaply later. And the rate is uneven and individual difference is normal: within one child one domain may be well ahead of another, and while the sequence is broadly common to all children, the rate, the intensity and the final pattern vary.

Which is why a stage describes what most children do, and is not a timetable on which any individual child is to be graded.

questions.question: Mention four tools of data collection. Describe with example how children's data helps the teacher. [5 Marks]
questions.answer:
The six tools of child study in this paper are naturalistic observation, interviews, case studies, anecdotal records, reflective journals and clinical methods. Four may be described here; clinical methods, the sixth, are diagnostic and belong to trained professionals.

- Naturalistic observation. Systematic, unobtrusive watching of a child in a setting where the child behaves naturally — the playground, the classroom, the home, the Anganwadi. The observer does not organise the situation but records what occurs. It becomes a tool only when the watching is planned, focused on a stated behaviour, timed and written down.
- Interviews. Conversations held with a purpose, in two forms. The parent interview elicits history, habits, the language used at home, feeding, discipline, health and developmental concerns — the indispensable source of information about the early years that the child cannot supply. The child interview elicits the child's own account of family, school, fears and worries.
- Case studies. A detailed, comprehensive, longitudinal study of a single child, family or group, built from many sources over time. Where an experiment isolates one variable by controlling everything else, the case study deliberately gathers everything.
- Anecdotal records. A brief written account of a single significant incident, recorded the same day, in plain descriptive language. Where a case study is a book, an anecdotal record is a postcard — and it is the tool most likely to be used every day by a working teacher.

How children's data helps the teacher — a worked example. In a Class II in a rural Assamese-medium school a teacher keeps a small notebook. One entry reads: 'Ranju asked three times to go to the toilet in one period and did not ask again.' That is data; 'Ranju was a nuisance' is not. A month of such entries, kept in columns for date, setting and observed behaviour, turns one impression into a pattern — and a pattern lets the teacher do four things she could not do before. It tells her the children in her charge individually, so that Ranju is no longer read as careless but as possibly anxious. It groups children by need instead of by ability, so that a child who has never handled scissors is given real material rather than another worksheet. It measures the effect of her own teaching, since a fall in teasing after she introduced a turn-taking routine is evidence rather than opinion. And it supplies the raw material for the work she is formally required to do, namely the case study in the School Internship and the report on the parent interviews.

One caution has to end the answer. Five of the six tools are tools of description, not diagnosis. Careful data does not make a teacher qualified to call a child autistic or disabled; what it lets her do is notice, record, consult and refer — which is exactly what is asked of her.

questions.question: What are the stages of cognitive development with reference to Jean Piaget? Write about their characteristics. [6 Marks]
questions.answer:
Cognitive development is the sequential and orderly change in the mental processes of a child — perception, attention, memory, thinking, reasoning, problem solving, understanding and symbolisation — by which the child acquires and organises knowledge. Jean Piaget (1896–1980), a Swiss psychologist who studied his own three children over years and asked not what children know but how they think and why their mistakes change with age, gave the most influential account of it. Three ideas run through the theory: children pass through an invariable sequence of qualitatively distinct stages, each with its own structure of thought; knowledge is constructed by assimilation, fitting new experience into an existing scheme, and accommodation, changing the scheme to fit the experience; and the sequence is invariable while the ages at which children enter the stages are not.

**Stage 1 — Sensorimotor (0 to 2 years).** The infant knows the world through the senses and through movement. Knowledge begins with the mouth and the hands, and everything is learned by doing rather than by being told. Two achievements mark the end of the stage: object permanence, the understanding that a thing continues to exist out of sight, which is why a child who drops a toy under a blanket will not look for it; and goal-directed action, in which several actions are coordinated into a plan, such as pushing a chair to reach a shelf. Implication: learn by doing.

**Stage 2 — Pre-operational (2 to 7 years).** The child acquires the symbolic function and can use one thing to stand for another — a piece of wood is a doll, a folded paper a boat — which is the foundation of pretend play, drawing, language and all later abstract thought. Five characteristics follow. Egocentrism, the inability to take another's point of view, which is a stage limitation and not selfishness, and is why a child who is 'wrong' in an argument genuinely cannot see the other side. Intuition rather than logic, so that it must be heavier because it is bigger. No conservation, so that water poured from a tall glass into a flat one is genuinely thought to have increased — the classic test of the transition. Centration, focusing on length or height and ignoring the rest. Irreversibility, the inability to undo an action mentally. Implication: learn through play.

**Stage 3 — Concrete operational (7 to 11 years).** Logical operations become possible, but only on material that is present and visible. Four operations characterise the stage: conservation; reversibility, the ability to undo an action mentally, which makes schoolwork checkable, revisable and self-correcting and is why the first real pleasure in arithmetic arrives at this age; classification, grouping by common properties and understanding that a thing belongs to several classes at once; and seriation, arranging objects along a quantitative dimension such as size. The child is still substantially egocentric but can now take another's view, which is why rule-governed team games and the peer group are so powerful. Implication: learn by doing, on concrete material.

**Stage 4 — Formal operational (11 years onwards).** Thinking becomes abstract and hypothetical, though unevenly until the mid-teens. The adolescent can reason about possibilities rather than facts, formulate and systematically test hypotheses, consider a system as a whole, detect inconsistency in an argument, and think about thinking itself. Mathematics, science, formal logic and abstract moral argument become genuinely accessible. Implication: learn by discussion and self-direction.

Two warnings follow directly for the classroom: a child cannot be taught a stage of thought they have not reached, and a child cannot be held back in a stage they have passed. In practice this means building the elementary curriculum on objects, blocks, apparatus and models, letting a Class III child perform the conservation experiment before naming it, and allowing dramatic and pretend play as a legitimate way of learning rather than a waste of time.

questions.question: Discuss in detail about the types of developmental delays. [5 Marks]
questions.answer:
Developmental delay is the persistent failure of a child to attain, within the expected period, a milestone that the majority of children reach by that age, in one or more of the areas of physical-motor, cognitive, language, social, emotional or adaptive development. It is a descriptive term and not a diagnosis, and the word delay is used rather than any older term both because it is more accurate and because it is now the required professional usage. A child can be growing normally and still be developmentally delayed; growth and development are not the same test.

Delay is classified along two axes — whether it is general or specific, and which domain it affects. This gives the following types.

- Global or general delay, affecting all or most domains: uniform slow development, milestones late across the board, usually evident before three years, requiring medical assessment.
- Speech and language delay: late babbling, no words at eighteen months, no two-word combinations, late grammar, and a child who understands and responds perfectly at home but appears mute in class.
- Motor development delay, affecting gross motor, fine motor or both: late sitting, standing and walking, late grasping, a pencil grip that never firms up, poor balance and coordination.
- Learning difficulty or specific learning disability: reading, writing or arithmetic lag markedly while intelligence and general development are normal, persisting despite instruction, and usually accompanied by restlessness and low self-esteem because the child can see that others find the same work easy.
- Intellectual disability: a significant limitation of intellectual functioning together with adaptive behaviour, present from early development, needing specialist assessment and carrying a legal entitlement to education.
- Autistic spectrum disorder: very limited or no eye contact, absence of joint attention, preference for routine and distress at change, unusual sensory responses, often a late talker, with abilities uneven across domains.
- Social-emotional or attachment delay: emotional regulation and relationships affected, the child very difficult or very withdrawn or indiscriminately friendly with strangers, often arising from early deprivation or repeated changes of caregiver.
- Sensory impairment affecting development: no response to sound or to a name, unrecognised deafness mistaken for dullness, visual difficulty mistaken for clumsiness.

Two distinctions carry marks. Delay versus disability: a delay means the child is behind the expected period and may yet catch up, whereas a disability is a lasting limitation of function. Delay versus disorder: a delay describes a gap in time, a disorder is the condition causing that gap.

And the sentence that should close any answer on this subject: the teacher observes, records and refers, and does not diagnose. A child who does not babble by about twelve months, has no meaningful words by eighteen months, does not respond to a name, or has lost a skill they once had must be referred. Loss of previously acquired skills is a medical matter needing immediate referral; a child who could speak and has stopped speaking has not merely become shy.

questions.question: Write short notes (any three, 4 marks each): (a) Naturalistic observations, (b) Functions of emotions, (c) Role of parents for physical development of children, (d) Types of developmental delay. [4 Marks each]
questions.answer:
(a) Naturalistic observation

Naturalistic observation is the systematic, unobtrusive watching of a child in a setting in which the child behaves naturally — the playground, the classroom, the home, the Anganwadi centre. The observer does not organise the situation; it is allowed to occur, and the observer records what happens. Every teacher does this informally all day, but it becomes a tool of data collection only when the watching is planned, focused on a stated behaviour, timed and written down.

In use: decide first what you are looking at and write it down — for instance, 'the number and kind of social interactions during free play in the first fifteen minutes' — then choose the setting and the time, obtain permission, and position yourself where you can see without becoming the centre of attention. Keep columns for date, setting and observed behaviour, and keep interpretation strictly separate from description, because mixing the two is the commonest way good observation becomes useless.

(b) Functions of emotions

Emotions are not nuisances to be suppressed. They serve at least seven identifiable functions in the life of a child.

- Signal. Emotion tells others what a child needs and how they are. The distress that brings a caregiver running is the child's first communication, and the whole system of attachment is built on it.
- Motivating. Emotion energises and directs behaviour. Interest and joy sustain attention; fear and anger produce avoidance or aggression.
- Communicating. Even before language, emotion is a message, and much of the emotional content of speech — tone, emphasis, expression — is read correctly by the listener before the words are.
- Adaptive and protective. Fear and anxiety have evolved to protect the child from danger. Losing the capacity for fear is not a developmental achievement.
- Social bonding. Shared emotion is the basis of attachment, sympathy, empathy and love. Friends are held together by common feeling rather than by shared tasks.
- Evaluating and decision-making. Emotion is part of what makes a person judge a situation as good or bad, safe or threatening, fair or unjust; guilt and pride are the emotional forms of moral self-assessment.
- Self-knowledge and stress. Emotion carries the child's sense of self-worth, and sustained emotional strain is expressed psychosomatically — in sleep disturbance, stomach aches, withdrawal, aggression or refusal to come to school. The body of a distressed child often speaks before the child does.

(c) Role of parents for physical development of children

A child develops motorically only through practice, and practice needs opportunity, material, time and safety. The young child's entire motor world is the home — the floor, the stair, the courtyard, the road, the charpai, the company of siblings — and the parent is the first and most frequent supplier of it.

Parents provide movement rather than restricting it: floor time for infants instead of continuous carrying, letting a toddler walk up a step instead of being carried, some outdoor space, messy active play even in bad weather, and no battery-operated toy standing in for running. They supply the nutrition and health care that are the material of growth, and protection from injury — a hazardous staircase, an unguarded well, an open road, a stored pesticide. They supply the emotional security without which no child will attempt a difficult movement; a child who expects to be shouted at for spilling will not try to hold a cup steadily. And parents model it: active parents transmit an active life, while parents who regard sport as unfashionable or unsafe for girls transmit that view just as effectively, and silently.

(d) Types of developmental delay

Developmental delay is the persistent failure to attain within the expected period a milestone most children reach by that age. It is classified along two axes — whether it is general or specific, and which domain is affected.

- Global or general delay, affecting all or most domains: motor, language, cognitive, social and adaptive. Development is uniformly slow, milestones are late across the board, and it is usually evident before three years. It requires medical assessment.
- Speech and language delay: late babbling, no words at eighteen months, no two-word combinations, late grammar, and a child who responds at home but appears silent in class.
- Motor development delay: late sitting, standing and walking, late grasping and pencil grip, poor balance and coordination, affecting gross motor, fine motor or both.
- Learning difficulty or specific learning disability: reading, writing or arithmetic lag markedly while intelligence and general development are normal, and the difficulty persists despite instruction.
- Intellectual disability: a significant limitation of intellectual functioning together with adaptive behaviour from early development, needing specialist assessment and carrying a legal entitlement to education.
- Autistic spectrum disorder: very limited eye contact, absence of joint attention, need for routine and distress at change, unusual sensory responses, often a late talker, with abilities uneven.
- Social-emotional or attachment delay: emotional regulation and relationships affected, arising often from early deprivation or repeated change of caregiver.
- Sensory impairment affecting development: unrecognised deafness mistaken for dullness, or visual difficulty mistaken for clumsiness.

Two distinctions carry marks: delay versus disability, since a delay is behind the expected period and may be overcome while a disability is a lasting limitation; and delay versus disorder, since a delay describes a gap in time and a disorder is the condition causing it.

questions.question: What is Growth and Development? Write any two principles of child development. [4 Marks]
questions.answer:
Growth and development are related but not the same, and the difference matters more in a classroom than the two words suggest.

Growth is a measurable, quantitative change in the physical — height, weight, girth, head circumference, or the number of vocabulary words a child owns. It can be expressed in objective units and recorded on a measuring scale. Development is the progressive series of orderly, coherent changes, qualitative as well as quantitative, by which the child comes to function at progressively higher levels of physical, mental, social and emotional organisation.

The two are supply and use. Growth supplies the raw material on which development builds. A child with healthy limbs may never learn to write because nobody taught them; a child with delayed growth may show entirely normal intellectual development in a responsive environment. Growth largely stops at the end of adolescence, while development continues well into adulthood. Development cannot proceed normally without adequate growth, and growth alone does not guarantee development.

Two principles of development, most commonly attributed to Edgar Arnold Hurlock:

**1. Cephalocaudal — development proceeds from head to toe.** Control appears first in the muscles of the head and neck, then the trunk and shoulders, then the arms, and last the legs and feet. An infant controls the head before the body, and the hands before the feet. The practical consequence is that an infant who is never allowed to lie on the floor and lift the head is being held back at the very start of the direction development will take.

**2. Proximodistal — development proceeds from the centre outward.** Control moves outwards from the central nervous system and trunk to the extremities: shoulder, then elbow, then wrist, then fingers. At first the whole arm moves as one piece; only later do the individual digits become controllable. This is why a young child holding a crayon in a tight fist eventually develops a proper pencil grip, and why rushing a child to write before the shoulder, elbow and wrist are steady produces a weak, painful grip and a lifelong dislike of writing.

Two further principles are commonly added: that development is a continuous process with no sudden jumps, so that gaps in the foundation cannot be repaired cheaply later; and that the rate of development is uneven, with physical growth rapid in infancy, language explosive between two and five, and abstract reasoning a late bloomer.

questions.question: What kind of facilities a teacher can provide for physical-motor development of students at school? [4 Marks]
questions.answer:
Motor development is the domain in which the school environment has the clearest and most immediate effect, because movement must be practised in order to exist. A child who is not given space, time, equipment and safety cannot practise, and the capacity stays unused whatever the genes may have provided for. So what a teacher supplies is provision, in five forms.

- Space. A safe indoor or covered space for movement, a marked playing area, and room to move between desks rather than a corridor into which a running child is a nuisance. In a school with no ground, a modest strip levelled and cleared is worth a great deal.
- Time. A play period protected in the timetable, protected meaning it will not be given away on a wet morning or before an examination. Free play is not a break from physical education; it is the main occasion on which most children get their gross motor practice at all.
- Equipment. Simple and cheap is enough: balls of several sizes, skipping ropes, rings and hoops, a climbing frame, two bricks laid as a balance beam, chalk for drawing courts, and targets for throwing. Nothing need be bought in bulk; much of it can be made by the children themselves.
- A developmental sequence. Order the skills from the one the class can do to the next, give each adequate practice, let it be practised at the easier level, and raise the demand only then. For fine motor, use real materials in ordinary routines — drawing, colouring, cutting paper, threading beads, gripping a brush, clay modelling, chalk on the slate — rather than worksheets asking a child to trace shapes their fingers cannot yet control.
- Correct seating and a limit on fatigue. Furniture that fits the child, with the desk at elbow height and the chair deep enough to support the popliteal space, and no long unbroken stretch of sitting. Chronic poor seating is a genuine cause of later postural and spinal problems.

Two qualifications make this real rather than decorative. Motor provision is usually unequal — the large clumsy child pushed to the back, the girl kept away from the climbing frame, the child with a disability seated apart — so the teacher's grouping decides whether every child actually practises. And the teacher must watch: a child well behind the class in motor development is not lazy, and observation plus a plain conversation with the parent extends that child's practice hours at home, where most of them happen.

questions.question: What are the different stages of cognitive development with reference to Jean Piaget? [4 Marks]
questions.answer:
Jean Piaget (1896–1980), a Swiss psychologist, proposed that cognitive development passes through an invariable sequence of four qualitatively distinct stages, each with its own structure of thought. The sequence is fixed; the ages at which children enter the stages vary.

1. Sensorimotor stage (0 to 2 years). The infant knows the world through the senses and through movement. Knowledge begins with the mouth and the hands, and everything is learned by doing rather than by being told. Two achievements mark the end of the stage: object permanence, the understanding that a thing continues to exist when it is out of sight, which is why a child who drops a toy under a blanket does not look for it; and goal-directed action, in which several actions are coordinated into a plan, such as pushing a chair to reach a shelf. Implication: learn by doing.

2. Pre-operational stage (2 to 7 years). The child acquires the symbolic function and can use one thing to stand for another, so a piece of wood becomes a doll and a folded paper a boat. Five characteristics follow: egocentrism, the inability to take another person's point of view, which is a stage limitation and not selfishness; intuition rather than logic; no conservation, so that the same water poured into a wider vessel is thought to have increased; centration, attending to one aspect and ignoring the rest; and irreversibility, the inability to undo an action mentally. Implication: learn through play.

3. Concrete operational stage (7 to 11 years). Logical operations become possible, but only on material that is present and visible. Four operations characterise the stage: conservation, reversibility, classification and seriation. Reversibility is what makes schoolwork checkable and self-correcting. The child is still substantially egocentric but can now take another's view. Implication: learn by doing, on concrete material.

4. Formal operational stage (11 years onwards). Thinking becomes abstract and hypothetical, though unevenly until the mid-teens. The adolescent can reason about possibilities, formulate and test hypotheses, consider a system as a whole, detect inconsistency in an argument, and think about thinking itself. Implication: learn by discussion and self-direction.

For a teacher there are two practical warnings: a child cannot be taught a stage of thought they have not reached, and a child cannot be held back in a stage they have passed.

questions.question: What is language development? Write any two factors influencing child's language development? [4 Marks]
questions.answer:
Language development is the orderly and progressive process by which a child acquires the ability to understand and produce speech and, later, to use symbols on a page — moving from crying, through cooing and babbling, to words, phrases, sentences, conversation, and finally language used for reasoning and planning. The order of it is remarkably consistent across languages and cultures, while the timing varies enormously from child to child. For a teacher it is also the most reliable index of development available: almost everything else can be hidden by a quiet child, but a child who cannot use language cannot manage a classroom, make a friend, or show what they know.

The stages run as follows: crying, 0 to 6 weeks, the cry differentiating into hunger, pain, tiredness and anger by about two to three weeks; cooing, 6 weeks to 6 months; babbling, 6 to 12 months, in the language of the household; one-word and two-word, 12 to 18 months, the first word falling in a normal range of roughly 9 to 15 months; sentences and grammar, 2 to 5 years, with vocabulary rising from about fifty words at two to well over a thousand by five; and refinement and expansion, 5 to 8 years and beyond, when technical vocabulary, the written word and language for reasoning arrive.

Two factors among the many that influence this:

**Quantity and quality of talk in the home.** This is the strongest predictor of all. Children who hear many words, in varied and responsive conversation, learn many words. What counts is adult talk directed at the child, not the noise of a television in the corner. A child who is answered when they speak keeps speaking; a child who is ignored, or spoken over, learns quietly that speech does not produce results.

**Mother tongue and the language of the classroom.** A child thinks, forms concepts and builds first sentences in the language of the home. In an Assamese classroom a child may speak Bodo, Mising, Karbi or Tiwa at home and be taught in Assamese or English. Where the two differ there must be a deliberate bridging strategy — songs, stories, rhymes and play in the mother tongue first — because a child asked to think in a language they do not yet think in is being asked to do two things at once. The common error is the reverse one: reading a child who is quiet in class but talks freely with friends in the mother tongue as delayed at all.

Two cautions belong with this. The sequence is common but the timing is not, and a child with no meaningful words by about eighteen months warrants careful attention and referral. And assessment must be done in the language in which the child thinks.

questions.question: What is child abuse? Write briefly about any three types of child abuse with special reference to Assam. [4 Marks]
questions.answer:
Child abuse is any act, or any failure to act, by a parent, caregiver, relative, institution or stranger that causes, or is likely to cause, harm to a child — physically, sexually, emotionally or psychologically — or that places the child at risk of harm. Two features of the definition do real work. It includes a failure to act, so that neglect — not providing food, care, medical attention, education or protection — is abuse in its own right. And it includes harm that is only likely, so a threat, a sexual proposition to a child, or a situation of evident risk counts even though nothing has yet happened.

The paper classifies abuse into nine forms: child marriage, child labour, child trafficking, corporal punishment, sexual abuse, emotional abuse, physical abuse, substance abuse, and stress with the risk of suicide. Three are worth describing here.

**Child labour.** The employment of a child below fourteen in any work, and below eighteen in hazardous occupations, that interferes with schooling, denies play and education, or is harmful to health, safety or development. In Assam the reported forms are work in tea gardens, brick kilns, domestic service, rag picking, roadside and agricultural work, sand mining and small workshops, with children from poor, riverine, marginalised, Scheduled Caste and Scheduled Tribe households heavily over-represented, frequently as 'brought' children who have no family to return to. The Child Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act 1986, amended in 2016, sets 14 as the general minimum and 18 for hazardous work, and provides that a child found working is to be rescued, educated and rehabilitated, not merely told to stop.

**Child trafficking.** The recruitment, transportation, harbouring, transfer or receipt of a child by any means for exploitation — sexual exploitation, forced labour, criminal activity, organ removal, forced marriage, or use in armed conflict. The recruitment alone is an abuse even if the child is never moved. Assam is a source, a transit and a destination state in the regional circuit running from the plains to the neighbouring North-Eastern states and beyond, for sexual exploitation, for domestic and bonded labour, and for the forced marriage of girls. Floods and seasonal displacement push families into vulnerability, and the riverine and border geography makes tracing a missing child genuinely difficult.

**Child marriage.** The marriage of a child below eighteen — below eighteen for a girl and below twenty-one for a boy under the Prohibition of Child Marriage Act, 2006. It is abuse because the child is denied childhood, schooling, health and free consent, and is exposed instead to early pregnancy, complications of childbirth, domestic violence and lifelong economic dependence. It continues in some rural, hilly and riverine communities of Assam, often tangled up with labour and trafficking rather than occurring alone. Beti Bachao Beti Padhao, launched in 2015, is the principal countermeasure, and the teacher's role is awareness among parents and adolescents, and prompt referral when a girl begins to miss school.

Whatever the form, four rules govern the teacher's response: notice and record the same day in neutral language; refer without delay to the school's child protection functionary, the Child Welfare Committee, or the child helpline 1098; never investigate, never promise secrecy and never doubt the child; and never return the child to the risk.

questions.question: Write one objective of ECCE.
questions.answer: One objective of ECCE is to promote holistic development — physical, cognitive, language, socio-emotional and aesthetic-creativity — by providing care and education together in a safe, inclusive setting where children learn through play and activity rather than formal instruction.

questions.question: According to the new academic structure as per NEP 2020, ECCE falls under which stage?
questions.answer: The Foundational Stage. Under NEP 2020 it runs for five years, ages 3 to 8: three years of anganwadi or pre-primary (Bal Vatika, 3–5 years) followed by Grades 1 and 2 (5–8 years) for foundational literacy and numeracy.

questions.question: Mention one characteristic of theme based activities.
questions.answer: A theme is never a single lesson. One broad theme is explored through many activities that together reach all five domains — language, physical, cognitive, socio-emotional and aesthetic-creativity — each beginning with a concrete experience.

questions.question: Write any two principles of a balanced curriculum on ECCE.
questions.answer:
- Developmentally appropriate: the activity is one a child of that age can actually do, with the materials actually available, without an adult's hand on it at every step.
- Holistic: every domain is represented, and preferably inside the same activity rather than in separate periods.

questions.question: Why is parental involvement important in ECCE?
questions.answer: Because the family is the child's first school. Parents give the earliest language, the food, the affection and the habits of self-care, and whatever is learned at the centre has to survive at home — so parents must be partners, not visitors.

questions.question: Write one significance of ECCE.
questions.answer: Development in the early years is cumulative. What is built between three and six stands under every lesson that follows, which is why a child who has been well cared for and played with is simply easier to teach for the whole of school.

questions.question: Mention one advantage of learning through Art and Craft in ECCE.
questions.answer: Art and craft give the child a symbol — the ability to represent an idea that is not actually present — and that is one of the most advanced things a small child can do. It is also the first safe avenue for expressing feeling.

questions.question: What is holistic progress card (HPC)?
questions.answer: The Holistic Progress Card is the official card maintained for every child in an ECCE programme. It carries dated notes of what the child actually did across all five developmental domains, and it describes behaviour rather than grades.

questions.question: Mention one key standard for ensuring quality ECCE.
questions.answer: A safe and secure environment: the building, furniture and material are safe, the fence, the well and any water point are secured, staff know the emergency procedure, and the centre's address is on record with the nearest health facility.

questions.question: Mention one theme-based activity for ensuring holistic development during ECCE.
questions.answer: Under the theme Water: carrying two buckets from the tank to the garden. Physical (balance, grip, endurance), cognitive (which container holds more), language (naming the parts of a matka), socio-emotional (taking turns at the tap) and aesthetic (arranging the vessels by size).

questions.question: Write in full the names of two major agencies associated with Early Childhood Care and Education (ECCE).
questions.answer:
- Integrated Child Development Services (ICDS), delivered through a network of Anganwadi centres.
- National Institute of Child Development and Nutrition (NIPCCD), which coordinates and trains for that system.
Both work under the Ministry of Women and Child Development.

questions.question: Write the principle of 3 'R' in ECCE.
questions.answer: The three R's of early education are Reading, wRiting and ARITHmetik. In ECCE these are not drilled as subjects; they grow out of picture books and stories, scribbling with big chalks and crayons, and counting real objects a child can touch.

questions.question: According to the new academic structure as per NEP 2020, ECCE falls under which stage?
questions.answer: It falls under the Foundational Stage — five years and ages 3 to 8: Bal Vatika and the anganwadi or pre-primary years (3–5), followed by Grades 1 and 2 (5–8). Under the older NCF 2005 this stage meant Grades 1 and 2 only.

questions.question: Write any two principles of a balanced curriculum on ECCE.
questions.answer:
- Contextualised: the plan grows out of what the children in this centre already have — their language, the local crops, the work of their parents, the festivals on the village calendar. A plan imported from a textbook is a plan that will not run.
- Play- and activity-based: it is written as experiences and activities, not as lessons.

questions.question: What is holistic development of a child.
questions.answer: Holistic development is growth in all five domains together — language, physical, cognitive, socio-emotional and aesthetic-appreciation and creativity. The domains overlap, so a child who can count to twenty but cannot sit with a group has not developed wholly.

questions.question: Write the full form: ICDS, UNICEF.
questions.answer:
ICDS — Integrated Child Development Services, launched in 1975–76 under the Ministry of Women and Child Development.
UNICEF — United Nations Children's Fund.

questions.question: Write one difference between ECCE and formal education.
questions.answer: In ECCE, play and activity carry the programme, no subject is taught formally, and progress is described from observation rather than scored. In formal education, attainment is taught to a fixed standard, tested and reported as a grade.

questions.question: Mention one objective of ECCE.
questions.answer: To give every child a safe, nourishing and inclusive place where curiosity, self-confidence, the habit of sharing and the willingness to try again are built through play. What ECCE produces is not information but dispositions.

questions.question: What is the general objective of a holistic ECCE Curriculum?
questions.answer: The general objective is all-round development — physical, cognitive, linguistic, socio-emotional and aesthetic — through integrated learning and learning by doing, meeting the child where he is instead of pushing him towards a fixed standard.

questions.question: What is Emergent literacy?
questions.answer: Emergent literacy is the reading, writing and print-awareness a young child picks up before he can read and write in the accepted way — through story and rhyme, big books, print around him and his own scribbling with chalk and crayons.

questions.question: Mention one principle of assessment.
questions.answer: Assessment is based on observation, and only on observation. The evidence is what a child does with a real material, over real time, with real people around — never what he merely says he can do.

questions.question: Write two major agencies associated with ECCE.
questions.answer:
- Anganwadi centres delivering the Integrated Child Development Services (ICDS) under the Ministry of Women and Child Development.
- The pre-primary and Bal Vatika sections of schools, with NCERT and the state SCERTs supporting the curriculum and the teachers.

questions.question: What is School readiness?
questions.answer: School readiness is the physical, social-emotional, language-cognitive and approach-to-learning competencies a child needs in order to benefit from school. It is a continuum, not a gate — and not the ability to read and write already.

questions.question: Write one objective of ECCE.
questions.answer: To bring about equality of outcome. A well-run pre-primary class gives a poor child the language exposure, nutrition, safe place, adult attention and peer experience that the same child would not otherwise have got.

questions.question: What is nurture?
questions.answer: Nurture is the care, warmth, food, responsive attention and stimulation a child receives from the adults and surroundings around him after conception. It is the environmental half of the nature–nurture equation.

questions.question: What is development milestone?
questions.answer: A development milestone is a marker of typical development that most children reach by a given age — walking, first words, holding a crayon in a working grip. Milestones are used to watch a child's progress, never to label or rank him.

questions.question: What is balanced curriculum?
questions.answer: A balanced curriculum is one in which all five developmental domains are represented — language, physical, cognitive, socio-emotional and aesthetic-creativity — preferably within the same activity, with nothing taught formally or ahead of what the child can do.

questions.question: Write two major agencies associated with ECCE. What are the functions of ICDS?
questions.answer:
Two major agencies: (i) Anganwadi centres delivering the Integrated Child Development Services (ICDS) under the Ministry of Women and Child Development, and (ii) the pre-primary and Bal Vatika sections of schools, supported by NCERT and the SCERTs.

Functions of ICDS, delivered through Anganwadi centres: pre-school education for children of about three to six, supplementary nutrition and a midday meal, health and nutrition check-ups, immunisation, health education, referral services and care of the under-three.

questions.question: Discuss the impact of family in child's holistic development.
questions.answer:
The family shapes development before any programme does. It gives the earliest language — how many words a child hears and in what quality of talk — together with attachment, the first self-care habits, and the values attached to girls' schooling, cleanliness and earning.

But the home also exerts pressure: child labour, early sibling care, harsh correction or over-protection crowd out play. So as a teacher I treat the family as a partner through home visits and parent meetings, knowing what the home offers can never be replaced by the centre.

questions.question: Write the influence of Nature and Nurture on development of a child.
questions.answer:
Nature is heredity — the genes, the build of the body, the temperament, the natural timing of walking, talking and reasoning. It sets the range of possibility, but it does not decide what is achieved inside that range.

Nurture is the environment — food, warmth, responsive caregiving, the language spoken at home, play, affection and opportunity. The two act together: heredity fixes the potential and its timing, and experience decides how far that potential is realised.

questions.question: Write two strategies for outside management of ECCE classroom.
questions.answer:
Outdoor space is not the leftover, so I would manage it on two lines.

- Zoning. Mark out separate areas for active play, quiet play, sand and water, a climbing or swinging structure and a garden bed, using plants, edges or low fencing rather than instructions to the children.
- Supervision without hovering. Position adults so that the whole space is visible, keep about one adult to ten children, and let the ground stay slightly risky — safe means a sound fence and a covered well, not a sterile concrete yard.

questions.question: Discuss about the role of song and rhymes in language and socio-emotional development.
questions.answer:
For language, a rhyme builds vocabulary in context, so a new word is heard inside a sentence where it is useful rather than on a flashcard, and it fixes sequences in memory — the days of the week, counting to twenty, the order of a story.

For socio-emotional development, song moves the body, which is a prerequisite for attention, and builds belonging: a child who knows the same songs as the rest of the group is part of the group. In Assam the folk songs, khona bhat and putuna naat give us all this free of cost.

questions.question: Mention any two tools of assessment in ECCE.
questions.answer:
- Observation. The teacher watches systematically during ordinary play — does she hold the crayon in a working grip, does he wait for his turn — and records what the child actually did. It costs nothing extra, because it happens while the children are playing.
- The Holistic Progress Card. The official child-level record, carrying dated notes of behaviour across all five domains. It tells the teacher what to change in the programme and the parent what to do at home.

questions.question: Write short notes (any two, 2 marks each): (a) Importance of parental and community involvement in ECCE, (b) Difference between Inclusion and Equality.
questions.answer:
(a) Importance of parental and community involvement in ECCE

It decides what the programme can actually do. What is learned at the centre has to survive at home, and parents are the source of the child's home language, so without knowing the family we cannot even plan the transition to school. Attendance, immunisation, sleep and feeding are school problems before they are health problems. And trust matters: a parent who has seen the room and spoken to the teacher will believe the teacher, where one handed only a diary will not. The community adds what no budget can buy — the potter's hands, a field, a folk song, the health centre.

(b) Difference between Inclusion and Equality

Inclusion is about who is in the room. The child with a disability, the child who speaks another language, the slower or faster child, the child from a poorer or a different caste or clan home is present and participating in the ordinary activity, with the space and material designed so that this happens by default. Equality is about how each child is treated — the same opportunity, respect, dignity and attention for everybody. Equality is the floor; equity goes further by giving extra support where a child needs it.

questions.question: Write short notes on (2 marks each): (a) Age appropriate learning opportunities to foster holistic development of child as per National Policy on ECCE 2013, (b) Influence of Nature and Nurture on development of a child, (c) Adverse effect of Early Formal Education.
questions.answer:
(a) Age-appropriate learning opportunities under the National Policy on ECCE 2013

The NECC Policy 2013 covers the child from before birth to six years, and it asks that every opportunity given be matched to what children of that age can actually do on their own with the materials available. For holistic development those opportunities must reach all five domains, preferably inside the same activity — carrying two buckets of water, sorting seeds, singing a rhyme. No child below six is to be taught letters, numbers or any subject formally; learning runs through play, activity and conversation in a setting planned with the family and the community.

(b) Influence of Nature and Nurture on development

Nature is heredity — the genes, the build of the body, the temperament, the natural timing of sitting, walking, talking and reasoning. It sets the limits within which a child can develop. Nurture is the environment — food, warmth, responsive caregiving, the language of the home, play, affection and opportunity. The two work together: heredity fixes the potential and its timing, and experience decides how far that potential is realised. This is why a child from a poor but caring home does well, and why a gifted child with no stimulation may not.

(c) Adverse effects of early formal instruction

Early formal instruction means teaching three- to six-year-olds by primary-school methods — fixed timetables, rows of desks, worksheets, recitation, copying and unit tests.
- Physical: long hours on adult-sized benches give poor posture, eye strain and tiredness, and remove the movement the brain needs to stay alert.
- Cognitive and motivational: reasoning through play is displaced by recitation, so curiosity and persistence weaken and the child concludes that only the teacher has the right answer.
- Social-emotional: stress appears as bed-wetting, withdrawal, aggression, shyness and refusal to attend.
- Long-term: the child can copy but not choose, obey but not cooperate, recite but not talk.

questions.question: Write short notes (any two, 2 marks each): (a) Emergent literacy, (b) Observation and evaluation in ECCE, (c) Project Method.
questions.answer:
(a) Emergent literacy

It is the reading, writing and print-awareness a child develops before he can read and write in the accepted way. It grows from listening to stories and rhymes, handling big books and picture cards, noticing print on packets and signboards, and scribbling with chalk, crayons and clay. That is why we show print as pictures before letters, and why a child's own name written on his cup or mat matters to him. Emergent literacy is the ground on which later decoding is built — and if it is ignored, children learn to copy letter shapes instead of learning sounds.

(b) Observation and evaluation in ECCE

Observation is deliberate watching during ordinary play: does she hold the crayon in a working grip, does he wait for his turn, can the group sort ten caps by size. The teacher records what the child actually did, with a date, and describes the behaviour rather than labelling the quality. Evaluation is the next step: what has moved since the last observation, which domain is still weak, and what the plan must therefore change. Planning and assessment are the same loop seen from two ends.

(c) Project method

This organises learning around a purposeful piece of work that a group of children plans, carries out and completes, the curriculum emerging from the work itself. The steps are: a need or question is felt, the children plan, they collect materials, they make, and they present and discuss what they have made. In ECCE it fits well, because it is play with a purpose and an end product. Its caution: it suits older pre-primary children, and a child who joins late finds nothing to do unless the teacher keeps the material within reach.

questions.question: Write differences: Project method of learning and theme based method of learning.
questions.answer:
- Organisation. In the project method one group works on a single self-chosen piece of work with an end product. In the theme-based method the teacher fixes a broad theme and many children explore it in different ways; there is no single end product.
- Who decides. The project is chosen by the children themselves; the theme is chosen by the teacher from what the children are already asking about.
- Outcome. A project ends in something made and presented; a theme ends in concrete experiences, new concepts and records across all five domains.

questions.question: Write differences: Authentic Assessment and Developmental Assessment.
questions.answer:
- What is watched. Authentic assessment watches the child doing real things in real activity — the leaf he sorts, the bridge he builds with blocks. Developmental assessment asks what the child can do now compared with what he could do earlier.
- The benchmark. Authentic assessment sets no standard beyond the ordinary demands of the activity. Developmental assessment uses the child's own previous level as the yardstick, never the class average.
- Together they answer the only question that matters here: what can this child do now that he could not do before?

questions.question: Mention two challenges of ECCE.
questions.answer:
- Staffing and training. Most centres run on one or two functionaries for a large group, and many have had no training in early childhood care and education at all. The recognised ratio is one adult to about ten children; below that the session becomes crowd control, so the number of children must be reduced instead.
- Formal instruction pushed down. Parents often ask for letters and numbers in the first term because they believe that is what school means, and then a small room starts running like a primary class.

questions.question: What are different domains of holistic development in children? Explain.
questions.answer:
Holistic development means the child grows as a whole person, and this syllabus works with five domains that overlap rather than compete.

- Language — listening to a story to the end, joining a rhyme, naming objects, asking why. Daily story and rhyme time, and conversation rather than interrogation.
- Physical — running and jumping, a working grip on a block or crayon, threading beads, washing hands. Daily outdoor time, fine-motor corners, self-care routines.
- Cognitive — matching, sorting, arranging by size, counting real objects, cause and effect. Real objects before pictures, open-ended material, no worksheets.
- Socio-Emotional — separating from the parent, waiting for a turn, sharing, pride in a finished product. A predictable routine and gentle handling of conflict.
- Aesthetic-Appreciation and Creativity — arranging leaves by colour, making a clay object, telling a make-believe story. Open-ended art material, displayed at child height.

A child sorting bottle caps is handling them, matching, taking turns and naming colour all at once. That gives us a test: an activity that does not move the child in at least three domains should be redesigned.

questions.question: What are the different types of Play? Write with suitable examples.
questions.answer:
The syllabus names three types of play. They differ in one respect only — who controls the direction — and a good day contains all three.

1. Free Play — the child chooses the goal, the material and the duration; the teacher observes. Example: two children building a bridge with blocks while a third watches. Give at least 25–30 uninterrupted minutes daily. Overused, skills stay incidental and some children never enter it.
2. Guided Play — the teacher sets the purpose, the child chooses route and pace. Example: a heap of fallen leaves is brought in and the teacher sorts none of them, saying only, put them however you like. Children sort by colour or size, and she narrows the task — can you make three piles from biggest to smallest? This is the largest block of the day.
3. Structured Play — the teacher sets the rules, the goal and the time and leads. Example: a circle song with every child's name in the rhyme, a story narration, a simple floor game. Short and frequent. Overused, it becomes formal instruction with a play label.

questions.question: Describe the principles of planning a balanced and contextualized ECCE curriculum.
questions.answer:
Planning an ECCE programme is not planning a primary programme: nothing is taught to a standard, nothing runs to a fixed period, nothing is completed. A plan must describe a range of experience and a rhythm. Six principles do most of the work.

- Developmentally appropriate — the activity is one the child can actually do, with the materials actually available, without an adult helping at every step. Writing before a child can hold a crayon is not enrichment; it is practice at failure.
- Holistic — every domain represented, preferably in the same activity. A child watering a plant is physical, cognitive, linguistic, socio-emotional and aesthetic at once.
- Contextualised — built on what these children have: their language, the crops of the season, the work of their parents, the local festivals, the village's water conditions. A plan imported from a textbook will not run.
- Play- and activity-based — written as experiences, not lessons, with the timetable protecting time for them.
- Child-centred and inclusive — children take part in choosing, and nothing assumes a single home language or an average body.
- Flexible and cyclical — a plan is a hypothesis; what the children actually did feeds the next one.

questions.question: Discuss why proper management of classrooms (both inside and outside) is an important factor in ECCE.
questions.answer:
At this age management is not discipline in the ordinary sense. A three-year-old cannot be reasoned with, cannot be made to sit still because a lesson demands it, and does not understand punishment. What we manage is not the child's behaviour but the conditions under which it changes.

Inside, arrange the room so that movement is the default: low shelves, reachable material, floor space, a book corner, a sand-and-water corner, display at child height. Keep materials few, mixed and open-ended. The flow of the day matters more than its content — arrival, free play, circle, snack, outdoor time, rest, group activity, story, departure — because a predictable rhythm lowers friction better than any rule. Work in groups of four to six and rotate them; whole-class instruction does not belong below six.

Outside, zone the space for active play, quiet play, sand and water, climbing and a garden bed, and keep it safe but not sterile. Adults stand where they can see the whole space, and the ratio is about one adult to ten children. Change the conditions before you change the child.

questions.question: Discuss the impact of family, community and school in child's holistic development.
questions.answer:
The syllabus names three settings as the factors influencing holistic development. In each case we ask the same questions: what opportunities does it offer, what models does it provide, what pressure does it place on the child.

The home is the first and most influential. It gives the earliest language — how many words the child hears and in how many languages — plus emotional security, the earliest self-care habits and the first relationships with other people. It transmits values too: the importance of a girl's schooling, of cleanliness, of earning. Home inputs are unequal, which is why good practice begins by enriching the home.

The community supplies the wider world — peers, the play area, the Anganwadi, the health centre, and the festivals, crafts and occupations of village life. It brings risks too: exclusion by caste, gender or disability, and children drawn into work or sibling care at the expense of play.

The school, read broadly to include the Anganwadi, the pre-primary section and the primary school, is the only environment fully under professional control. It acts through what is taught and how, through the adult–child relationship, the peer group, the environment and the daily schedule. It is also where the other two can be brought in — where a pond, a field or a baker's workshop becomes the classroom.

questions.question: Describe briefly three principles of planning a balanced and contextualised curriculum for ECCE.
questions.answer:
Any three of the six planning principles will do, but these three do the most work.

1. Developmentally appropriate. The activity must be one the child of that age can actually do, with the materials the centre really has, without an adult helping at every step. A five-year-old who cannot hold a crayon is not being stretched by lacing cards; he is being taught to fail. The test: can a child do it without an adult's hand on it?

2. Holistic. Every domain is represented, preferably in the same activity rather than in five separate periods. A child watering a plant is at once physical (grip, balance), cognitive (this plant is dry), linguistic (naming, describing), socio-emotional (caring for something dependent on him) and aesthetic (arranging, noticing colour). Balance does not mean equal time per domain; it means every domain alive in the same hour.

3. Contextualised. The plan must grow out of the children actually in the centre — their language, the crops of the season, the work of their parents, the local festivals. An activity built on a dhaki, on a hu, or on counting the paddy seeds parents bring home passes the test of name three things a child here already knows.

questions.question: "Play and active learning is very essential in early childhood"- illustrate with reason.
questions.answer:
I agree, and the strongest reason is structural rather than sentimental. Real play has three conditions: it is self-chosen, self-directed and purposeless in the child's own estimate. Strip away self-choice and you get drills. Strip away self-direction and you get obedience. Strip away both and you have removed the play while keeping the children sitting still — exactly the failure mode that early formal instruction represents.

Beyond that, movement is a prerequisite for attention, so a child who has run outside for forty minutes can sit and listen afterwards. Exploration of real material builds reasoning in a way no explanation can at this age — a three-year-old learns the word cold by touching cold water. Language, too, is built in play, because it is the only place a child must negotiate a turn. And the dispositions that matter most later — curiosity, self-confidence, the ability to try again — are built, not taught.

An illustration. A teacher brings a heap of fallen leaves into an Assamese pre-primary class and sorts none of them, saying only, put them however you like. She then narrows the task: can you make three piles from biggest to smallest? One succeeds, one asks for help, one says the smallest pile has lots. Nothing was taught and a great deal was learned.

questions.question: Briefly write about the need of theme based activities in case of ECCE.
questions.answer:
A theme is a subject broad enough for children to explore from several directions and narrow enough to hold their attention. The syllabus is explicit that activities in ECCE be planned on a theme, cover all five domains, and use integrated learning and learning by doing. The official themes are flowers, vegetables, birds, water, family, transport, community helpers and animals.

The need is threefold.

- It gives the day a spine. A four-year-old cannot be given forty unrelated things, and a teacher who plans isolated activities ends up with nothing running. A theme holds them together, so a child joining on the second day still gets something to do. A theme that makes sense only to the planner is an activity, not a theme.
- It integrates the domains. On the theme water, one child carries two buckets from the tank (physical), asks which container holds more (cognitive), waits his turn at the tap (socio-emotional), names the parts of a matka (language), and block-prints a ripple pattern (aesthetic-creativity) — in the same hour, not five periods.
- It begins with concrete experience, which is what learning by doing means.

questions.question: Explain why it is necessary to maintain progress records of children.
questions.answer:
Assessment in ECCE answers one question: what can this child do now that he could not do before? The record is the only place where that answer is written down, and without it the teacher is left with memory and impression.

The reasons records are necessary are these.

- They are the evidence assessment rests on. Assessment here is continuous, observation-based and play-based, and the evidence is what a child does with real material over real time. A useful entry carries a date and a behaviour — sorted ten bottle caps by size unaided. Words like good and average are not entries, because nobody can act on them.
- They change the programme. The Holistic Progress Card carries five dated columns, one for each domain, and the next plan is built on what the card shows is missing.
- They are the meeting point with the family. A register entry helps the teacher; a report reaches the home and changes what the family does. So reporting begins with a strength, describes behaviour rather than quality, covers all five domains, uses the parent's language, and never compares the child with others.
- They give continuity and protection. The admission, attendance and stock registers are official records, and attendance at this age is a health and nutrition indicator, not merely administration. They must never be used for selection or ranking.

questions.question: What activities would you design for language development in early childhood stage? Prepare a table.
questions.answer:
Language runs through everything else, so these are not a separate language period — most are embedded in the daily routine. The principle in all of them is that a new word must be heard in a sentence where it is useful, never on a flashcard, and the home language is the medium.

| Activity | What the child does | What it builds |
|---|---|---|
| Story and rhyme time, daily | Listens to a story to the end, joins the refrain, retells it his own way | Listening, vocabulary, sequencing |
| Naming in everyday routines | Names the parts of a tap, a matka, a leaf; describes the sky at circle time | Vocabulary in context, descriptive speech |
| Conversation, not interrogation | Asks why, where did the water go; the teacher waits and extends with what would happen if | Curiosity, sentence length, turn-taking |
| Songs and counting rhymes | Sings in the home language, counts to twenty, sequences the days of the week, claps to a beat | Phonological awareness, memory, self-regulation |
| Role-play and make-believe | Plays the shopkeeper, the driver, the mother at the well, with a friend | Narrative language, negotiation, symbolic thought |
| Print as picture before letters | Handles big books and picture cards, turns pages, matches name cards | Print awareness, early reading behaviour |
| Peer talk while sorting and building | Talks to another child rather than only to the adult | The language most four-year-olds actually do |

Two rules I hold to: any rhyme must end with something the children do, and I never stop a child mid-sentence to correct his grammar.

questions.question: Write short note (any one): (a) Adverse effect of early formal instruction, (b) Multilingualism.
questions.answer:
(a) Adverse effects of early formal instruction

Early formal instruction means teaching children aged three to six by the methods of the primary school — a fixed timetable, rows of desks, a worksheet, letters and numbers as subjects, recitation and copying, unit tests and ranking. NCF-FS 2022 makes it explicit that Bal Vatika and the pre-primary years are play-based, that Bal Vatika has no formal textbook, and that formal instruction has no place before six. The effects group into four kinds:
- Physical — long hours on benches sized for adults give poor posture, weak core strength and eye strain, and remove the movement the brain uses to stay alert.
- Cognitive and motivational — exploration is displaced by recitation; the child learns that a right answer exists and the teacher finds it, weakening curiosity and persistence.
- Social-emotional — stress appears as bed-wetting, withdrawal, aggression, shyness and refusal to attend.
- Long-term — the child becomes school-ready in the narrowest sense and otherwise unprepared: able to copy but not to choose, to obey but not to cooperate. We should not claim it damages the brain; the defensible claim is that it is unnecessary, developmentally misplaced and on balance harmful.

(b) Multilingualism

India has no single home language, and most children grow up with several in the air — a mother tongue, a father's language, a community language, and now English or Hindi through television and phone. The curricular question is not which language we shall use, but how we use what the child already has. A child talked to in a familiar language understands a new one; a child forced to receive all instruction in an unfamiliar language switches off, because comprehension is the condition of everything else. The national position is that the home language is the medium of the Bal Vatika and pre-primary years, the regional language is brought in alongside, and English is introduced to be heard and enjoyed rather than used as the language of the classroom.

So: greet the child in his own language first, let him answer in any language he has, learn his name correctly, never ridicule an accent, and use the second language for the fun parts.

questions.question: Discuss the importance of play in ECCE.
questions.answer:
Play is not a break from learning; at this age it is the natural form of learning, and the syllabus makes it the primary medium through which children acquire knowledge, skills, attitudes and values.

First, play is how the five domains are actually developed. Nothing else touches all of them in the same hour. A heap of leaves on the floor gives physical handling, cognitive matching and seriation, socio-emotional turns and coping with losing, language for size and colour, and aesthetic pleasure in arrangement. The planning test is that an activity which does not move the child in at least three domains should be redesigned.

Second, play is the structure of the day, not an event inside it. A good day holds all three types — 25–30 minutes of uninterrupted free play, guided play as the largest block where the teacher provokes and extends, and short structured episodes of song, story and circle.

Third, the material matters. Open-ended material — plain blocks, a bucket of sand, a tray of mixed shells and buttons — serves a hundred purposes and twenty children; a battery toy with four sounds serves none.

Fourth, what play produces is not information but disposition: curiosity, attention, self-confidence, the ability to wait and try again. Those are built, not taught.

questions.question: "There is a close relationship between primary education and ECCE"- Justify the statement.
questions.answer:
The statement is true, and since NEP 2020 it is true in a stronger sense than before. NEP 2020 defines the Foundational Stage as five years and ages three to eight — three years of Anganwadi or pre-primary plus Grades 1 and 2 — and NCF-FS 2022 details it as Bal Vatika (3–4 and 4–5) followed by foundational literacy and numeracy. Under NCF 2005 the foundational stage meant only Grades 1–2, with early childhood outside the school system under the welfare sector. Bringing ECCE into the school system is one of the most significant changes in Indian education policy in the last decade.

The relationship is justified on four grounds.

- Cumulative. Later learning stands on what was built earlier. A child who can hold a book, follow a two-step instruction, wait for a turn and express a need in words faces a very different classroom from a child who cannot.
- Continuity of method and teacher. The difference between ECCE and primary is one of method, not subject — play carries the programme, assessment is descriptive rather than a score, and the child meets the same adult in Grade 1.
- School readiness, the physical, socio-emotional, language-cognitive and approach-to-learning competencies needed to benefit from school — a continuum, not a gate.
- Practical returns. Children with a good pre-primary experience are less likely to repeat a class or drop out, and that matters most for the poorest children.

questions.question: Write three principles in planning ECCE programme.
questions.answer:
Any three of the six planning principles will carry the answer. These are the ones I would write.

1. Developmentally appropriate. The activity must be one a child of that age can actually do, with the materials the centre really has, without an adult helping at every step. The test: can a child do it without an adult's hand on it?

2. Play- and activity-based. The plan is written as experiences and activities, not as lessons with outcomes attached, and the timetable actively protects time for them. A programme that is 80 per cent teacher-led is a primary programme in a small room, and the useful question is whether the plan would still run if the board and the textbook disappeared.

3. Child-centred and inclusive. Children take part in choosing and in evaluating, and nothing assumes a single home language, a single family structure, a physically average body or a particular amount of adult help at home. Would the activity work for a child who speaks only Mising, or for a child who cannot walk?

questions.question: Give your opinion with justification about the importance of ECCE.
questions.answer:
My position is that ECCE is not a useful addition to primary education but the foundation on which the whole of the eight years stands — and the highest-return investment a state can make in its own future. Three arguments carry it.

The first is the critical period. Language, responsive caregiving, nutrition and safe stimulation in the early years have disproportionate later effects, and deprivation in this window is much harder to make up for. A child arriving at Grade 1 after two years at an Anganwadi can remove his own sandals, wash his hands, wait in a line without pushing, join a game with two other children, and hold a book the right way up. None of that came from a lesson; all of it came from meals, routines, songs and being trusted with small tasks.

The second is equality of outcome, and this convinces me most. A well-run pre-primary class gives a poor child language exposure, nutrition, a safe place, adult attention and peer experience that the same child would otherwise never have, because it reaches the child before school has sorted them by family income.

The third is that the product is the right thing: dispositions such as curiosity, attention and self-confidence, which are built, not taught.

questions.question: How toy-based teaching benefits the learners of ECCE? [4 Marks]
questions.answer:
For a four-year-old a toy is a tool of thinking, not a pastime. Toy-based teaching earns its place in ECCE for four reasons.

- It gives concrete material for ideas that cannot yet be handled in words. You cannot explain conservation to a four-year-old, but you can let her pour water from a wide bowl into a narrow one and watch the amount stay the same. Sorting bottle caps by size, threading beads in order — each is seriation and classification performed rather than recited.
- It prepares the hand for writing. Every crayon grip, every peg pushed into a card, every piece of clay pressed flat works the small muscles a pencil will later need. Stringing beads is a fine-motor intervention for a five-year-old who cannot hold a crayon; the same beads frustrate a three-year-old, which is why toys must be matched to a developmental target.
- It gives children something to do with each other. Two children building one bridge negotiate, take turns and fail together. That is where language stops being words addressed to an adult and becomes talk with a peer.
- It builds persistence, because a child can see the evidence of his own effort. The tower he built is a fact; a teacher telling him that he did well is only an opinion.

Two cautions go with this. Choose open-ended material over closed toys — blocks, sand and stones serve twenty children a hundred ways, while a battery toy repeating four sounds serves one child four ways. And never tidy away a construction the child made yesterday; if it is swept into a box every evening, he quietly learns that making is not worth the trouble.

questions.question: What are the benefits and challenges of promoting multilingualism in early childhood care and education? [4 Marks]
questions.answer:
India has no single home language, and most children grow up with more than one in the air — a mother tongue, a father's language, a community language, and now English through a phone screen. Multilingualism is therefore not an enrichment we add; it is the condition the child already lives in.

Benefits
- Transfer of learning. A child who grasps that a dhaki is heavy in Mising has the concept already, and carries it into Assamese almost free.
- Bigger vocabulary and more flexible thinking: more than one language means more words for the same thing.
- Identity and belonging. The language of home carries food, work and festivals; speaking it at the centre tells the child that what he came from is valued here.
- A bridge home and school. The home language is how the teacher reaches the family at all.

Challenges
- The teacher's own competence; many centres are staffed in one language while the children speak three.
- Materials. Story books and rhymes exist mainly in Assamese and English; in Bodo, Mising or Dimasa they are simply unavailable.
- Curriculum pressure. The upper stages want English, so somebody decides English must start at four — formal instruction disguised as language policy.
- Parents, who often treat the second language as a rung on a ladder and make the child who talks only in the mother tongue feel behind.

The position to hold is the one the national curriculum documents take: the home language is the medium of the Bal Vatika and pre-primary years, the regional language comes in alongside it, and English is heard and enjoyed rather than demanded. So greet each child in his own language, let him answer in any language he has, keep rhymes and stories in the language he speaks best, and never correct a child's grammar mid-sentence. A child whose sentences are constantly interrupted stops talking, and a child who stops talking stops learning language.

questions.question: Discuss 8 key standards to ensure quality Early Childhood Care and Education. [4 Marks]
questions.answer:
The syllabus names eight standards against which an ECCE programme is judged — and against which we should judge our own plan. They concern the environment, the process and the people.

1. Safe and secure environment. Sound fencing, a covered well, secured water points, safe furniture and material, a known emergency procedure, and the centre's address on record with the nearest health facility.
2. Health and nutrition. Check-up on admission, monthly growth monitoring, drinking water, sanitation, a midday meal, and absence followed up and referred.
3. Developmentally appropriate curriculum. Activities matched to the age; all five domains covered; nothing taught formally or ahead of the child's capacity.
4. Learning through play and activity. Long periods of free and guided play with materials the children reach themselves; the teacher extends the play rather than instructing.
5. Trained and adequate staff. Trained in ECCE, present in the room, not pulled away to other duties, with the adult–child ratio held at about one adult to ten children.
6. Family and community partnership. Parents known, visited and welcomed, their knowledge of the child recorded, and the community used as a resource.
7. Inclusive programme. Every child welcome regardless of disability, gender, language, caste, religion or income, with a space and material designed so that every child can actually take part.
8. Continuous assessment and improvement. Progress observed, entered on the Holistic Progress Card and used to change the programme, with the admission, attendance and stock registers complete.

Read together, the eight describe one thing: a programme that keeps the child safe, keeps the child fed, keeps the child playing, and pays attention to what the child can now do. A centre that satisfies standard 8 while failing standard 5 is only documenting bad practice.

questions.question: What is Holistic Progress Card (HPC)? Prepare a sample holistic progress report proforma for pre-school children. [4 Marks]
questions.answer:
The Holistic Progress Card is the official child-level document of an ECCE programme. It is a card maintained for every child, recording dated evidence of progress across all five developmental domains — language, physical, cognitive, socio-emotional, and aesthetic-appreciation and creativity. It informs the programme and reports to the parent. It carries descriptions of what the child did, never scores. A child who cannot do anything on the day you test him is not a child who knows nothing; he is a child you did not watch.

Sample proforma:

1. Child identification — Name; date of birth; date of admission; centre enrolment number; parent/guardian name, address and contact.
2. Period covered — From ____ to ____ (Term I / Term II); class/age group ____.
3. Attendance during the period — Present ____ days; absent ____ days; reason and follow-up.
