4. Domain-wise dated observation sheet:
- Language — vocabulary, sentence length, sequencing a story, listening to the end.
- Physical — gross motor, fine-motor grip, self-care and independence, participation in outdoor activity.
- Cognitive — attention span, matching, sorting, seriation, persistence.
- Socio-emotional — confidence, cooperation, separation from parent, tolerance of frustration.
- Aesthetic and creativity — expression, design, willingness to try, care taken with the work.
5. Health and nutrition note — growth measured, any referral made.
6. Teacher's overall remark for the term, beginning with a strength and ending with one action the family can carry out.

An entry is useful only if it carries a date and describes a behaviour somebody else could also see: '4 March — sorted ten bottle caps by size unaided; tried the pulley four times before asking for help.' Words like good, average and needs improvement are not entries; they cannot be acted on, and they tell the parent nothing she can do on Monday.

questions.question: Write about the necessities for planning and design of theme-based activities for ECCE. [4 Marks]
questions.answer:
A theme is a subject broad enough for children to explore from several directions and narrow enough to hold their attention. Planning a theme is a five-step job, and the order matters.

1. Find the thread. Start from the children, not from the textbook. Ask what they have noticed recently — the rain, the buffaloes in the field, the new shop on the road — and choose the theme they are already asking about. A theme imported from a book is a theme that will not run.
2. Set the concepts. List the three or four big ideas the theme can carry, stated as concepts and not as activities. For flowers: living things need water and light; plants can be sorted and grouped; the same word can be a name, a colour and a shape. Concepts, not tasks.
3. Plan the concrete experiences first, before writing anything down. What will children actually do, see, handle and say? A seed soaked in a plate, a leaf rubbed and pressed, a rhyme sung, a story told, a visit to a garden. Concrete experience is the foundation; everything else is built on it.
4. Spread the activities across all five domains — language, physical, cognitive, socio-emotional and aesthetic-creativity — preferably in the same activity rather than in five separate periods.
5. Sequence, and decide in advance what you will record. Seeing comes before naming, naming before comparing, comparing before classifying. That record is what the Holistic Progress Card will later be made of.

Materials go with this: low-cost, locally available, safe, non-toxic and age-appropriate — nothing small enough to swallow, nothing sharp, no water without an adult present.

questions.question: What is Inquiry-based learning? Discuss how method of inquiry help in Early Childhood Education. [4 Marks]
questions.answer:
Inquiry-based learning is learning organised around questions children ask, or around questions a teacher deliberately provokes, and answered by looking, handling, comparing and testing rather than by being told. The syllabus names four elements: questioning, observation, exploration and experience. All four begin with the child's own action; the teacher supplies the material, the time, the vocabulary and the follow-up question.

How it helps a young child:
- It turns a passive listener into an active thinker. A child who has poured water from a wide bowl into a narrow one has conservation in his hands, not in his memory.
- It builds language, because a child who has seen something must find words for it.
- It develops curiosity and persistence. Children allowed to pursue a question to the end come to school expecting the day to contain something interesting.
- It makes assessment free. Observation in ordinary activity costs nothing extra, and it is the only reliable evidence we have of what a child can do.
- It makes the child's errors useful. A wrong answer spoken aloud and examined teaches more than a right one merely stated, because the thinking behind it has been made visible.

The sequence a good pre-primary teacher runs almost unconsciously is: notice, name, question, handle, compare, sort, find a rule, tell someone. The last step matters as much as any other, because saying what he found out is how language, pride and conceptual clarity are built together. A programme that stops at finding the rule has produced a discovery nobody knows about.

And it works only if the teacher's habits support it: wait for the child to finish his question, extend it with 'what do you think would happen if', invite the others in, and never shame an error. The worst response to a child's question is an impatient question in return.

questions.question: Discuss the key principles of assessment in ECCE. [4 Marks]
questions.answer:
Assessment at this stage has one job: to describe what a child can now do, so that the programme can be changed and the parent can be told something true. Seven principles follow from that job.

1. Continuous and part of the programme, not an event. It happens while the children are playing and costs nothing extra. A test week in an ECCE centre is a lost week.
2. Based on observation, and only on observation. The evidence is what a child does with a real material, over real time, with real people around — never what he says he can do.
3. Play-based and embedded, not separated from the children. The activity that is assessed is the activity they believe they are playing in.
4. Holistic. All five domains, no single label. A child is five things at once, and a report that says average without saying average in what is worse than no report.
5. Developmentally appropriate, and measured against the child's own previous level. At this age the gain over time is the finding.
6. Qualitative and descriptive, not quantitative and competitive. Words, examples and a description of behaviour — not a number out of ten, and never a ranking on a wall.
7. Used for support and programme improvement, never for selection or labelling. Records must never travel outside the centre as a verdict on a child.

Every one of these is a consequence of a single question: what can this child do now that he could not do before? If our answer to a child's progress is a mark out of twenty, we have stopped asking that question and started asking a different one, whose answer helps nobody.

questions.question: Write a note about the importance of 'school' as an influencing factor for children's holistic development. [4 Marks]
questions.answer:
The syllabus names three settings that influence holistic development — home, community and school. Home is the earliest and the deepest, and community supplies the wider world. But school, read broadly to include the Anganwadi, the pre-primary section and the primary school, is the only one of the three completely under professional control. That makes it both the most powerful and the most responsible.

School influences development in five ways.
- Through what is taught and how. Play, conversation and exploration on one side; sitting in rows and copying from the board on the other. The method decides whether a child learns to think or only to obey.
- Through the adult–child relationship. A warm adult who notices each child by name produces a child who risks things; an impersonal and controlling adult produces a child who hides.
- Through the peer group. In a mixed room a four-year-old learns to wait, to share, to lose and to be liked — none of which can be taught at home.
- Through the physical environment. Space to move, shade, light, low shelves, furniture scaled to a child's body. A room with no floor space produces stiff bodies and bored minds.
- Through the daily schedule. A rhythm of varied activity, or four unbroken hours of a worksheet. The timetable is a curriculum in disguise.

School also has a second importance: it is the setting in which the other two can be brought in. A mother learns about nutrition because the Anganwadi told her. A pond, a paddy field or a potter's workshop becomes a classroom when the teacher walks out of the door.

The honest difficulty is that school can also do harm — formal instruction pushed down on children who cannot yet sit through it, harsh correction, overcrowding, no materials. So the importance cuts both ways, which is precisely why teacher education comes before a person stands in front of a three-year-old. The child who has been well cared for and well played with is teachable; the child who has not will cost the primary teacher several times the effort for the same outcome.

questions.question: Discuss 8 key standards to ensure quality Early Childhood Care and Education (ECCE). [4 Marks]
questions.answer:
The eight standards are best read as three groups — the environment, the process and the people — because quality in an ECCE centre is never only about what goes on inside the room.

On the environment: (1) a safe and secure setting, with sound fencing, a covered well, secured water points, safe furniture and material, a known emergency procedure and the centre's address recorded with the nearest health facility; and (2) health and nutrition, with a check-up on admission, monthly growth monitoring, drinking water, sanitation, a midday meal, and absence followed up and referred.

On the process: (3) a developmentally appropriate curriculum covering all five domains and teaching nothing formally; (4) learning through play and activity, with long free and guided play periods and materials the children reach themselves; (8) continuous assessment and improvement — progress observed, entered on the Holistic Progress Card and actually used to change the programme, with the admission, attendance and stock registers complete and open to inspection.

On the people: (5) trained and adequate staff, present in the room, not diverted to other duties, with the ratio held at about one adult to ten children in supervised activity; (6) family and community partnership, with parents known, visited and welcomed and the community used as a resource; and (7) an inclusive programme, in which every child participates regardless of disability, gender, language, caste, religion or income.

Take them one at a time in a rural centre and they become concrete. Standard 2 means a growth chart on the wall with last month's weight beside this month's. Standard 5 means that when the teacher is called away to the office, the number of children present falls rather than the standard of care. Standard 7 means that the child who cannot walk has a chair at the table because the room was designed for her, not because a special arrangement was made after she arrived.

questions.question: Discuss in details the appropriate practices to ensure holistic growth and development of various domains in a child. [5 Marks]
questions.answer:
Holistic development means all five domains moving forward together — language, physical, cognitive, socio-emotional, and aesthetic-appreciation and creativity. The domains are overlapping windows onto one child, so the practices below are not five separate periods. A child watering a plant is exercising her grip and balance, working out that a dry plant needs water, naming and describing, caring for a living thing, and arranging the pot where it looks good.

Language. Provide daily story and rhyme time, big books handled by the children, and naming aloud during every routine — the matka is round and heavy, the fish is silver. Talk with the child rather than at him; questions that invite an answer beat questions that catch a mistake. Let him retell the same story for days, because repetition is where sequence is built. Print appears as pictures before it appears as letters.

Physical. Give a real outdoor period every day and treat it as non-negotiable. Zoning matters: active play, quiet play, sand and water, a climbing structure, a garden bed. Provide open-ended apparatus and a fine-motor corner — beads, pegs, large chalks, clay, dough — because the hand that writes is made long before the pencil arrives. Build self-care into the timetable as a real routine: washing hands, removing sandals, eating with a spoon. Keep floor space clear and furniture small enough for a child to move.

Cognitive. Work with real objects before pictures. Put out enough open-ended material that the child must decide, because deciding is the cognitive work. Give him time to sort, arrange by size and count what he can touch; ask what do you think will happen if we pour it out; allow a wrong attempt to be examined rather than stopped. Whole-class instruction does not belong below six — work in groups of four to six and rotate them.

Socio-emotional. Build a predictable rhythm, because a child who knows what happens next is not anxious. Use the circle daily to give every child a turn and a name in a song. Redirect rather than punish. Take a special interest in separation at drop-off, and say good-bye predictably even on the days you are tired. Watch who is always the leader, who is always the outsider, and who is always cast as the villain in pretend play.

Aesthetic and creativity. Put out open-ended art material daily and hold one firm rule: the process is the point, not the product. Never draw for the child, never correct the drawing, never say that does not look like a flower. Display the work at children's eye level.

One test keeps this honest. If a proposed activity does not move the child in at least three domains, redesign it.

questions.question: Prepare a sample progress report proforma for pre-school children. [4 Marks]
questions.answer:
The progress report turns a teacher's records into something a family can use. A record kept in the register helps the teacher; a report reaches the home and changes what the family does. A good proforma therefore leaves a place for the parent's own comment as well as the teacher's.

Sample proforma — Pre-school Progress Report

Part A. Identification
Name of child ____ ; date of birth ____ ; admission date ____ ; class/age ____ ; parent or guardian ____ ; address and contact ____ ; attendance this term ____.

Part B. Observation summary (dated behaviour, not grades)
- Language — ____
- Physical — ____
- Cognitive — ____
- Socio-emotional — ____
- Aesthetic and creativity — ____
- Health and nutrition — ____

Part C. Present level in my words — What your child can now do: ____ (begin here, with a strength)

Part D. Change since last report — What she could not do in September and can do now: ____

Part E. One activity for home — ____ (something the family can do this week, in the home language)

Part F. Teacher's signature and date ____ ; Parent's comment and signature ____

Three rules govern the filling of it. Report what the child can do, not what she lacks, because a parent told only about failure will look for a remedy everywhere except where the remedy is. Use the child's own behaviour in concrete terms — she has started sharing is a report; she has improved in sharing is a judgment nobody can act on. And never compare one child with another, because that comparison belongs in the teacher's head, not on paper a family keeps for years.

questions.question: What is meant by long-term and short-term programme planning in regard to ECCE? Explain with appropriate examples. [5 Marks]
questions.answer:
At this stage nothing is completed, so planning describes a range of experience and a rhythm rather than a sequence of lessons with outcomes attached. Planning happens at two horizons, and the two must agree with each other.

Long-term planning is the wider frame: the annual or term-wise programme, built around the children's age group, the local season, the agricultural calendar and the festivals on the local calendar. It answers the question, what should this group of children have experienced by the end of the year? An annual plan for a pre-primary section in an Assamese village might put the monsoon and paddy in September, the harvest and the post-harvest folk songs in November and December, Bihu and the seasonal foods in January, the new seedlings in March, with a block on water, sanitation and hygiene running through all of it. It also allocates the practical things: the term's themes, the visits, the parent meetings, the growth-monitoring schedule and the material budget.

Short-term planning is the daily and weekly working plan — what we will actually do in this room tomorrow. A weekly plan on the theme of water might spread across five days: Monday bringing real water containers and asking which holds more; Tuesday carrying two buckets from the tank; Wednesday the story of the thirsty crow and words for water in the home language; Thursday painting the reflection and block-printing a ripple; Friday talking about why the queue at the tap is long. Each day also fixes the daily rhythm: arrival and free play, circle time, snack, outdoor activity, rest, group activity, story and song, departure.

The two are joined by the principle of flexible and cyclical planning. A plan is a hypothesis, not a promise. If the children spent four days chasing a scooter in the yard, the week is re-sequenced around outdoor games. If the group sorts bottle caps by size without being asked, the next plan pushes seriation further. The long-term plan sets the direction, the short-term plan sets the road, and what the teacher observes while driving changes both. A term plan that observation cannot alter is not a plan; it is a schedule that has been mistaken for one.

questions.question: Write the principles of preparing a balanced and contextualized programme of Early Childhood Care and Education (ECCE). [4 Marks]
questions.answer:
Planning an ECCE programme is not the same work as planning a primary programme, and six principles do most of the job. This is the list an examiner is looking for.

1. Developmentally appropriate. The activity must be one a child of that age can actually do, with the materials actually available, without an adult hand on it. Writing before a child can hold a crayon well is not enrichment; it is practice at failure.
2. Holistic. Every area of development is represented, preferably in the same activity rather than in separate periods. The test: point to the physical, cognitive, language, socio-emotional and aesthetic strand of this one activity.
3. Contextualised. The plan grows out of what the children in this centre have — their language, the crops of the season, the work of their parents, the festivals on the local calendar, the water and sanitation conditions of the village. The test: name three things in this plan a child here already knows. An activity built on a dhaki or a hu will pass; one built on a shape-sorting set from a catalogue will not, and the children will say so within ten minutes.
4. Play- and activity-based. The plan is written as experiences, not as lessons, and the timetable protects time for them. The test: could this run if the board and the textbook disappeared?
5. Child-centred and inclusive. Children participate in choosing and in evaluating; nothing assumes a single home language, a single family structure, an average body or a particular amount of adult help at home.
6. Flexible and cyclical. The teacher observes, notes what the children actually did, and adjusts the next week's plan. Planning and assessment are the same loop seen from two ends.

Balanced and contextualised, then, are not two separate virtues. A balanced programme covers all five domains; contextualised means the balance is drawn from the children in front of you, not from a textbook written three thousand kilometres away.

questions.question: "Early childhood is a significant period for life long learning and development"- Justify the statement. [4 Marks]
questions.answer:
The claim has four supports, and each has a consequence for what we do on Monday morning.

First, development is cumulative. Later learning stands on what was built earlier. A child who can hold a book the right way up, follow a two-step instruction, wait for a turn and say 'my head hurts' walks into a very different Grade 1 classroom from a child who cannot. None of those skills came from a lesson; all came from meals, routines, songs, games and being trusted with small tasks.

Second, this is the critical period. Language, responsive caregiving, nutrition and safe stimulation in the early years have disproportionate later effects, and deprivation in this window is harder to make up for than deprivation at ten. A language not acquired conversationally at six rarely becomes fluent later; a child who has spent years without being talked to does not catch up by being taught to read. What is not built early is expensive to build later, if it can be built at all.

Third, equality of outcome. A well-run pre-primary class gives a poor child language exposure, nutrition, a safe place to spend the day, adult attention and peer experience that the same child would not otherwise get. It does not ask poor children to become richer; it gives them the same starting room everyone else has.

Fourth, retention and health. Children who have had a good pre-primary experience enter school better prepared and are less likely to repeat a class or drop out; and an ECCE centre is among the few points of contact an Indian child has outside the home before school, which is why it is used for growth monitoring, immunisation and early identification of disability.

So the statement is not saying that children are born knowing more, but that this is when the foundations are poured. And it is why the dispositions of the stage — curiosity, attention, self-confidence, the ability to wait and try again — matter more than any alphabet.

questions.question: Mention four challenges of early learning. [4 Marks]
questions.answer:
The four challenges I would put first are these.

1. Early formal instruction pushed down into the pre-primary years — desks in rows, worksheets, letters and numbers taught as subjects, recitation, copying and unit tests — often because parents believe that is what school means, and private pre-schools respond to that belief. The child learns to sit still and copy, and loses the play through which reasoning, language and motivation are actually built.
2. Shortage of trained teachers and of materials. Most teachers of the three-to-six group have not been trained in ECCE; they arrive from the primary system with its habits of timetable, instruction and discipline. Where materials are scarce the room becomes verbal — a teacher talking — and talk without objects or movement cannot hold a four-year-old's attention.
3. Language mismatch and weak home–school continuity. Many children in rural Assam come speaking a home language the teacher does not use. If all instruction comes in an unfamiliar language the child switches off, because comprehension is the condition of everything else. Add to it a home where no one sits and talks with the child, and school becomes the only place formal language is heard — which is the wrong place for it.
4. Poverty, nutrition and attendance. A child who is undernourished, who has no safe play space at home, who is pulled in to sibling care or work, or who is simply absent for a quarter of the term cannot be reached by any curriculum. At this age attendance is a health indicator before it is an administrative one.

These four reinforce one another, which is why solving any one alone changes very little. But all four are workable, which is what the next question is about.

questions.question: Why home-school linkage is necessary in ECCE? For effective home-school linkage what different activities would be carry out? Discuss? [4 Marks]
questions.answer:
At this age the parents are the first educators, and a programme that treats them as visitors has misunderstood the stage. Four reasons make the linkage necessary.

- Continuity. What is learned at the centre has to survive at home, and what happens at home has to be understood at the centre. Neither half can do it alone.
- Language. Parents are the source of the child's home language, and a programme that does not know what language a child speaks at home cannot plan for the transition to school.
- Health and nutrition. Attendance, immunisation, sleep and feeding are school problems before they are health problems. The Anganwadi can weigh a child; only the family can change what she eats.
- Trust. A parent who has seen the room and spoken to the teacher will believe the teacher.

The activities that make it real:
- Home visits, with an interpreter or community worker where the home language is not the school's. Nothing else gives the true picture of the child's language, care, nutrition and interests.
- An open day and visiting hours, where parents watch the ordinary day rather than a performance. This also corrects the common belief that a good pre-primary class teaches letters.
- Parent meetings and a parent council — regular meetings on health, growth and development, and a council that can carry messages back to families who never attend.
- Take-home materials: simple, low-cost activities in the home language, requiring nothing the family must buy.
- Homework done together — talking about the day, reading any book at all, visiting a market, doing a small household task side by side. This reaches the poorest home, because it costs nothing.
- Local people as guests: a potter, a boatman, a weaver, a grandmother, sitting in the room talking about the work.

One caution: involve parents as partners with knowledge, never as unpaid helpers assigned cleaning duties. The moment a parent is treated as labour, the relationship is over.

questions.question: What are the early learning challenges? Discuss briefly four strategies to overcome these challenges. [6 Marks]
questions.answer:
Early learning challenges are the obstacles that stand between a child of three to six and the learning that age is capable of. Let me name the main ones, then give four strategies, each tied to a particular challenge.

The challenges
- Early formal instruction: worksheets, rows, letters and numbers as subjects, recitation and unit tests, pushed down into years when the child should be playing.
- Untrained teachers and scarce materials, which turn the room verbal and leave the child copying instead of doing.
- Language mismatch: the child speaks a home language the teacher does not use, so comprehension — the condition of everything else — is missing.
- Poverty, malnutrition, absence, sibling care and child work, which make the child physically unavailable for learning.
- The absence of play space, either because the home is crowded and work-bound, or because the school yard is treated as a leftover.
- Assessment done as testing — a test week, ranking, prizes — which teaches children that learning is a performance to be judged rather than something to be explored.

Four strategies

1. Protect play, and make it developmental rather than decorative. Give every day at least 25 to 30 minutes of uninterrupted free play and two or three guided-play episodes, with open-ended materials the children reach themselves — stones, sand, bangles, blocks, clay, a tray of water. Nothing goes on the shelf a four-year-old cannot open. This answers both formal instruction and material scarcity, because a tray of mixed bottle caps serves twenty children as well as an expensive catalogue set serves one.

2. Use the child's language, and treat the home as the first school. Greet each child in his own language, allow him to answer in any language he has, learn to pronounce his name correctly, keep rhymes, stories and counting games in the language he speaks best, and bring in the second language for the fun parts. Never interrupt a child's sentence to correct his grammar; a child whose sentences are constantly interrupted simply stops talking. This answers the language challenge and opens the channel home.

3. Work with families and the community, deliberately. Home visits with an interpreter where needed, an open day, a parent council, take-home activities in the family's language, and local people — a farmer, a potter, a grandmother — as guests in the room. Attendance, immunisation, sleep and feeding are followed up from the centre, because attendance at this age is a health indicator before it is an administrative one. This is where poverty and absence are actually met.

4. Train the teacher and redesign the room. An untrained teacher carries primary-school habits into a pre-primary room. So: orientation in the five domains and in play-based methods, one adult to about ten children in supervised activity, whole-class instruction abandoned below six in favour of groups of four to six, low shelves, clear floor space and zoned outdoor space supervised from a point of full visibility. And assessment by observation entered on the Holistic Progress Card, never by test or prize — which removes the last pressure that pushes formal instruction back in.

The four work together. Play without language support stays shallow; language support without family contact stops at the gate; and a trained teacher with no material has nothing to be trained for.

questions.question: Discuss with example the role of play and active learning for holistic development of a child. [5 Marks]
questions.answer:
Play is what young children do when they are given the chance, the space and the time — and that sounds obvious only because children are rarely given it. In many rooms play is chopped into a fixed twenty minutes in the timetable and forty-five minutes of worksheet. Real play has three conditions: it is self-chosen, self-directed, and purposeless in the child's own estimate. Strip away self-choice and you get drills; strip away self-direction and you get obedience; strip away both and you have removed the play while keeping the children sitting still.

That is why the syllabus insists on three kinds, which differ only in who controls the direction: free play, where the child decides everything; guided play, where the teacher sets the purpose and the child chooses the route; and structured play, where the teacher sets the goal, rules and time. A good day contains all three, and moving between them is a teaching decision, not an accident.

Take one ordinary morning. Twenty-five minutes of free play: two children build a bridge with blocks and a third watches. The teacher joins the bridge-builder and asks only, how will it not fall down? — and a guided episode begins. The day closes with a structured circle song in which every child's name goes into a rhyme. In those thirty minutes, language (names, questions, talk between the builders), physical (the grip and balance of building), cognitive (spatial relations, planning, revising when it falls), socio-emotional (negotiating, waiting, coping with failure) and aesthetic (colour, form, the pleasure of a thing that works) have all been served. Nothing was taught, and a great deal was learned.

Active learning is the same idea taken more seriously: the child does the doing. Carry two buckets of water from the tank and physical development — balance, grip, endurance — comes free, along with the cognitive idea of how much the pot holds and the social habit of queueing at the tap. A leaf that was picked, smelled, crushed between the fingers, compared with another leaf and stuck in a book is an experience; a worksheet about a leaf is not.

My position is straightforward. Play is not a break from learning or a reward for finishing the work; it is the form learning takes at this age, and every skill we want later — attention, persistence, the ability to negotiate — is built in it.

questions.question: What is curriculum? Mention the principles of constructing a balance and contextualized curriculum for ECCE. Write a note any one of it. [7 Marks]
questions.answer:
Curriculum is the whole range of experiences a child is offered — what is planned, what the environment offers, what the adults say and do, what the children bring from home and community, and what the materials invite them to do. It is not the syllabus and not the textbook. In ECCE the textbook is usually absent by design, because nothing at this age is taught to a standard, nothing runs to a fixed period and nothing is completed.

The principles for constructing a balanced and contextualised ECCE curriculum are the six planning principles, and each is a corrective to a familiar failure.

1. Developmentally appropriate. The activity must be one a child of that age can actually do, with the materials actually available, without an adult hand on it. Writing before a child can hold a crayon well is not enrichment; it is practice at failure.
2. Holistic. Every area of development is represented, and preferably in the same activity rather than in separate periods. A child watering a plant is at once physical, cognitive, language, socio-emotional and aesthetic.
3. Contextualised. The curriculum grows out of what these children have — their language, the crops of the season, the work of their parents, the festivals on the local calendar, the water and sanitation conditions of the village.
4. Play- and activity-based. Written as experiences, not as lessons, with the timetable protecting time for them.
5. Child-centred and inclusive. Children participate in choosing and in evaluating; nothing assumes a single home language, a single family structure, an average body or a particular amount of adult help at home.
6. Flexible and cyclical. The plan is a hypothesis. The teacher observes, notes what the children actually did, and adjusts the next week — planning and assessment are the same loop seen from two ends.

Balance also carries a second meaning that examiners expect: balance across the six curricular issues the syllabus names — multilingualism, inclusion, gender, equality, the adverse effects of early formal instruction, and school readiness. A curriculum can cover all five domains beautifully and still be unbalanced in the sense that matters, if it runs entirely in one language, sorts materials by gender, or leaves the child who cannot walk standing at the edge.

A note on one principle in detail: contextualisation.

Take a rural Assamese pre-primary centre and the theme water. Contextualisation means concept and material both come from the children's own world. They carry buckets from the school tank, because that is the work they watch at home; the word for the container is the word their mother uses, not the word in the textbook; the story is about a queue at a tap, which is a queue they have stood in. Concept formation then happens without a lesson: which vessel holds more, why is one pot heavier than another of the same size, where is the leak, what will happen if we cover it. The concepts are conserved volume, capacity and cause and effect — genuine cognitive structures — but they were arrived at through material the children own.

The practical test takes one minute. Name three things in this activity a child here already knows. An activity built on a dhaki, a hu, or the paddy-seed count the parents bring home at harvest will pass. One built on a shape-sorting set from a catalogue will not, and the children will say so within ten minutes.

So I would put it this way. The curriculum of the early years is not what we decide children must learn, but the environment, the material, the conversation and the day we build around them — and it must be their own, or it will not take.

questions.question: Prepare a sample progress report for a pre school child. [4 Marks]
questions.answer:
Here is a filled-in sample, so that the difference between a record and a judgement is visible.

Sample Progress Report
Child: Manju Das. Age: 4 years 4 months. Class: pre-primary. Period: September to December. Attendance: present 78 of 86 days; absent 8, of which 5 were with fever and followed up.

Language — Manju now uses four- and five-word sentences where in September she used single words. On 4 December she narrated the whole sequence of what happened at the pond without prompting. She answers in Mising at home and Assamese in class, and is beginning to join the Assamese rhyme for bathua-bhat.

Physical — She pedals the tricycle up the slope unaided and holds her crayon in a tripod grip. She buttons her own coat now. She was shy about the rough-and-tumble corner in September; on 14 November she was last to leave it.

Cognitive — She sorted ten bottle caps by size unaided and can then re-sort by colour when the rule changes. Attention has lengthened from about two minutes to about ten. She tried the pulley four times before asking for help, and then succeeded.

Socio-emotional — She joined the group game after ten minutes and stayed to the end, and coped with losing the race without crying. Separation at drop-off is still difficult on Mondays; on other days she walks in and greets the group.

Aesthetic and creativity — She chose colours deliberately and stayed with the block-printing to the end of the session. Her clay pot from the theme water was displayed at child height.

Health and nutrition — Weight 13.1 kg against 12.4 kg in September; height 100 cm. No referral needed.

One thing you can do at home: please keep talking with her in Mising at home about the stories we are reading here. She retells them to her grandmother in Mising, and that retelling is where the words are settling.

Teacher: (signature)  Parent: (signature)

Note what makes this a report and not a score. Every entry carries a date and a behaviour somebody else could also see, it begins with a strength, and it ends in an action the family can carry out. There is no comparison with the class anywhere in it.

questions.question: Mention few programmes that can be undertaken in school for establishing healthy home school linkage. [4 Marks]
questions.answer:
A linkage programme is a set of regular, scheduled activities, not an occasional meeting. The forms below are the ones the syllabus names, and they are worth running in this order, because each makes the next easier.

- Home visits, with an interpreter when the home language is not the school's. This is the only activity that gives the true picture of the child's language, care, nutrition and interests, and it brings back information the school badly needs.
- Open days and visiting hours. Parents come into the room and watch the ordinary day, not a performance arranged for them. This corrects the widespread belief that a good pre-primary class teaches letters and numbers, and it is where the teacher's own practice gets corrected too.
- Parent meetings and a parent council. Regular meetings on health, growth, nutrition and what the children are actually learning. The council advises the centre and, more usefully, carries messages back to families who never attend meetings.
- Take-home materials in the home language: a story to retell, a game to play with stones, a song. This keeps the learning going at home and quietly makes the child the family's teacher.
- Homework done together — talking about the day, reading any book that exists at home, visiting a market, doing a small household task side by side. Family time is the vehicle, and it is the form that reaches the poorest household, because it costs nothing.
- A weekly or fortnightly din's diary in the family's own language, with no written part: a picture of what the child made, the sentence the child spoke, and one question the parent answers. Short enough to be filled, which is why it is read.
- Using the community as a resource — the Anganwadi, the panchayat, the health centre, the library, local artisans and folk singers as guests in the room, and convergence meetings that put the Anganwadi and the pre-primary section in the same conversation.

One caution closes this: never enlist parents as unpaid helpers for cleaning duties. The moment a parent is treated as labour, the relationship is over.

questions.question: Define assessment? How ECCE assessment is different from other learning levels. Explain with example. [4 Marks]
questions.answer:
Assessment means judging the extent to which learning has taken place. That definition is too thin for the early years, and the difference matters.

Testing measures a child against a standard, in a situation someone designed, and produces a number. Assessment observes what a child can already do, in ordinary activity, and produces a description. At every level the distinction exists, but below six it becomes a matter of principle, because a test administered to a four-year-old measures the examiner more than the child: a strange adult, a strange room, questions with no material in the hands, and a demand to produce an answer on demand rather than in play.

So ECCE assessment differs in these ways.
- It is continuous, not periodic. It happens while children are playing and costs nothing extra. A test week in an ECCE centre is a lost week.
- It is based only on observation. The evidence is what the child does with a real material, over real time, with real people around.
- It is embedded in play, so the activity assessed is the activity the children believe they are playing in.
- It covers all five domains and gives no single label.
- It is measured against the child's own previous level, not against the class.
- It is qualitative, not competitive. No marks out of ten, no ranking on a wall.
- It is never used for selection, labelling or admission.

An example. In a Grade 3 classroom the teacher gives a unit test, marks it out of twenty, and finds that twenty-eight children can subtract within a hundred. In a pre-primary class the teacher watches four children fit ten bottle caps from largest to smallest, and sees that three manage it unaided and can then re-sort by colour, while the fourth still confuses size with number. That observation is worth more than any test: it is dated, repeatable, names the actual difficulty, and tells the teacher exactly what to do next — more guided play with the same material, not a worksheet.

questions.question: Prepare a progress report proforma for pre school children. [4 Marks]
questions.answer:
Progress Report Proforma — Pre-school (Holistic Progress Card)

A. Identification: Name ____ ; DOB ____ ; Admission date ____ ; Enrolment no. ____ ; Class/age ____ ; Parent/guardian ____ ; Address ____ ; Contact ____

B. Period: From ____ to ____ (Term I / Term II) ; Attendance ____ days present of ____ ; Reason for absence ____ ; Follow-up made ____

C. Growth and health: Weight ____ kg ; Height ____ cm ; Date ____ ; Immunisation up to date: Yes / No ; Referral if any ____

D. Domain-wise evidence (write dated behaviour, not grades)
- Language — vocabulary ____ ; sentence length ____ ; sequencing a story ____ ; listening to the end ____
- Physical — gross motor ____ ; fine-motor grip ____ ; self-care ____ ; participation in outdoor activity ____
- Cognitive — attention span ____ ; matching ____ ; sorting ____ ; seriation ____ ; persistence ____
- Socio-emotional — confidence ____ ; cooperation and turn-taking ____ ; separation from parent ____ ; frustration ____
- Aesthetic and creativity — expression ____ ; design and colour ____ ; willingness to try ____ ; care taken with the work ____

E. What your child can do now (begin with a strength) ____

F. Change since the last report: what she could not do then and can do now ____

G. One thing to do at home, in your language ____

H. Teacher's remark and signature ____ ; Date ____ ; Parent's comment and signature ____

Three rules govern the filling of it. Write what the child can do, not what she lacks — a parent told only about failure will look for the remedy everywhere except where it is. Use behaviour, not judgment: she has started sharing is a report; she has improved in sharing is unanswerable. And never compare one child with another on paper. Fill it in on the day, not from memory at the end of the term.

questions.question: What is theme based activity. Prepare a weekly plan by taking a single theme for holistic development of child of early childhood. [5 Marks]
questions.answer:
A theme-based activity is one built around a broad subject — flowers, vegetables, birds, water, family, transport, community helpers or animals — that children explore from several directions across all five domains. A theme holds many activities and spans the whole week; an activity is one event inside it. The essence of the approach is integrated learning and learning by doing: the child meets the same idea through the hand, the eye, the ear and the mouth, and the concept forms out of the experience rather than out of an explanation.

Weekly plan — Theme: Water (class: 3–6 years, 25 children, one teacher with one helper)

Concepts carried by the theme: water comes in many forms; the same amount fits in different shapes; living things need water; water is shared, so we take turns.

Monday — Bringing water in. Real matkas, bottles, a bucket and a mug are placed out and the children simply play. Later the teacher asks, which one holds more? We watch who pours and who only watches. Domains: cognitive, physical, language. Materials: household containers, a bucket.

Tuesday — Carrying and building. Two children carry a bucket each from the tank to the plants; a relay with water pots; a block bridge over a water tray. Domains: physical (balance, bilateral coordination, endurance), cognitive (spatial planning), socio-emotional (turns, shared task). Materials: buckets, pots, blocks.

Wednesday — Words and story. Collect words for water in the home language; name the parts of a tap and a matka; the story of the thirsty crow, retold over two days; a rhyme with actions. Domains: language, socio-emotional. Materials: none beyond voice, and a few picture cards.

Thursday — Making and noticing. Floating and sinking with a stick, a leaf and a stone; finding where the tray leaks and mending it with cloth; painting the reflection on the surface; block-printing a ripple pattern. Domains: cognitive, aesthetic and creativity, physical. Materials: clay, cloth, washable colour, blocks.

Friday — Care and sharing. Why is the queue at the tap long? Taking turns to fill the school's pots; watering the shade corner; a circle song using every child's name. Domains: socio-emotional, language, aesthetic. Materials: song, plants.

Throughout the week, a wet-weather plan: the same water play indoors in trays, since in Assam rain cannot be scheduled out of a plan.

What we record while it runs: dated notes of who sorts, who persists, who waits, who speaks — the raw material of the Holistic Progress Card. And the test of the plan is simple: a child who joined on Thursday must still find something here to do.

papers.title: UNDERSTANDING LANGUAGE AND EARLY LANGUAGE DEVELOPMENT

questions.question: What are the vowel sounds of the Assamese language according to the mode of pronunciation?
questions.answer: Classified by the mode of pronunciation, Assamese has eleven vowels: অ (a), আ (ā), ই (i), ঈ (ī), উ (u), ঊ (ū), এ (e), ঐ (oi), ও (o), ঔ (ou) and ঋ (ri). They are grouped as short, long, nasalised and diphthongal, the last with a glide element such as ঔ.

questions.question: What do you mean by language?
questions.answer: Language is a conventional and systematic symbol system used by a human community for exchanging messages, for representing thought and for creating meaning, made of sounds and written symbols and governed equally by rules of combination and conventions of use.

questions.question: What is the full form of BICS?
questions.answer: BICS stands for Basic Interpersonal Communication Skills. It is the everyday face-to-face language of greeting, asking, thanking, apologising, arguing and joking, and it is contextual, meaning carried by gesture, tone and shared situation.

questions.question: What is multilingualism?
questions.answer: Multilingualism is the condition in which more than one language is in use in a community or a setting, and more than one of them is needed for full participation in it. This paper treats it as a resource to be used, not a problem to be solved.

questions.question: Write a definition of language.
questions.answer: Language is a system of human communication consisting of a limited set of sounds combined systematically into words and sentences according to agreed rules, and used by a group of people to convey their ideas, feelings and experiences.

questions.question: What are the structures of language?
questions.answer: Language has a chain structure of levels: phonetics and phonology at the sound level, orthography and phonics at the written level, morphology for meaningful word parts, lexis for vocabulary, syntax for the arrangement of words, and semantics and pragmatics for meaning and meaning in use.

questions.question: What is voiceless sound?
questions.answer: A voiceless sound is one produced without vibration of the vocal cords. In Assamese, ক, ট and ত are voiceless unaspirated stops, while the voiceless aspirates খ and ছ are produced with a puff of breath after the release.

questions.question: What is the smallest unit of language?
questions.answer: The phoneme is the smallest unit of sound in a language that can change the meaning of a word. In mat, pat and rat only the initial consonant changes, and the meaning changes with it, so that consonant is a phoneme.

questions.question: What is the origin of the word 'language'?
questions.answer: The word comes from the Latin lingua, meaning tongue, because speech was long held to come from the tongue. It passed through Old French langage and entered English in that form during the Middle English period.

questions.question: What is multilingualism?
questions.answer: Multilingualism is the state of a community, region or classroom in which more than one language is spoken and more than one is required for full participation in daily life. A single Assamese classroom may hold Assamese, Bodo, Mising, Hindi and Bengali in one morning.

questions.question: In which year did 'Right to Education Act' came into force in Assam?
questions.answer: The Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act, 2009 came into force on 1 April 2010, and it applies in Assam as it does everywhere else, making elementary education free and compulsory for children of six to fourteen years.

questions.question: Write an acceptable definition of language.
questions.answer: Language may be defined as a conventional system of vocal symbols used by a community for communication and thought, in which a limited number of sounds combine systematically into words and words into sentences, each governed by rules shared and understood by its speakers.

questions.question: How many vowels in Assamese language?
questions.answer: Assamese has eleven vowel sounds: অ, আ, ই, ঈ, উ, ঊ, এ, ঐ, ও, ঔ and ঋ. If the nasalised vowels য় and ৰ are counted as separate, many grammars give the number as twelve.

questions.question: What is sound?
questions.answer: In language, a sound is the smallest element produced by the vocal apparatus and perceived by the ear. Sounds are the raw material of speech, which a language organises into phonemes, words and sentences, so that speech is built out of them.

questions.question: What is Multilingualism?
questions.answer: Multilingualism means the use of more than one language within a single family, school or society, with each used for its own purposes and all of them needed for full participation. Assam is a good example, with tea-garden, tribal and migrant communities side by side.

questions.question: Name the only tribal language which is recognised by Indian Constitution.
questions.answer: Bodo. It was placed in the original Eighth Schedule of the Constitution in 1950 and is the only tribal language so recognised, though Assamese, spoken by many tribal people, is classed under the Indo-Aryan branch.

questions.question: Where does the word 'language' derived from?
questions.answer: It is derived from the Latin lingua, meaning tongue, on the old belief that speech is produced by the tongue. The Latin form became Old French langage, from which the English word language was taken.

questions.question: Give a definition of speech sound.
questions.answer: A speech sound is a brief and definite vocal production made by a speaker and perceived by the listener. In any language, such sounds as can change the meaning of a word are called phonemes, and the rest are allophones.

questions.question: Mention any two secondary components of language.
questions.answer: Two secondary components are syntax, the rules by which words are arranged into sentences, and semantics, the system of meaning carried by those sentences. Pragmatics, which deals with meaning in actual use, is usually named as the third.

questions.question: What is unaspirated sound?
questions.answer: An unaspirated sound is produced with a clean stoppage of the airflow and no puff of breath after the release of the stop. In Assamese, ক, ট and ত are unaspirated, in contrast with খ and ছ, which carry a breath.

questions.question: In which year, Bodo language was included in the eighth schedule of the constitution of India?
questions.answer: Bodo was in the original Eighth Schedule of the Constitution of India, 1950, one of the fourteen languages listed from the very beginning. It was never added later, unlike Sindhi, Konkani, Manipuri and Nepali.

questions.question: Write any two primary elements of language.
questions.answer: The two primary elements are speech sounds, organised into the phonemes that distinguish one word from another, and words, the smallest units that carry meaning on their own. Words in turn combine under grammatical rules to make sentences.

questions.question: What is the trilled sound of Assamese language?
questions.answer: The trilled sound of Assamese is র, the letter r. It is a clear trill at the beginning of a word and after certain consonants such as ড় and ঢ়, but in other positions it is realised as a soft flap, a quick tap of the tongue.

questions.question: Mention the name of a language of Sino-Tibetan language family found in Assam.
questions.answer: Bodo. It belongs to the Sino-Tibetan, or Tibeto-Burman, family and is spoken mainly in Bodoland and northern Assam, with Mising, Karbi and the languages of the hill districts belonging to the same family.

questions.question: Who wrote the book, 'Asomiya Sahityar Ruprekha'?
questions.answer: Dr. Maheswar Neog wrote 'Asomiya Sahityar Ruprekha', the standard survey of Assamese literature. He is also known for his study of the Assamese language itself, 'Nika Asamiya Bhasa'.

questions.question: Give one scientific definition of language.
questions.answer: Scientifically, language may be defined as a system of signs in which a finite set of phonemes is combined according to fixed rules into morphemes, words and sentences, and is used by a speech community to convey meaning.

questions.question: What is the central vowel phone of Assamese language.
questions.answer: The central vowel phoneme of Assamese is /a/, written অ. It is realised with a rather open, central quality, and unlike many Indian languages it can occur in any syllable position, not only in the first.

questions.question: Name the only tribal language of Assam which is recognised by the constitution of India.
questions.answer: Bodo, spoken across Bodoland and northern Assam, is the only tribal language recognised by the Constitution of India, having been listed in the Eighth Schedule in 1950.

questions.question: Which core linguistic family does Assamese language belongs to?
questions.answer: Assamese belongs to the Indo-Aryan branch of the Indo-European family of languages, historically descended from Sanskrit through Prakrit and Apabhramsha, which is why it is classed with Bengali and Hindi.

questions.question: What is the full form of LAD?
questions.answer: LAD stands for Language Acquisition Device, the term used by Chomsky for the inborn mental structure that makes every normal child able to acquire any human language, given enough exposure to it.

questions.question: Write one function of language.
questions.answer: One function of language is communication: it enables a speaker to convey a message to a hearer and so to share knowledge, feelings and intentions. Another, running close to it, is the expression of thought.

questions.question: Briefly explain the nature of language.
questions.answer: Language is a conventional and systematic symbol system, and it has four basic natures. It is dynamic, since new words enter it and old ones change or die as the things they name change. It is creative, because a speaker who has never heard unbelievable can still build it from un- + believe + -able. It is arbitrary, since the word water does not sound like water. And it is perpetual, so it is never finished.

questions.question: State two ways in which language helps in acquiring knowledge.
questions.answer: First, subject knowledge cannot be had apart from language. Before a child can count he must know the number words, and before he can do a sum he must understand the words in which the problem is written. Second, knowledge is cumulative and social: it is stored in language and handed down in compressed words, so that nobody has to discover afresh that water boils or that a seed grows.

questions.question: What is meant by home language?
questions.answer: The home language, or mother tongue (matribhasa), is the language a child acquires first, naturally and without formal teaching, in ordinary family and community life. It is learnt by need, interaction and sheer volume of talk rather than from a textbook, and it gives the child linguistic security, authority and identity. In an Assamese-medium school the home language and the school language are often two different languages, and the gap between them is the real difficulty.

questions.question: What is Foundational Literacy and Numeracy (FLN)?
questions.answer: Foundational Literacy and Numeracy is the early stage of schooling in which every child acquires the basic capabilities of reading, writing, speaking and number, to the level needed for further learning. NEP 2020 makes it the first priority area for the foundational stage, on the ground that a child who cannot read, write and count cannot do anything else in school. The national mission for it is NIPUN Bharat, whose guidelines came out in 2022.

questions.question: What is phonology?
questions.answer: Phonology is the study of language as a system of sounds. Instead of asking how a sound is produced, it asks which sounds the language treats as different and which sequences of them it permits. Its central unit is the phoneme, the smallest unit of sound that can change the meaning of a word, as in mat, pat and rat. Phonetics studies actual production; phonology studies the pattern.

questions.question: Mention any two constitutional provisions related to language.
questions.answer: Article 350A says that every effort shall be made to promote the mother tongue of mother-tongue-medium institutions at the primary stage, English being allowed where necessary; it was inserted by the Seventh Amendment Act, 1956. Article 343A provides that Article 343 applies, with adaptations, to States that adopt their own official language, which is the basis on which Assamese became the official language of Assam under the Assam Official Language Act, 1963.

questions.question: Write any two objectives of Foundational Literacy given by NEP 2020.
questions.answer: NEP 2020 states two linked objectives. The first is universal foundational literacy and numeracy, so that every child learns to read and write with actual fluency by Grade 3 rather than merely reciting the alphabet, and becomes numerically capable by Grade 5. The second is reducing learning gaps: a Foundational Literacy and Numeracy cell in every district is to work with a national mission, so that the child who is worst served gets the most attention.

questions.question: "Language is dynamic" - Explain the statement.
questions.answer: Language is dynamic because it is alive and keeps changing with the life it is used to describe. New things have to be named, so new words enter it, such as laptop or solar inverter, and old words narrow their sense or disappear when what they named is gone. The practical consequence for us as teachers is that no word list is ever complete, and the vocabulary of a Class III textbook is only a fraction of the language its children already speak.

questions.question: What is aspirated sound? How many aspirated sounds are there in Assamese language?
questions.answer: An aspirated sound is produced with a puff of breath immediately after the stop is released, so the air is heard as a small hiss. Assamese has five aspirated sounds: খ (kh), গ (gh), ছ (chh), ঢ় and জ (jh). Assamese is unusual in keeping voiced aspirates, which Bengali and Hindi have lost, and this is one reason Assamese has a slightly larger consonant inventory than its close relatives.

questions.question: Write two provisions provided by Indian Constitution for language.
questions.answer: Article 345 provides that only Hindi and English shall be used for the official purposes of the Union, with the President free to specify others by rules; that is why central documents reach an Assamese school in English or Hindi. Article 350B declares that the languages specified in the Eighth Schedule are the languages recognised by the Constitution, and the Eighth Schedule now lists 22 languages, Assamese among them.

questions.question: What is the full form of BICS and CALP.
questions.answer: BICS is Basic Interpersonal Communication Skills, the everyday contextual spoken language of social life, acquired very early and mostly before school. CALP is Cognitive and Academic Language Proficiency, the decontextualised language of reading, writing, textbook and examination answers, which has to be taught and is learnt slowly. Both terms come from Jim Cummins. A child may be fluent in BICS and still be unable to read a line of the textbook.

questions.question: "Language is arbitrary"- Explain.
questions.answer: Arbitrary means there is no necessary connection between the form of a word and what it means. The word water does not contain water and does not sound like water, and it could have been called anything at all; only the agreement of the community holds the connection steady. A few signs are motivated, such as an imitation of a cow's call or a shrug, but print is the most arbitrary form of all, which is why reading has to be taught and cannot simply happen.

questions.question: Write the three language formula.
questions.answer: R-1 is the regional language of the State, R-2 is the mother tongue or local language of the child, and R-3 is a modern European or foreign language, in India ordinarily English. The formula was recommended by the Kothari Commission, 1964-66, and adopted nationally in the National Policy on Education, 1968. In Assam, R-1 is Assamese, R-2 is the child's own language such as Bodo or Mising, and R-3 is English.

questions.question: Write two provisions provided by Indian Constitution regarding language.
questions.answer: Article 343 fixes Hindi in Devanagari script as the official language of the Union and expressly denies that it is the official language of any State. Article 347 obliges every State to endeavour to promote the Eighth Schedule languages and allows Parliament to make special provisions for any language; it is the source of the special protection given to languages such as Assamese, Bodo and Mising.

questions.question: Write how does language works as a tool for self expression.
questions.answer: Language works as a tool of self-expression by selecting among words, and each choice sets one perspective against another. To say the garhi is broken is to make a statement; to say she broke my pen is to make a claim; to say I could not finish it is to make an excuse. That is why a small vocabulary is also a small reasoning power, and why words such as because, if and instead have to be taught deliberately.

questions.question: Briefly mention the constitutional provisions for regional language of India.
questions.answer: Article 345 allows only Hindi and English for the official purposes of the Union, the President naming others by rules, so the regional language of Assam does not travel with central documents. Article 347 obliges every State to endeavour to promote the Eighth Schedule languages and allows Parliament to make special provisions for any language. Article 350 lets a member address the chair in the mother tongue with the Chairman's permission, which is the constitutional basis for treating a regional language as equal.

questions.question: How does a child's home language influence in learning school language?
questions.answer: The home language gives the child the scaffolding in which concepts first form, through everyday talk, questions, stories and songs, so a new subject arrives as an addition to what is already understood. It also gives confidence, since a child who is answered in his own language is willing to risk a wrong answer. This is why withdrawing the home language early does not speed the transition; it removes the security, and the school language is then learnt more slowly, not faster.

questions.question: Write any two differences between phonetics and phonology.
questions.answer: Phonetics studies speech sounds as they are actually produced, describing how the vocal organs work and dealing with accent, clarity and mumbling; it is concerned with production. Phonology studies the same sounds as a system, asking which sounds the language treats as different and which sequences it permits. So phonetics describes how bat is actually pronounced, while phonology explains why bat, pat and rat are three different words.

questions.question: Why language is called dynamic?
questions.answer: Because it is a living thing that changes with the life it describes. New objects need names, so new words enter the language, and old words narrow their meaning or die out when what they named is gone; Assamese has taken in laptop and solar inverter within one generation. That is a practical warning for the teacher: the textbook vocabulary is only a fraction of the language the children are already using, and a Class IV child bringing a new word is not making a mistake.

questions.question: Write briefly about the importance of Assamese language as a lingua franca of the North East.
questions.answer: Assamese matters as the lingua franca of the North-East because it is spoken over the widest area as both a first and a second language, in the plains and in the tribal districts, and it is the official language of Assam under the 1963 Act. It is the language of the market, the school, the courts and the radio, so it is the language in which speakers of Mising, Karbi, Bodo or Sadri usually meet a stranger. It carries the folk song and folk tale of many communities, so it belongs to everyone who uses it.

questions.question: Briefly write what aspects of learners linguistic development are possible through the activities inside the classroom.
questions.answer: Classroom activity can develop three aspects of a learner's linguistic growth. Oral language comes first, since storytelling, role play, debate and group discussion give every child an occasion to speak and to be listened to. Vocabulary and word formation follow, when children handle word walls, picture cards and word families. Metalinguistic awareness comes last, when sentences in the texts they read are named, compared and corrected. All three need the home languages of the class to be welcome rather than suppressed.

questions.question: 'Language is arbitrary' - describe the statement briefly.
questions.answer: The statement means that the form of a word has no natural connection with its meaning. Water does not contain water and does not sound like water, and the letters of table look nothing like a table; the link exists only because a community agreed on it. Arbitrary does not mean meaningless, however. A sign has meaning because the agreement is binding within the community, which is why every new speaker has to learn it.

questions.question: Mention two natures of language.
questions.answer: Language is creative and it is arbitrary. Creative means it is not a closed list but a rule-governed capacity, so a speaker who has never heard unbelievable can still produce it from the un- + believe + -able pattern. Arbitrary means there is no necessary connection between the form of a word and its meaning; the word water could have been called anything, and only convention keeps it steady.

questions.question: What is aspirated sound? What are the aspirated sounds of Assamese Language?
questions.answer: An aspirated sound is produced with a puff of breath immediately after the stop is released, so that the airflow is heard as a slight hiss; place the hand before the mouth and the breath is felt. The five aspirated sounds of Assamese are খ (kh), গ (gh), ছ (chh), ঢ় and জ (jh). Assamese keeps voiced aspirates, which Hindi and Bengali have lost, so its consonant inventory is slightly larger.

questions.question: Describe briefly about the three language formula.
questions.answer: The formula recommends that every child learns three languages in a graded sequence rather than all at once: R-1 the regional language, R-2 the mother tongue or local language, and R-3 a foreign language, ordinarily English. In an Assamese-medium school of Assam, R-1 is Assamese and the medium from the primary stage, R-2 is the child's own language such as Bodo or Mising, used from the beginning, and R-3 is English, introduced progressively and emphasised in the upper primary stage.

questions.question: Write the provisions provided by Indian constitution about Language.
questions.answer: Article 343 fixes Hindi in Devanagari as the official language of the Union and denies that it is the official language of any State. Article 350 allows members to address the chair in Hindi or English, with the Chairman's permission to use the mother tongue; read with the Eighth Schedule, it is the basis of the view that any citizen may address the President or the Governor in an Eighth Schedule language such as Assamese.

questions.question: 'Language is arbitrary'- Explain.
questions.answer: Language is arbitrary in the sense that the shape of a sign and its meaning are fixed by convention alone, not by anything in the object itself. The letter b does not look or sound like the sound it names, and a printed page is the most arbitrary form of all. This is the theoretical reason a child cannot infer meaning from print and why reading has to be taught. It does not mean language is meaningless, only that its signs have to be agreed upon.

questions.question: Write two differences between phonetics and phonology?
questions.answer: Phonetics is a branch of physics-based study of speech sounds as they are produced, and its questions are about the vocal organs, accent and clarity. Phonology is a grammatical study of sounds within a particular language, and its questions are about contrast and permitted sequences. In short, phonetics tells us how a sound is made, while phonology tells us what difference that sound makes in the language.

questions.question: Write two suggestions according to NCF-2005 about multilingualism.
questions.answer: NCF 2005 makes two recommendations. First, the home language or mother tongue should be the medium of instruction at least until the early elementary stage, and certainly in the foundational years, so that the child learns concepts in a language already under command. Second, schools should build a multilingual environment in which children learn several languages, use each for its own purpose, and respect the languages the community speaks, rather than treating the home language as a handicap to be corrected.

questions.question: Briefly explain about 'Three language formula'.
questions.answer: The three-language formula says that a child should learn the regional language, the mother tongue or local language, and a foreign language, in a graded sequence instead of all together. The Kothari Commission recommended it in 1964-66 and the National Policy on Education of 1968 adopted it. It guards against three failures: reducing the child to the mother tongue alone, to the majority language alone, or to the foreign language alone. NEP 2020 keeps the mother tongue or regional language as the medium until at least Grade 5, preferably Grade 8.

questions.question: What is language learning and learning through language?
questions.answer: Learning about language treats language itself as the content of the lesson, so the child names its parts, compares constructions, applies a rule and corrects punctuation. Learning through language uses language as the tool of some other purpose, such as learning about plants, the water cycle or the difference between 46 and 39. The first belongs to the language period and the second to every other period, and most of school happens in the second, which is why a child can know the rules of grammar and still answer in one word.

questions.question: As a language teacher design an activity to develop patriotism among the learners at the elementary level.
questions.answer: I would run a three-day activity called My Language, My State, My India. Each group takes one Assamese poem or folk song praising the State or the country and one folk song from a home language in the class, and every child writes four lines about it, in Assamese and in the home language, with a small drawing. We display the writings on one class chart, so that every language in the room is honoured, and then each child answers one question about a State other than Assam. The patriotism comes from the children doing the work, not from being told about it.

questions.question: Explain language as an important part of culture and identity.
questions.answer:
Culture is the whole way of life of a community — its food, dress, work, festivals, forms of address and rules of politeness — and language is integral to it in a double sense. It records culture in proverbs, folk tales, songs and the names of plants, animals and kinship; and it carries culture, because the manner of speaking is itself a cultural act. In Assamese, forms of address differ by age and relationship, and the choice of code between two speakers carries respect or closeness.

From this comes identity. A person's name, mother tongue, script and idiom travel with them, and in an unfamiliar setting they are marked as outsiders. This is why NEP 2020 and NCF-SE 2023 place the home language at the centre of the foundational stage — and why a school that takes away the language a child brings is making a statement about who is at home.

Plurality, though, is not betrayal. The tea-garden worker who speaks Sadri at home and Assamese in the bazaar is using a repertoire, not losing a culture.

questions.question: Describe how children move from home language to school language.
questions.answer:
The home language (matribhasa) is what a child acquires first, naturally and informally, in family life. The school language is the one in which the textbook is written and the child examined — normally Assamese in an Assamese-medium school. They have different jobs: the home language gives the linguistic scaffolding within which concepts are first formed, while the school language opens the printed curriculum.

The transition from one to the other is a period, not a moment. During it the child understands a great deal but answers in short phrases, reverts to the home language when the school language fails, and avoids tasks needing speech. A well-informed teacher reads this as the normal stage of a bilingual child, not as a child who cannot learn. Three things make it go well — time, two or three years of sustained exposure; understandable input, slower and tied to things the child can see; and continued use of the home language. Withdrawing the home language early does not speed the transition, it removes the child's confidence.

questions.question: Explain the importance of multilingual classrooms.
questions.answer:
Multilingualism means more than one language is in use in a setting and more than one is needed for full participation. In an Assamese classroom a single morning may contain Assamese, Bodo, Mising, Hindi, Bengali and a tea-garden community language. Three things follow.

First, the languages are additive, not remedial. A language the child brings adds to the school's repertoire rather than correcting a deficit; there is no weak language and strong language, only different ones. Second, more than one language means more than one set of comparisons, and comparison is the origin of grammar — the child sees two word orders, two ways of marking tense and two scripts, and so develops metalinguistic awareness far sooner than a monolingual peer. Third, functions are distributed: one language carries explanation, another affection or play, and the child learns to shift.

Two conditions must hold: a shared language for common purposes, and patient time for those who do not yet know the school language.

questions.question: Describe language diversity in the context of Assam.
questions.answer:
Assam is a small state with a long history of trade, migration and settlement, and it holds a remarkable density of languages. Assamese (Asamiya Bhasa, also called Bamar) is the official language of the State under the Assam Official Language Act, 1963; it is written in the Baamuniya script, of the Brahmic family, and is one of the 22 languages of the Eighth Schedule. It serves as the lingua franca of the State.

Alongside and within it are many tribal and linguistic communities — Bodo, also in the Eighth Schedule with its own script, Mising, Karbi, Dimasa, Hmar, Zakhai, Khasi, Garo, Rabha, Tiwa, and the hill communities of Dima Hasao and Karbi Anglong. The tea gardens brought workers from eastern and central India, and with them Sadri or Mundari and Nepali; Bengali and Hindi are widely used in commerce.

So one district, sometimes one school compound, holds half a dozen mother tongues. For us this is concrete: a Bodo-speaking and a Hindi-speaking child in an Assamese-medium Class II are learning a second language while learning to read.

questions.question: How can foundational literacy and numeracy be acquired at the elementary level.
questions.answer:
Foundational Literacy and Numeracy (FLN) is the early stage in which every child acquires the basic capabilities of reading, writing, speaking and number to the level required for further learning. Under NEP 2020 it is the first priority area of the foundational stage, because a child who cannot read, write and count cannot do anything else in school. The national mission is NIPUN Bharat, whose guidelines came in 2022.

I would build the period around the twelve competencies NIPUN Bharat lists: oral skills, decoding (print concepts, phonemic awareness) and encoding (forming letters and composing words); counting and cardinality, and operations done with meaning using real objects.

So reading begins with phonics taught in the language the child already speaks, starting with letters in a meaningful context such as the child's own name, then regular three-phoneme words, holding irregular words back.
