Emergent writing is respected — squiggles and repeated marks come before joined letters. And counting is done with seeds and stones, with the child saying the story behind the answer.

questions.question: Write any three functions of language outside the classroom.
questions.answer:
Outside the classroom and beyond the school, language performs at least three functions.

First, the affective and social function. In the family and among neighbours, language carries affection, instruction, narration, comfort, gossip and quarrel. It is warm, repetitive, intimate and heavily dialectal — the register in which a child first learns to argue, to apologise and to be comforted.

Second, the transactional and informative function. In the market and on the phone, language carries bargaining, enquiry, news and greeting. The register is fixed and formulaic, speech is reduced, and the market is usually multilingual, so the child practises switching codes without noticing.

Third, the cultural and commemorative function. In folk song, festival and worship, language carries collective memory, devotion and identity. It is rhythmic, formulaic, archaic and oral, and many of these forms survive nowhere else. A fourth function is the public and imaginative one of newspaper, radio and literature. Note that these are exactly the languages children are examined in inside school.

questions.question: "Teaching through language refers to that teaching, where a language plays role of a medium of instruction?" Justify the statement.
questions.answer:
The statement is correct, and it can be justified from three directions.

First, language is the vehicle of thought, not a label stuck on it. Vygotsky held that the higher mental functions — abstract reasoning, planning, self-awareness — have no natural existence apart from language, and concepts such as fair or possible have no meaning outside a language. A child still acquiring words in a second language is still acquiring the concepts those words carry.

Second, subject knowledge arrives through language. Before a child can count they must know the number words; before they can add they must understand the words of the operation; before they can understand that a plant needs water they must understand the sentence holding the fact.

Third, where the child does not yet control the medium of instruction, the examination measures the child's language, and marks attributed to the subject are really marks attributed to language. Hence a language-sensitive pedagogy: teach the subject in the child's own language first.

questions.question: Write the needs of language learning in acquiring knowledge of other subjects.
questions.answer:
Nothing in a school happens except through language, and the child's first acquisition of any subject is linguistic. The needs are concrete and subject-specific.

For reading, the child needs print concepts and the relation of the spoken word to the written word; without them decoding fails and the child reads out words instead of meaning. For mathematics, the child needs counting words, the terms of the operation and the language of the problem statement; otherwise the child can manipulate objects but cannot read the problem. For science, the child needs the names of materials and processes and the phrasing of cause and effect; without it observation becomes guesswork. For social studies, narrative and expository comprehension and place and time vocabulary, or facts are memorised without connection. For classroom life itself, imperatives, questions and warnings — otherwise behaviour becomes noise.

The need cuts both ways: knowledge itself is inherited through language. No child invents the alphabet or the number system.

questions.question: Discuss the role of a language teacher in a multilingual classroom.
questions.answer:
In a multilingual classroom the language teacher is not only a teacher of grammar but a planner and a bridge person.

As a planner, the teacher first maps the languages actually present — the step the practicum project on the languages of the neighbourhood trains us to do — and then plans for them. A child explains a concept in the language in which they know it best, and the teacher moves it afterwards into the school language. This planned movement is translanguaging, not random code-switching. Children bring their own words for a plant or a tool, and the class holds all of them beside the textbook word.

As a bridge, the teacher's own competence in two or three of the classroom's languages is a resource no methodology replaces. Where the teacher lacks it, the honest move is to ask — invite a parent, an elder or an older pupil to contribute.

As a setter of tone, the teacher decides what happens to interference and ridicule: L1 interference is treated as evidence of what the child knows, meaning first and form gently.

questions.question: What is the meaning of learning language and learning through language.
questions.answer:
The word “language” hides two different activities, and a primary teacher must be able to say which one a lesson is doing.

Learning about language treats language as the content. The child names the parts of a sentence, compares constructions, applies a rule, revises, summarises and translates. The child is doing something to language, and the teacher's talk is metalinguistic — “this is a compound sentence”. Its usual failure is that the rule is learned but not used: grammar without text.

Learning through language treats it as the tool of another purpose. The child is learning about plants, or the water cycle, or the difference between 46 and 39, with language used to think, organise, discuss and write. The teacher's talk here is scaffolding — “first tell me what you see”. Its failure is the reverse: content learned but not articulated, answers of one word.

Most of school happens in the second mode with little attention paid to it, which is how a child can know the grammar and still not explain a process in a paragraph.

questions.question: Write about the importance of language in curriculum.
questions.answer:
Language occupies three distinguishable places in the curriculum, and confusing them is the commonest error in discussion of the subject.

It is first a subject. Assamese or English has its own periods, textbook, syllabus, examination and body of knowledge — literature, grammar, composition, comprehension. It is secondly a medium: the vehicle through which every other subject is taught, every lesson explained and every answer given, and through which the child shows what has been learnt in science or mathematics. It is thirdly a resource and cross-curricular competence — listening, speaking, reading, writing, reasoning about language and using language to learn — which every other subject both assumes and develops.

The tension is real: time given to “language” looks like time taken from mathematics, yet a child who cannot read the question cannot do the mathematics. The answer is not to choose but to plan for the overlap. NCF-SE 2023 and NEP 2020 both move this way, treating language as the medium of the whole curriculum.

questions.question: 'Language acquisition and language learning is complementary to each other'- explain the statement.
questions.answer:
Acquisition and learning are not rivals; each does what the other cannot.

Acquisition is how the first language arrives. It is natural, implicit and incidental — the child picks it up in ordinary family life, from need and interaction, with no textbook and no correction. The child is a full speaker with authority, and the volume of talk around it is enormous. Learning, by contrast, is explicit and deliberate: the school language is taught from a textbook, with rules, exercises and reward, and the child is a learner, often a slow and silent one.

They are complementary for three reasons. First, acquisition builds the scaffolding — the home language is where everyday talk, questions and stories happen, and within that scaffolding concepts are first formed; discard it in a hurry and the child cannot climb. Second, Cummins' interdependence hypothesis holds that proficiency developed in one language transfers to another. Third, the stages themselves are common to both — one-word, two-word, basic structures, complex structures. Only the pace differs.

questions.question: Discuss which aspects of learning can be developed through outside actions of a language classroom.
questions.answer:
Much of language learning happens outside the four walls, and a good part of what is credited to the classroom is really learnt on the playground, in the market and at home. Four aspects stand out.

Oral fluency and listening. Conversation, teasing, quarrels and group games produce far more talk than a language period does, in an informal register — incomplete sentences, slang, humour, non-verbal cues. A child who can argue about a football match has the interactional fluency the classroom rarely calls for.

Vocabulary and world knowledge. Children pick up names of plants, birds, foods and tools from the field and the bazaar, words no textbook lists.

Social learning. Sharing, negotiating and resolving conflict among peers is where the language of cooperation is practised; a child will not learn to negotiate by being told about it.

Identity. Folk songs, festival talk and the home language give the child a voice; a child whose language is ridiculed learns to be silent, and that is the loss not of a vocabulary but of a self.

questions.question: 'The need of language learning is important in acquiring other subject knowledge'- Describe it.
questions.answer:
The child acquires every subject in school linguistically first, so language is not a service to other subjects — it is the route through which they arrive.

Consider mathematics. The child needs the number words before counting, and the terms of the operation — “more”, “left”, “in all” — before adding. Given a word problem in an unfamiliar language, a child who has understood the counting may still be unable to read what is asked, and will be marked wrong for a language failure. Science needs the names of materials and the phrasing of cause and effect; without the sentence the child cannot connect what was observed with what is explained. Social studies needs narrative comprehension and place and time vocabulary, or facts are memorised without connection. Even classroom discipline runs on imperatives and warnings.

So teaching the subject in the child's own language first is not sentiment. It is the only route that does not lose the child.

questions.question: Describe the processes about language learning and learning through language.
questions.answer:
The two processes are different, and each needs its own moves.

For learning about language, the process runs through noticing and handling the language itself: listening to the text, reading it aloud, identifying what each part does, comparing two constructions, working out what changes if a word is removed, then applying a rule and revising one's own sentence. Grammar is handled inside a text rather than on a separate list, so the child meets the rule as a fact about this sentence.

For learning through language, the process runs through the subject, with language as the tool of thinking: listening to the explanation, organising what was seen, discussing with a partner, sequencing with first, then, next, finally, and writing or dictating the outcome. Three moves make this deliberate — plan the language demands in advance, use the subject text itself as language material, and read across subjects. A subject period is mostly the second process with none of the first, and that gap explains the child who knows the grammar but cannot explain a paragraph.

questions.question: Explain the importance of language as a carrier of heritage and culture.
questions.answer:
Language is the storehouse in which a community's heritage is kept and the carrier by which it is handed on.

It records heritage in fixed forms — proverbs, folk tales, folk songs, place names, oral traditions and the loan words a community carries, which show who traded with whom and worshipped what. It also carries everyday heritage in the vocabulary of a way of life: a mother, a grandmother, a rice-paddy, the first-flood rains, a particular loom, a particular folk song. These cannot be borrowed without loss. A community that stops using them loses the practice, and then the memory, because once the name is gone the custom becomes hard to describe.

The school has a footing here. Article 350A obliges every effort to promote the mother tongue in mother-tongue-medium institutions, and NEP 2020 places the home language at the centre of the foundational stage. What endangers heritage is not borrowing, but the loss of occasions to use a language in public.

questions.question: Explain the importance of story telling for the development of speaking skill of children.
questions.answer:
Storytelling is one of the cheapest and most powerful ways to develop children's speaking skill, and it is on the syllabus as part of the compulsory literary activity.

It builds vocabulary in context. A child hearing a story meets words such as “hesitated” or “succeeded” attached to a person and a happening, and later uses them the same way. It builds sentence length and structure, because a story cannot be told in single words — the child must join an action to a reason with “because” and “so”. It builds sequencing, which is the same skill as organising a paragraph.

It also develops voice and audience. A teller must be heard, must pause at the right moment and must change tone for a comic character. And it builds confidence, because a story gives the child something to stand behind; the child is not speaking about themselves, and that freedom is exactly what the silent child needs. So I record stories in the mother tongue as well, and give every teller a real audience task.

questions.question: Write the challenges in a multilingual classroom while using school language among the learners.
questions.answer:
When the school language is used with children who do not yet have it, six difficulties recur, and each has a practical answer.

The silent child, who understands but does not answer, replies in one word and looks at the floor. Allow a first response in the home language, accept gesture and pointing, give processing time, and never force an oral answer before the class.

The child who “makes mistakes” — interference from L1 and mixed sentences are normal here. Treat them as evidence of what the child knows, and correct meaning first and form gently.

Ridicule by peers, which silences a child for good. Make the multilingualism useful in public by asking that language for a word, and make respect a class norm.

Accent and script, where Bamuniya-style or Roman forms are marked wrong. Accept the child's script for a draft and teach the school script through phonics. And blocked concepts: explain the task in the home language first, because the content is the goal, not the code.

questions.question: Explain the Three Language Formula and its importance. [4 Marks] OR Write about Cognitive Academic Language Proficiency (CALP)? [4 Marks]
questions.answer:
The three-language formula was recommended by the Kothari (Education) Commission, 1964-66, and adopted as national policy in the National Policy on Education, 1968. It says that a child should learn three languages in a graded sequence — the regional language (R-1), the mother tongue or local language (R-2), and a foreign or modern European language (R-3), in India ordinarily English.

In an Assamese-medium school in Assam the three slots are filled like this.

- R-1, the regional language, is Assamese, the official language of the State and the medium of instruction from the primary stage itself.
- R-2, the mother tongue or local language, is the child’s own home language — Bodo, Mising, Karbi, Hmar, Sadri, Bengali or another — used from the beginning and, where possible, in school too.
- R-3, the foreign language, is English, introduced progressively and formally emphasised in the upper primary and secondary stages.

Its importance lies in what it protects. It avoids reducing the child to the mother tongue alone, which cuts the child off from the wider State; to the majority language alone, which makes a large part of the country learn slowly; and to the foreign language alone, which produces an educated elite that cannot talk to the society it is to serve. Because the three come in sequence, no child carries the whole load at once. In Assam the formula is not equally easy for everyone: where the home language is Assamese the school simply reinforces R-1, but a Bodo- or Mising-speaking child is learning R-1 and R-2 as two separate languages while R-3 waits ahead. The position has also moved — NEP 2020 asks that the medium be the home or regional language at least up to Grade 5 and preferably till Grade 8, and NCF-SE 2023 treats language as the medium of the whole curriculum.

If CALP is chosen instead: Cognitive and Academic Language Proficiency, as Jim Cummins named it, is the language of the textbook, the definition, the argument and the examination answer. It is decontextualised — the words must carry the meaning without gesture or shared situation to help — and academically demanding in precision and structure. It does not arrive by itself; it has to be taught, in every subject, which is why teaching the concepts in the language the child already has is the surest road to CALP in the second one.

questions.question: What is the place of language in the curriculum? [4 Marks] OR State two functions of language inside and outside the classroom. [4 Marks]
questions.answer:
Language occupies three distinguishable places in the curriculum, and running them together is the commonest error in discussions of the subject.

As a subject, language has its own periods, textbook, syllabus, examination and body of knowledge — literature, grammar, composition and comprehension. Without that period, grammar is never taught systematically.

As a medium, it is the vehicle through which every other subject is taught, every question asked and every answer given. A Class III child learns the life cycle of a butterfly in language and shows what was learnt in language.

As a resource and cross-curricular competence, it is the set of abilities — listening, speaking, reading, writing, reasoning about language and using language to learn — which every subject both assumes and develops.

The tension between these is the daily experience of every school. Time given to the language period looks like time taken from mathematics, yet a child who cannot read the question cannot do the mathematics, and a child who cannot write the answer cannot show that it was done. The resolution is not to choose but to plan for the overlap.

Two functions inside the classroom. Instructionally — explaining, describing, defining, directing, questioning and summarising, as when a teacher asks the class to write four stages in order using first, then, next and finally. Discip­linarily and socially — praising, warning, correcting and evaluating, as in sit down, or a word of approval that keeps a hesitant child trying.

Two functions outside. In the family and among neighbours, language carries affection, instruction, narration, comfort and quarrel, together with proverbs and stories; it is warm and heavily dialectal. In the market and the community it carries transactions, bargaining, greetings and news, often with several languages mixed together.

The two lists are linked: the languages used outside school are exactly the languages the child is assessed inside it.

questions.question: What is phonetics and phonology? Explain. [4 Marks]
questions.answer:
Both terms belong to the sound level of language. The difference between them is the difference between a sound as a physical event and a sound as a unit of a system.

Phonetics studies speech sounds as they are actually produced by the vocal organs. It asks how a sound is made — where the tongue, lips and velum sit, whether the vocal cords vibrate, how the air is released. The p of pat and the b of bat differ because the cords do not vibrate in the first and do in the second. Phonetics is description and measurement, and it is what a teacher reaches for when clearing a child’s mumbling.

Phonology studies the same sounds as a system. It asks not how a sound is made but which sounds the language treats as different, and which sequences are permitted. Its central unit is the phoneme — the smallest unit of sound that can change the meaning of a word. In bat, pat, rat and mat the initial consonant does exactly that work: change it and the meaning changes while the rest stands still. Such sounds are contrastive or phonemic.

Other sounds do no such work. The clear l at the end of milk, where the grammar expects a nasal, is a predictable variant; both are allophones of one phoneme, and the child treats them as one. A language’s phoneme inventory is therefore finite and countable — commonly between twenty and several dozen — while its word list runs into thousands. That efficiency is what makes the phoneme the true atom of spoken language.

The classroom consequence is direct. Phonics teaches the grapheme–phoneme relationship, turning the arbitrary mark on the page into a sound and so into a meaning; and because the correspondence is not one-to-one, it is a set of recurring patterns that must be learnt in the language the child is actually reading.

questions.question: Describe the need of international transmission of language and culture. [4 Marks]
questions.answer:
International transmission of language and culture means the movement of words, meanings, stories and ways of living across national borders, and it is needed for four reasons.

First, language carries culture, so what travels in the language travels with the culture attached. A proverb brings a whole world with it, a kinship term brings a family structure, a folk song brings a festival. A reader who has only the translated word has the object but not the world, which is why translation always loses something.

Second, language is a mark of cultural identity, and shared language is what lets a person from another country be met as a person rather than treated as an outsider. Our own Constitution accepts this logic: Article 351 lays a duty on the Union to promote harmony and common enquiry among all the people of India in the mother tongue, and Article 350 allows a member to address the President in an Eighth Schedule language.

Third, science, medicine, law and commerce have outgrown any single language. A research paper or a treaty has to travel, and it travels best in a language a wide community already reads. This is the practical need for English as R-3 in our own three-language formula, and nobody objects to that on cultural grounds.

Fourth, for a child in a primary class a second language is a window. A child who meets a story first in Assamese and then in English learns that the world is larger than one classroom, and picks up comparison by the way.

The caution is real: transmission is not replacement. A Jughon speaker mixing Mising and Assamese, or a tea-garden worker who speaks Sadri at home and Assamese in the bazaar, is using a repertoire, not making a choice. What harms a language is not the foreign language beside it but the disappearance of opportunities to use its own.

questions.question: Explain the challenges faced by learners' in using mother tongue in a multilingual classroom. [5 Marks]
questions.answer:
A single Assamese-medium class can hold Assamese, Bodo, Mising, Hindi, Bengali and a tea-garden language in one morning, and every one of those children is outnumbered in the language of the school. The challenges they face are of six kinds, and none is the child’s fault.

- The silent child. The commonest difficulty. The child understands the instruction perfectly but does not answer, or answers in one word, or looks at the floor. This is not stupidity; it is a child with no ready words in the school language who will not risk being laughed at for the few that come.
- Interference from the first language. Sentences come out mixed, word order follows L1 rather than L2, and local vocabulary appears where the textbook word was expected. Unlike a developmental error in the mother tongue, an interference error persists, because the first system is still fully active.
- Ridicule from peers. If other children laugh at the home language, the child stops using it, and the school has removed the very scaffolding the child needed.
- Accent and script. The child writes Bamuniya-style forms or Roman script, is marked wrong for them, and concludes that what it knows is worthless in this room.
- No material. There may be no reader, no chart, no wall card and no text in the home language, so nothing can be read in it at all.
- Concepts blocked behind the instruction. The child cannot do the task because the task cannot be understood, and both the subject content and the child’s ability are then marked as absent.

Two further difficulties sit at the teacher’s level. The transition from home language to school language is a period and not a moment, and during it the amount and quality of the child’s talk falls — it reverts to the home language when the school language fails, avoids tasks needing speech, and can appear to have gone backwards. And the teacher is often the only adult in the room who cannot bridge, because the languages present are not the ones the teacher studied.

The last of these matters most. A child whose language meets a blank face learns not only that it cannot use the language but that it is not the kind of person who has one. Silencing is not the loss of a vocabulary; it is the loss of a self permitted to exist.

questions.question: Which skills of language are known as "active and productive skill" and Why? [4 Marks]
questions.answer:
The four basic skills of language divide into two pairs, and the division turns on what the learner does with the language. Speaking and writing are the active or productive skills, because the learner produces language. Listening and reading are the receptive or passive skills, because the learner receives and interprets language that somebody else has produced.

Speaking is productive because the speaker generates the sounds, arranges them into words and sentences and puts meaning into them for somebody else. Nothing is given to the speaker; the utterance is built from nothing in the moment of speaking. It is the hardest of the four for a second-language learner, because planning and execution happen together — the child must choose the word, remember the rule, pronounce it and hear the effect all at once.

Writing is productive in the same way, with the difference that execution can be slowed down and revised. The writer produces a visible record that nobody else will correct unless the writer does, which is where grammar, organisation and precision are genuinely tested.

Why the naming matters. These terms are not a ranking; an active skill is not better than a receptive one, only a different relation to language. But the classroom implication is serious, because productive skills can only be learned by using them. A child cannot learn to speak a language by being told about speaking. Every function must be given an occasion: to teach the language of negotiation, give children a real disagreement about who does which task and make them resolve it; to teach narrative, give them a sequence to order; to teach description, give them an object to describe to a partner who cannot see it. That is why the compulsory practicum activity is a debate, an extempore speech, a storytelling and a role play — in all four the speaker must hold a position, give a reason, answer a challenge and read an audience.

questions.question: Write the role of a teacher in transition of home language to school language. [4 Marks]
questions.answer:
The transition from home language to school language is a period and not a moment, and the teacher’s work is to walk the child across it without destroying the scaffolding on the other side.

First, diagnose and respect the home language. Find out what each child speaks and with whom. A child who speaks Bodo with a grandmother, Assamese in the shop and Mising with a friend is not confused; the child is sorting languages by situation, and that awareness is an asset the teacher should name openly.

Second, expect the dip and read it correctly. During the transition the child understands a great deal but answers in short phrases, reverts to the home language when the school language fails, and avoids tasks that need speech. This is the normal stage of a bilingual child, not a child who cannot learn.

Third, give comprehensible input — slower than usual, literal, in short sentences, with every new word tied to something the child can see or hold.

Fourth, bridge rather than replace. Explain the task first in the language the child has, then move to the school language for the key terms. This planned movement is translanguaging; the content is the goal, not the code of explanation.

Fifth, give time and keep the home language alive. Two or three years of sustained exposure are needed, and withdrawing the home language early does not speed the crossing — it removes confidence, so the school language is then learned more slowly.

Two habits do more than the rest: allow a first response in the home language, accept pointing and gesture, and never put a silent child on the spot; and correct meaning first and form gently, reading interference as evidence of what the child knows.

questions.question: "Culture transfers from generation to generation through language"- Discuss. [4 Marks]
questions.answer:
The statement is true, and it is truer of some things than of others. Culture — food, dress, dwelling, work, festivals, religious practice, music, forms of address and rules of politeness — is carried to the next generation almost entirely by words.

Consider what travels. Proverbs carry a community’s moral judgements; the Assamese saying that a river is judged by its course tells a child something about conduct that no rule book states. Folk tales and songs carry the older generation’s fears, jokes and local knowledge in a rhythm the child remembers without being taught. Kinship terms — mother, grandmother, younger sister, elder brother — carry the shape of the family. The names of plants, animals, tools, looms and fishing gear carry the ecology and the work. Forms of address carry politeness itself, because in Assamese the word used for another person changes with age and relationship, and so does the intonation that goes with it.

Notice what happens when the word goes. Words like a rice-paddy, a particular loom or a particular folk song cannot be borrowed without loss, because they mark a way of life. A community that stops using them does not merely lose vocabulary; it loses the practice, and then the memory, because once the name is gone the custom becomes hard even to describe. Language is an archive that outlives the century in which the events happened.

Two qualifications keep this honest. Transmission is never pure copying; each generation selects, alters and adds, and that is how culture stays alive. And culture is not a sealed box — language change is not cultural loss, and borrowing is not betrayal. What damages a culture is the disappearance of opportunities to use its language in public.

questions.question: "Language plays an important role as a carrier of culture and heritage"- Justify the statement. [4 Marks]
questions.answer:
The statement can be justified on two grounds that the syllabus separates deliberately: language records culture, and language carries culture.

As a record, language preserves a culture in its vocabulary and its sentences. Proverb by proverb the moral code of a community is written down. Folk tales, folk songs, the names of plants and animals, the kinship terms and the words for weaving and fishing hold the whole material life of a people. Language is an archive: place names tell of settlement, loan words tell of trade and contact, and old ritual formulae tell of what was once worshipped.

As a carrier, it does something an archive cannot. It enacts culture every time it is used. The manner of speaking is itself cultural — forms of address in Assamese differ by age and relationship, certain intonations carry politeness, and the choice of code between two speakers is a cultural act. A child learns what counts as respectful simply by being addressed respectfully for three years.

The justification sharpens if we ask what is lost when a language is lost. Words such as a mother, a grandmother, a younger sister, a rice-paddy, the first-flood rains, a particular loom or a particular folk song cannot be borrowed without loss, because they mark a way of life. Lose them and you lose the practice, and then the memory.

This is also why language is a mark of cultural identity. When a school takes away the language a child brings, it is making a statement about who in the community is at home — which is why NEP 2020 and NCF-SE 2023 place the home language at the centre of the foundational stage, and why bringing a folk tale into the classroom is an act of recognition rather than decoration.

questions.question: As a language teacher what are the strategies you will adopt to overcome the challenges faced in using learners mother tongue in a multilingual classroom. [4 Marks]
questions.answer:
I treat the languages the children bring as the raw material of the lesson, not as an obstacle to it. Six strategies follow.

First, find out before teaching. I want to know what each child speaks at home, with whom, and what else the child understands, because what a teacher assumes about a class is usually wrong.

Second, never punish the mother tongue. I permit a first response in the home language, accept pointing and gesture as answers, give a child time to think before I take the class’s response, and never put a silent child on the spot in front of thirty people. Ridicule from peers stops a child speaking its language at all, and then the scaffold is gone.

Third, make the plurality public and valued. I ask, deliberately and often, for a word from another language in the room — the name of a plant, a bird, a food, a festival, a tool — and put it beside the textbook word on the word wall. What is asked for is honoured, not tolerated.

Fourth, bridge deliberately. A child may explain a concept first in the language in which the child knows it best, and I then move to the school language for the key terms and the written work. This planned movement is translanguaging, and it is different from random code-switching.

Fifth, teach the school script additively. I accept Bamuniya-style or Roman forms in a first draft and move on to the school script by phonics, beginning with the child’s own name.

Sixth, use my own competence and ask when I lack it. Where I do not speak the child’s language, I invite a parent, an elder or a bilingual older pupil to come and tell a story or teach a greeting.

For assessment I insist on one thing: a child who cannot yet write in the school language may dictate and must be credited for the content.

questions.question: Design a suitable activity to assess the listening skill of students in the lower primary level. [4 Marks]
questions.answer:
Here is an activity I would actually run in a Class II classroom. It is called the Listening Corner, and it takes about twenty-five minutes.

Aim. To find out whether the children can attend to an oral message, hold it in mind and act on it — which is what listening actually is in a classroom.

Material. A card with a simple picture on it, kept from the class; three or four objects or pictures on the table; an assessment chart with three columns.

Procedure. In the warm-up, the teacher says a familiar line from the folk song the class has been learning, and the children clap when they hear it; three minutes, and everyone’s ears are on. In the main task the teacher speaks for one minute without interruption. It is connected talk, not a list: how to fold a paper boat, what a shopkeeper said, or a short account of the first-flood rains in the village. Then the children do three things in order, so the memory load stays small: they point to or draw what was described, they answer three oral questions, and they carry out two instructions from it — for instance, placing three pictures in the order given. Finally the talk is heard a second time and each child adds one thing missed, which shows whether the earlier failure was of attention or of comprehension.

What is assessed. I record three things per child: how many of the three questions were answered, how many of the two instructions were carried out correctly, and whether the second hearing was needed. That record separates attention, vocabulary and memory, which are three problems with three different remedies.

Why it suits the lower primary level. Listening needs no script and no reading ability, so no child is excluded for what he cannot yet do on paper, and the response is physical as well as verbal, so a shy child can succeed by pointing.

questions.question: "Teaching through language refers to that teaching, where a language plays the role of a medium of instruction?"- Justify the statement. [4 Marks]
questions.answer:
The statement is correct, and it rests on a distinction a primary teacher must be able to make: teaching through language, as against teaching about language.

Teaching through language is the activity in which language is the tool and the subject is the point. The lesson is about plants, or the water cycle, or the difference between 46 and 39, and language is what the child thinks with, organises with, discusses with and writes with. Almost all school happens this way and very little attention is paid to it, which is exactly why a child can be taught minute details of grammar and still be unable to explain a process in a coherent paragraph. Teaching about language is the other activity, where the language itself is the content: the child names the parts of a sentence, changes the voice, corrects punctuation or translates. That is the language period.

The justification is that in teaching through language the medium is not neutral. A child cannot do science without the names of materials and the language of cause and effect; cannot do mathematics without counting words and the language of the problem; cannot read a history paragraph without narrative comprehension. And because the teacher’s talk carries meaning, it teaches language whether planned or not: a teacher who says only tell me what you see gets descriptions, one who says tell me what you see, then what changed, then why gets reasoning.

So the two must be connected deliberately. Plan the language of the subject in advance — for the butterfly lesson, decide that the children will write four stages in order using first, then, next, finally. Use the subject text as language material, since its headings and cause-and-effect markers are grammar taught in context. And read across subjects: a history paragraph is comprehension work, a word problem is inference work.

questions.question: What do you mean by home language and school language? What should be the role of a language teacher in transforming home language to school language? [4 Marks]
questions.answer:
The home language, or mother tongue (matribhasa), is the language a child acquires first, naturally and without formal teaching, in ordinary family life. The school language is the language in which the school teaches, in which the textbook is written, in which the teacher explains and in which the child is examined. For an Assamese-medium school in Assam the school language is normally Assamese, and the two are frequently different.

The difference shows in almost every respect. The home language is picked up in the family and community, incidentally, by need and interaction; the school language is learned in a classroom, from a textbook, deliberately and by examination. The child is a full speaker with authority at home and a silent, slow learner in school. Their values differ too: the home language is the foundation, giving linguistic security, identity and continuity; the school language is the instrument, giving access to the curriculum and the examination.

The two are colleagues with different jobs, not rivals. The home language gives the scaffolding — everyday talk, questions, stories and songs — inside which concepts are first formed. The school language opens the printed curriculum. A programme that discards the first in a hurry to install the second removes the scaffolding and then finds the child cannot climb.

My role as a language teacher is fourfold. I begin from what the child has, using the home language to explain and letting the child bring words and stories from it. I bridge deliberately by translanguaging: explain in the home language, give the school-language term, ask the child to use it in a sentence of his own. I give time and comprehensible input — slower, literal speech tied to visible things, and two or three years of exposure before expecting fluency. And I accept the temporary silence, reading a child who reverts to the home language as a bilingual child in a normal stage. What I will not do is withdraw the home language early in the hope of speeding the transfer. It does the opposite.

questions.question: What is multilingualism? Discuss the strategies to be undertaken by language teacher in using multilingualism as a resource in the language classroom. [5 Marks]
questions.answer:
Multilingualism is the condition in which more than one language is in use in a community or a setting, and in which more than one is needed for full participation. A multilingual classroom is one in which those languages are the medium through which culture, relationship and learning go on; it is better described as multilingual than as multicultural. A class in Assam may hold Assamese, Bodo, Mising, Hindi, Bengali and a tea-garden language in a morning.

Three things distinguish a genuinely multilingual classroom from an ordinary class that happens to contain children of several languages. The languages are additive and not remedial — a language the child brings enlarges the school’s repertoire instead of correcting a deficit, and there is no weak language and strong language, only different ones. Their functions are distributed, so one language may carry explanation and another affection or play. And all of them are used deliberately, for content, comparison and enrichment.

The strategies I would take up as a language teacher are these.

- For content, let the child explain a concept first in the language in which the child knows it best, and then bridge to the school language. This planned movement is translanguaging, not random code-switching.
- For vocabulary, hold the children’s own words beside the textbook word. Ask each child to bring the name in their home language of a plant, a bird, a food or a tool, and put them all on the word wall.
- For grammar, put two languages side by side and let the children find where they differ in word order, in how tense is marked, or in which script is used. More than one language means more than one set of comparisons, and comparison is the origin of grammar, so grammar becomes visible as something languages do differently rather than as an arbitrary list of rules.
- For literature, treat a folk tale told in a home language as a text to be analysed, not as a distraction.
- For assessment, allow a child who cannot yet write in the school language to dictate and credit the content, or the examination measures the child’s English instead of the child’s history.
- For social relations, use structured pair work across language groups, so every child has to use the school language for a real purpose.
- For materials, make them yourself. Where no reader or chart exists in a home language, transcribe from the child and the family.

Two conditions must be stated, or the idea becomes an excuse. There must be a shared language for the classroom’s common purposes, or no lesson can proceed; and the children who do not yet know the school language must be taught it patiently. A classroom that is multilingual but has abandoned the goal of teaching the school language has solved nothing.

questions.question: 'Language helps learners gathering over all knowledge'- Discuss. [4 Marks]
questions.answer:
The claim is not that language is one source of knowledge among others. It is stronger: in a school, language is the route by which every other kind of knowledge arrives. The child’s first acquisition of any subject is linguistic. Before a child can count they must know the number words; before they can add they must understand the words of the operation; before they can understand that a plant needs water they must understand the sentences in which the fact is embedded. Subject knowledge does not sit beside language in the timetable — it comes through it, and in an early primary class it is it.

Look subject by subject. To learn to read, a child needs print concepts and the relation of spoken to written word; without them decoding fails and the child reads words aloud without meaning. To learn mathematics the child needs counting words, operation terms and the language of the problem statement; without them the child can handle objects correctly and still cannot read the problem. To learn science the child needs the names of materials and the language of cause and effect. And classroom discipline needs language — imperatives, questions, praise, warnings, rules — or behaviour becomes noise rather than communication.

Look at that last case, because it decides how a child is examined. Where the child does not yet control the medium of instruction, the examination measures the child’s language, and marks attributed to the subject are really marks attributed to language.

There is a second reason. Knowledge is cumulative and collaborative: each generation begins with the work of the last, and no child invents the alphabet, its value system or the number system. This is why a word and a concept are bound together, and why a child still learning words in a second language is also still learning the concepts those words carry.

questions.question: Prepare a table of the vowel phone of Assamese language according to the position and place of the tongue while pronouncing. [4 Marks]
questions.answer:
A vowel phoneme is judged by two things: the place of the tongue in the mouth, and the degree of its opening or height. Where the tongue stands decides front, central or back; how high or low it stands decides close, close-mid, open-mid or open. Rounding separates the back vowels from the front ones in an otherwise parallel pair.

| Vowel phoneme | Usual Assamese spellings | Position of the tongue | Height of the tongue | Rounding |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| /i/ | ি, ঈ | front | close | none |
| /e/ | ে, এ | front | close-mid | none |
| /ɛ/ | short e, chiefly in borrowed words | front | open-mid | none |
| /a/ | অ, আ, া | central | open | none |
| /ɔ/ | short o, chiefly in borrowed words | back | open-mid | rounded |
| /o/ | ো, ও | back | close-mid | rounded |
| /u/ | ু, ঊ | back | close | rounded |
| /əi/ (diphthong) | ঐ, ৈ | front, closing towards the centre | moves from /e/ to /i/ | none |
| /ɔi/ (diphthong) | in borrowed words | back, closing towards the centre | moves from /o/ to /i/ | rounding at the start |
| /ɛ̃/, /õ/ (nasalised) | a vowel with ঁ or ং attached | as the base vowel, but air escapes through the nose | as the base vowel | as the base vowel |

Two points belong with the table. First, the exact inventory is given a little differently in different linguistic descriptions, particularly over the short e and short o of borrowed words. What is not in dispute — and what an answer should make clear — is the shape of the system: a front unrounded series at three heights, a central open a, and a back rounded series at three heights, with diphthongs closing towards i.

Second, phonemes are not letters. Assamese is written in the Baamuniya script, where a written vowel sign need not correspond one-to-one with a phoneme. That gap is precisely what phonics has to bridge in Class I, and the table is what the child must learn to hear before the mapping to print is attempted.

questions.question: Which Governor General played a key role in promoting English Education in India?
questions.answer: Lord Macaulay, Governor-General of Bengal. His Minute of 1835 visualised English as the language of administration, of the higher courts and of higher learning, and gave the political justification for an English-educated administrative class in India.

questions.question: Which commission recommended English as a medium of higher education in India in 1854?
questions.answer: Wood's Despatch of 1854, issued by Charles Wood, President of the Board of Control. It is sometimes called the Magna Carta of English education in India, because it also created the departments of public instruction and the inspectorate.

questions.question: Which Act made English the associate official language of India after Independence?
questions.answer: The Constitution of India, 1950. Part XVII names English the Associate Official language for official purposes alongside Hindi, and the Official Languages Act, 1963 gave it continuing official status.

questions.question: How many vowel sounds are represented in IPA for English?
questions.answer: Twenty vowel phonemes — twelve monophthongs (pure vowels) and eight diphthongs. Together with the twenty-four consonant phonemes this gives English forty-four phonemes in all, as shown in the IPA chart.

questions.question: Name the suprasegmental features of English language.
questions.answer: Stress (word and sentence stress), rhythm, intonation, juncture or pausing, and linking. These are features that work over a stretch of speech longer than a single phoneme, and they carry as much meaning as the sounds do.

questions.question: Put an appropriate prefix for the words: -write, -connect.
questions.answer: re- gives rewrite ('to write again'), and dis- gives disconnect ('to undo the connection'). A prefix is placed before the root and modifies its meaning, but it never changes the part of speech.

questions.question: Write two synonyms for the word 'small'.
questions.answer: Little and tiny. 'Little' is the everyday word and is often used affectionately, while 'tiny' carries the extra suggestion of a very small size, as in a tiny insect.

questions.question: Frame a sentence using the phrasal verb 'look after'.
questions.answer: She looks after her younger brother every evening after school. Here 'look after' is a clausal phrasal verb meaning 'to take care of'.

questions.question: Write the antonym for the word 'hot'.
questions.answer: Cold. Hot and cold are complementary antonyms — they are strictly opposite in meaning, with no middle ground between the two of them.

questions.question: Write true or false: 'Miscue analysis is used to assess a reader's oral reading errors.'
questions.answer: False. Miscue analysis is used to examine errors made in silent reading, since it is there that the reader's decoding strategy is visible. Oral reading is better assessed by running records and by reading aloud.

questions.question: Write the full form of IPA.
questions.answer: IPA stands for the International Phonetic Alphabet — a single agreed set of symbols that removes the ambiguities of ordinary English spelling and shows how a word is actually pronounced.

questions.question: Define function word.
questions.answer: A function word is a grammatical word that expresses a relationship between other words rather than carrying meaning of its own, such as the, in, is or and. Function words belong to the closed classes.

questions.question: How many diphthongs are there in English sound system?
questions.answer: Eight diphthongs: /eɪ/, /aɪ/, /ɔɪ/, /aʊ/, /əʊ/, /ɪə/, /eə/ and /ʊə/. Each is a glide in quality from one vowel to another within a single syllable, as in face, time, boy, cow, go, near, hair and tour.

questions.question: Mention the categories of vocabulary.
questions.answer: Lexical, phrasal and clausal. Lexical vocabulary consists of single content words and compounds; phrasal vocabulary of fixed multi-word phrases with no clause structure; clausal vocabulary of multi-word units that do have a subject and a predicate.

questions.question: Name the suprasegmental features.
questions.answer: Word stress, sentence stress, rhythm, intonation, juncture (pausing) and linking. They operate over stretches of speech rather than over single sounds, and a change in one of them can change the meaning of an utterance.

questions.question: Put an appropriate prefix for the words: -activate, -close.
questions.answer: de- gives deactivate ('to stop something being active'), and en- gives enclose ('to close something in'). The prefix changes the meaning but keeps the word a verb in both cases.

questions.question: Write two synonyms for the word "create".
questions.answer: Make and produce. 'Make' is the plainer word and is preferred in speech; 'produce' suggests bringing something into existence by a planned process.

questions.question: Frame a sentence using the phrasal verb "break into".
questions.answer: The children broke into the room laughing and holding a bundle of papers. Here 'break into' means 'to enter suddenly', often with a group.

questions.question: Write two words with the suffix 'ness'.
questions.answer: Kindness and darkness. The suffix -ness usually forms an abstract noun — the state or quality of being something — so happy gives happiness and dark gives darkness.

questions.question: Write two words with the suffix 'ment'.
questions.answer: Agreement and movement. The suffix -ment also forms abstract nouns: it turns the verbs agree and move into the nouns agreement and movement.

questions.question: Write two words with the prefix 'inter'.
questions.answer: International and interchange. The prefix inter- means 'between' or 'among', so international means 'between nations' and interchange means 'to exchange between two persons'.

questions.question: Frame a sentence using the phrasal verb- 'goes out'.
questions.answer: The lamp goes out at nine, and the whole hall falls silent. Here 'go out' is a phrasal verb meaning 'to be extinguished' or 'to stop burning'.

questions.question: Frame a sentence using the idiom - 'feel under the weather'.
questions.answer: I have been feeling under the weather since yesterday. The idiom means 'unwell' or 'slightly ill', and its meaning cannot be worked out from the words under and weather.

questions.question: Write two synonyms for- 'cold'.
questions.answer: Chilly and cool. 'Chilly' describes a temperature that makes one shiver, while 'cool' suggests a pleasantly mild temperature rather than an extreme one.

questions.question: Write the full form of IPA.
questions.answer: International Phonetic Alphabet. It gives one agreed symbol for each English phoneme, which is why we can write /ʃiːp/ and know at once that the word is sheep and not ship.

questions.question: How many pure vowels are there in English sound system.
questions.answer: Twelve pure vowels, or monophthongs. They are plotted in a quadrilateral by height and backness: /iː/, /ɪ/, /e/, /æ/, /ə/, /ɜː/, /ʌ/, /uː/, /ʊ/, /ɔː/, /ɒ/ and /ɑː/.

questions.question: Put appropriate suffixes for the words: (i) manage (ii) faith.
questions.answer: (i) manage + -ment = management. (ii) faith + -ful = faithful. A suffix goes at the end of a word and usually decides its part of speech — here both answers are nouns.

questions.question: Construct sentences using the following phrases/idioms (any two): (i) Out and out (ii) Raining cats and dogs (iii) Look into.
questions.answer:
(i) Out and out — He is out and out the best player in our school team.
(ii) Raining cats and dogs — It was raining cats and dogs when we reached the tea estate, and the road turned to mud.
(iii) Look into — The teacher looked into the problem of absent children and found that most of them had no shoes in the monsoon.

questions.question: Put appropriate prefix for the words: (i) Happy (ii) Possible.
questions.answer: (i) un- gives unhappy ('not happy'). (ii) im- gives impossible ('not possible'). In both cases the prefix reverses the meaning of the root without changing its part of speech.

questions.question: Construct sentences using the following phrasal verbs (any two): (i) Look after (ii) Switch off (iii) Bring forth (iv) Show up.
questions.answer:
(i) Look after — She looks after her younger brother every evening.
(ii) Switch off — Please switch off the fan when you leave the classroom.
(iii) Bring forth — The teacher brought forth an old map of Assam to show where the old kingdoms lay.
(iv) Show up — Half the class did not show up for the Sunday remedial class.

questions.question: Name the supra-segmental features.
questions.answer: Stress, rhythm, intonation, juncture and linking. They are supra-segmental because they are not carried by a single phoneme but by a stretch of speech — the whole word, phrase or utterance.

questions.question: Write the full form of IPA.
questions.answer: The International Phonetic Alphabet. It was devised so that the sounds of any language could be written down unambiguously, with one symbol standing for one phoneme and the angle brackets [ ] marking physical sounds.

questions.question: How many pure vowels are there in the English sound system?
questions.answer: Twelve. These pure vowels, or monophthongs, keep one steady vowel quality throughout; the remaining eight vowels of English are diphthongs, which glide from one quality to another.

questions.question: Define function words.
questions.answer: Function words are the grammatical words of English — pronouns, articles, determiners, prepositions, conjunctions, auxiliaries, modals and negative particles — which express relationships such as time, number, cause and contrast rather than content.

questions.question: Mention the categories of vocabulary.
questions.answer: Three categories: lexical vocabulary (single content words and compounds), phrasal vocabulary (fixed idiomatic phrases) and clausal vocabulary (multi-word units that contain a subject and a predicate, such as look after).

questions.question: Put appropriate suffix for - begin, intern.
questions.answer: begin + -ning gives beginning, and intern + -ment gives internment. Both -ning and -ment form nouns here, which is the usual work of a suffix.

questions.question: Write two synonyms for the word - "beautiful".
questions.answer: Lovely and attractive. 'Lovely' carries a warm, approving feeling and is common in speech about scenery and people, while 'attractive' is the plainer word of approval.

questions.question: Construct sentences using the following phrasal verbs (any two): Bring up, Put away, Look into, Back out.
questions.answer:
(i) Bring up — She was brought up in a village near Dibrugarh and speaks fluent Assamese and Hindi.
(ii) Put away — Put your books away when the bell rings, please.
(iii) Look into — The head teacher looked into the complaint and promised an answer within a week.
(iv) Back out — He backed out of the race at the last moment because his leg was still sore.

questions.question: Construct sentences using the following idioms (any two): A piece of cake, Under the weather, Green fingers, Raining cats and dogs.
questions.answer:
(i) A piece of cake — The whole exercise was a piece of cake for the Class IV children.
(ii) Under the weather — Our head teacher is under the weather today, so the assembly has been cancelled.
(iii) Green fingers — My aunt has green fingers; her mustard plants crop even in winter.
(iv) Raining cats and dogs — Outside it is raining cats and dogs, and the children have been stuck in the classroom since morning.

questions.question: What is NEP 2020's stance on English as a medium of instruction in schools?
questions.answer: NEP 2020 does not reject English; it refuses to let English displace the language of the child's own life at the stage when the child is still learning to read. An English-medium or Indian-language-medium environment may be provided from the foundational stage wherever possible, but the mother tongue or the local/regional language must remain the medium at least till Grade 5 and preferably till Grade 8. English therefore enters early as a subject, a bridge and a link language, not as a replacement for the medium.

questions.question: Describe the importance of a language rich classroom?
questions.answer: A language-rich classroom is not one where the teacher talks a great deal of English. It is one in which the density of meaningful language that children hear, use and have to think in is high, across the whole day and across every subject. Such a classroom has print on the walls, talk in every subject, dialogue instead of recitation, and language used to get real things done. New words are met before they are needed, and home languages are honoured for thinking and drafting, so that no child is taught that the language in his head is worthless.

questions.question: Write the difference between intensive and extensive reading?
questions.answer: Intensive reading is close, slow and careful reading of a short, difficult text to extract all of its meaning — vocabulary, structure, argument, tone and the writer's attitude — with frequent re-reading and dictionary use. Extensive reading is wide, rapid and largely uninterrupted reading of many easy texts, undertaken for fluency, vocabulary growth and the sheer habit of reading. A poem analysed line by line each week is intensive; a class library of graded readers is extensive.

questions.question: Define function words with examples.
questions.answer: A function word is a grammatical word that expresses a relationship between other words rather than meaning of its own. In 'She has put the book on the table', she is a pronoun, has an auxiliary, the an article, on a preposition. The closed classes — pronouns, articles, determiners, prepositions, conjunctions, auxiliaries, modals and negative particles — number only about 100 to 150 items, make up half of all running text, and are picked up by absorption rather than memorised.

questions.question: How do role-playing activities enhance language learning in a contextual setting?
questions.answer: Role play puts English to work inside a situation the children can actually see, so the language stays in memory in a way a grammar drill does not. A child acting out a complaint to the head teacher must use the exact phrases the situation demands and must adjust them when the partner does not understand. It also forces shy speakers to take a turn and fluent speakers to listen. Afterwards I note which chunks the class needed and drill only those.

questions.question: Distinguish between extensive reading and intensive reading.
questions.answer: Extensive reading aims at fluency, speed, volume and the habit of reading; the learner chooses many easy texts and reads them fast without stopping. Intensive reading aims at accuracy and depth; the text is short, difficult and carefully chosen, and the reader re-reads, consults a dictionary and analyses the language itself. In outcome terms, extensive reading is measured by how much is read and by the willingness to continue, while intensive reading is measured by close analysis and a written product.

questions.question: Distinguish between scanning and skimming.
questions.answer: Skimming is reading fast to get the general idea of a text without stopping at unfamiliar words. The eyes move in a zig-zag, taking in the first line of each paragraph, the headings and the last line; the reader leaves with the topic, the organisation and the main point. Scanning is searching for one specific item — a date, a name, a price, a number. The eyes move in a straight line down a column and the search stops the moment the item is found.

questions.question: Design an activity to develop listening skill.
questions.answer: I use the 'thrice-listened' announcement activity. First I play a thirty-second railway-style announcement once and ask only global questions: what is this about, and is the speaker giving information or making a request? I play it again for selective listening — what time, which platform, what change. Third time I ask detail questions: why was the train delayed. Between rounds I signal the boundaries and the key words on the board. Each pass has one job, so no child is lost for the whole minute.

questions.question: Explain language as a means of communication and thought.
questions.answer: Language does two jobs at once. As a means of communication, it lets one person share an idea or a feeling with another. As a means of thought, it lets a person work inside an idea — a child who has no word for 'compare' cannot easily hold two objects side by side and judge between them. This is why education is limited by the conceptual resources of the language it is done in, and why the medium of instruction is a pedagogical question and not merely an administrative one.

questions.question: State three language formula.
questions.answer: The three-language formula, introduced by the National Policy on Education 1968, requires every child to learn three languages: the mother tongue or regional language; a language of the 'other' regional group or another Indian language; and English or a foreign language. NEP 2020 restates it as the home or local language, the regional or another Indian language, and a foreign or additional language, with English often placed in the third slot or introduced early as a bridge.

questions.question: Differentiate between open word classes and closed word classes.
questions.answer: The distinction is how readily new members can be added. Closed (function) classes are finite and fixed — about 100 to 150 items across pronouns, articles, determiners, prepositions, conjunctions, auxiliaries, modals and negative particles — and no new ones can be coined; they express grammatical relationships. Open (lexical or content) classes have no known limit and grow daily by derivation, compounding and borrowing; they are the nouns, verbs, adjectives and adverbs that carry the content of the message.

questions.question: Mention two benefits of loud reading.
questions.answer: First, it forces the reader to pronounce rather than to guess: because the voice must actually produce the word, wrong sounds, wrong stress and ignored punctuation all surface at once, and sentence stress and phrasing come under the reader's own control. Second, it makes the text public, so the whole class hears and discusses the same passage together and can compare how different readers gave it voice — which is where suprasegmental awareness begins.

questions.question: Examples of two closed word and two open word.
questions.answer: Closed word classes: 'the' (article), 'in' (preposition), 'because' (conjunction), 'have' (auxiliary). Open word classes: 'river' (noun), 'write' (verb), 'silent' (adjective), 'carefully' (adverb). The closed classes are a fixed set of about 100 to 150 words and no new one can be coined; the open classes can be added to every single day.

questions.question: Write two homophones and two homonyms.
questions.answer: Homophones share the sound but not the meaning: pair /peə/ and pear /peə/; two /tuː/ and too /tuː/. Homonyms share both form and general area of meaning, but differ in sense: the bark of a tree and the bark of a dog; a school as an institution and a school of fish. A quick test: if the pronunciation can be predicted from the meaning, it is a homonym.

questions.question: Write a short note on (any three, 2 marks each): (a) Three language formula, (b) Skimming and scanning, (c) Miscue analysis, (d) Intonation, (e) Use of dictionary.
questions.answer:
(a) Three-language formula
Introduced by NPE 1968, it asks every child to learn the mother tongue or regional language; a language of the 'other' regional group; and English or a foreign language. NEP 2020 restates it as the home or local language, the regional or another Indian language, and a foreign or additional language. It is a policy of the education system, not of the Constitution, and it makes English one language among three rather than the sole gateway.

(b) Skimming and scanning
Skimming is fast reading for the general idea, the eyes taking in headings, the first line of each paragraph and the last line, without stopping at unfamiliar words. It is done before a test and in the first ten seconds with any new text. Scanning is a much narrower search for one specific item — a date, a name, a price, a number — with the eyes moving down a column and stopping the moment the item is found. One lesson can teach both: skim a paragraph for its main idea, then scan it for five hidden items.

(c) Miscue analysis
A miscue is a reading error that reveals the strategy the reader is using: reading house as 'hose' shows decoding by shape; saying 'beau-ti-ful' shows syllable chopping on the way to blending; reading 'ship' for 'sheep' shows the first language's vowel system at work. The teacher collects the miscue, identifies the strategy, judges whether it is productive or non-productive, and intervenes. The goal is self-correction, not a clean page.

(d) Intonation
Intonation is the melody of pitch movement over a stretch of speech, and it does three jobs: it marks a boundary, it marks grammatical role, and it signals attitude. Four patterns cover almost all classroom speech — fall (statement, certain), rise (yes/no question, offer), fall–rise (sharing information, checking) and rise–fall (warning, insistence). 'You are coming.' with a fall is a fact; the same words with a rise are a question.

(e) Use of dictionary
A dictionary is a reference tool, not a crutch to be used on every word. The habit to build is: read to the end of the clause, decide whether context settles the meaning, then look up only what matters. A good dictionary entry gives the headword, the part of speech and numbered senses, so the reader chooses the sense that fits. The companion tools are the thesaurus, the encyclopaedia and the internet, used in that order and always judged against context.

questions.question: Define Phoneme.
questions.answer: A phoneme is the smallest unit of sound in a language that can change the meaning of a word. Two sounds count as different phonemes only if substituting one for the other produces a different word — hence the minimal pairs ship /ʃɪp/ and sheep /ʃiːp/. The phoneme is thus an abstract contrastive unit, whereas the phone is the actual sound a speaker produces, which varies with accent and context.

questions.question: Define local comprehension.
questions.answer: Local comprehension is work at the level of the word, the phrase and the sentence: the literal meaning, the reference of a pronoun, the relation between subject and verb, the connotation of a word and the meaning of an idiom. Its questions are of the form 'What does this word mean here?' and 'What does the pronoun it stand for?' A child can be perfect at local comprehension and still miss the point of a paragraph, which is a failure at the global level.

questions.question: Differentiate between intensive reading and extensive reading.
questions.answer: Intensive reading is narrow, slow and analytic; it is done on a short, difficult, carefully chosen text, with re-reading and dictionary use, and it is judged by depth of response and close analysis. Extensive reading is broad, fast and uninterrupted; it is done on many easy, often self-selected texts, with little re-reading, and it is judged by volume read, reading rate and the willingness to continue. A class that reads four easy texts a week is doing extensive reading.

questions.question: Describe the process of critical reading.
questions.answer: Critical reading is a staged process. Before reading, the reader settles the purpose, activates prior knowledge and predicts from the title and headings, producing a prediction and a list of questions. While reading, the reader marks up the text, monitors comprehension at each paragraph end and asks what claim is being made and on what grounds. After reading, the reader reconstructs the argument in one's own words, evaluates it through the four lenses — concepts, soundness of argument, assumptions and tradition — and responds in a suitable form.

questions.question: Write briefly about three language formula.
questions.answer: The three-language formula is the policy, first given its canonical form in NPE 1968 and reiterated in NPE 1985, that every child learns three languages: the mother tongue or regional language, a language of the 'other' regional group, and English or a foreign language. NEP 2020 reframes the three as the home or local language, the regional or another Indian language, and a foreign or additional language. Its purpose is to keep English within reach without letting it crowd out the child's first language.

questions.question: Describe strategies to teach different categories of vocabulary OR Discuss the role of the teacher to enhance active vocabulary of the students.
questions.answer: I teach the three categories in three different ways. Lexical vocabulary is extended through roots, affixes and topic banks: a word family tree from one root, and a picture bank on 'clothes' or 'farming' for the topic words. Phrasal vocabulary is taught through situation, picture and story, so that under the weather arrives attached to a picture of a pale child rather than as a definition. Clausal vocabulary is taught through example sentences and contrast within the family — turn down the radio against turn it down — and every new chunk is rehearsed until it is automatic.

questions.question: Write short notes on (2 marks each): (a) Three-language Formula, (b) Language-rich classroom, (c) Reading for global comprehension.
questions.answer:
(a) Three-language Formula
A policy of the education system rather than of the Constitution, introduced by NPE 1968 and reiterated in NPE 1985. Every child is to learn the mother tongue or regional language; a language of the 'other' regional group; and English or a foreign language. NEP 2020 restates the three as the home or local language, the regional or another Indian language, and a foreign or additional language, with English often in the third slot or introduced early as a bridge. Its purpose is additive multilingualism: the child ends up with more languages, not fewer.

(b) Language-rich classroom
Not a classroom in which the teacher speaks a great deal of English, but one in which the density of meaningful language children hear, use and think in is high, across the day and across the subjects. Its marks are print in the environment, talk in every subject, dialogue instead of recitation, language used to get real purposes done, vocabulary pre-taught before it is needed, and home languages honoured for thinking and drafting.

(c) Reading for global comprehension
Work on the text as a whole rather than word by word: its purpose, its structure, its main idea, its tone, its genre and the writer's implied attitude. Its questions are 'What is the main point of this paragraph?', 'Why has the writer put this example here?' and 'Which of these headings would the writer accept?' It is worth teaching separately because a child can read every sentence correctly and still miss the whole point of the paragraph.

questions.question: Design an interactive oral discourse on any one: (a) Telephonic conversation to invite someone for a family function, (b) Discussing about today's weather, (c) Seeking information regarding availability of bus seats at ticket counter.
questions.answer:
Since all three are worth preparing, here are working models of each. I would rehearse them in pairs, record one, and have the students transcribe their own recording to see what they actually said.

(a) Telephonic conversation — inviting someone to a family function
A: Good morning. May I speak to Mrs Barua, please?
B: Speaking. Good morning, who is it?
A: My name is Hemen. I am ringing from Guwahati. Is this a convenient moment?
B: Yes, Hemen, go ahead.
A: The 21st is free for you, and we are expecting you at my sister's wedding.
B: That is very good of you. What time should we leave?
A: The marriage is at eleven, but do come by ten.
B: We shall be there by half past nine. Is there anything we should bring?
A: Nothing at all. We will arrange everything.
B: Then thank you for the invitation. Goodbye.
A: Goodbye, and a safe journey.

(b) Discussing today's weather
A: The sun is beating down today, isn't it?
B: Yes, and there is not a cloud in the sky. It is the hottest day this season.
A: The wind is blowing from the east, so it may turn cloudy by evening.
B: I hope not. We have a match on the ground this afternoon.

(c) At the ticket counter
Passenger: Good morning. Do you have a bus to Dibrugarh at four this afternoon?
Clerk: Yes, one on platform six.
Passenger: How many seats are still available?
Clerk: Six window seats and a few in the middle.
Passenger: Then two tickets, please. What is the fare?
Clerk: Three hundred and fifty rupees each.
Passenger: Can I pay by card?
Clerk: Certainly. May I see your card, please?

questions.question: Describe the process of critical reading.
questions.answer: Critical reading is staged. Before, the reader settles the purpose, activates what he already knows and predicts from the title and headings. While, he reads actively — underlining claims, boxing examples, marking doubts, and pausing at each paragraph end to ask what has happened and why it was placed there. After, he makes three moves: reconstruct the argument in his own words, evaluate it through the four lenses, and respond in a form suited to the text. Fifteen minutes of this record is a piece of critical reading.

questions.question: Elaborate on the differences between skimming and scanning.
questions.answer: The difference is one of purpose, eye movement and stopping. Skimming serves the purpose of getting the shape of a text; the eyes move in a zig-zag and take in headings, the first line of each paragraph and the last line, sweeping over everything else, so unfamiliar words are passed by rather than looked up. Scanning serves the purpose of finding one item; the eyes move in a straight line down a column, the rest of the page is ignored, and the search stops the instant the item is found. The first ten seconds with any new text want a skim; a timetable wants a scan.

questions.question: Design an activity to teach homonyms to the students at the elementary level.
questions.answer: I use a picture-card sort. I draw or paste six pictures and write the same word at the head of each pair — bark, school, match, bat, ring, spring. Children first say the word aloud, so they hear the shared pronunciation, and then sort the cards by meaning, putting a circle round the two senses in each group. Then I give one sentence for each sense, and a pair of sentences for the class to fill in. The rule I leave them with: same spelling, same sound, same general area of meaning, different sense.
