questions.question: How will you increase the vocabulary of your students?
questions.answer: I meet words before they are needed — five new words with pictures and gesture before a story, then each word used three times in the same day. I extend them through roots, so one root gives a family of words, and through topic banks of twenty high-frequency words with pictures on a word wall. I insist on use rather than definition: the word must appear in the child's own sentence that day. And I read aloud to the class every day, because vocabulary grows by exposure and by context, not by lists.

questions.question: Explain the process of critical reading.
questions.answer:
Critical reading is not a flash of insight at the end of a text; it is a staged process, and the staging is what makes it teachable. It moves through three stages.

- Before reading: build a frame. What kind of text is this, who wrote it, for whom, when and why? What do I already believe about the topic, and what am I reading for? The purpose — gist, argument, fact or pleasure — decides the strategy. The product is a prediction and a list of questions.
- While reading: read actively, marking up and monitoring. Underline the claims, box the examples, put a question mark beside what is not understood, and pause at each paragraph end to ask what has just happened and why it was placed there.
- After reading: reconstruct, evaluate and respond. Put the book down and write the argument in your own words, then test its concepts, the soundness of the argument, its assumptions and the tradition it belongs to, and finish by saying what you think.

That last move is the one that proves the reading was critical.

questions.question: Describe the process of critical reading.
questions.answer:
Reading critically means holding a text at a distance and asking questions of it that a reader does not normally ask. The process has three stages, and each produces something on paper.

1. Before reading — set a purpose and activate prior knowledge. Skim the title, the headings and the first paragraph, and form a frame: this text is probably about water, because the heading says so and I know water freezes at zero.
2. While reading — read actively. Mark up the text, monitor your comprehension paragraph by paragraph, and keep a running question list. Notice which words are doing the work of persuasion and what has been left out.
3. After reading — reconstruct, evaluate, respond. Write the argument in your own words and check it against the text. Then apply the four lenses: the concepts taken for granted, the soundness of the argument, the assumptions, and the tradition the text belongs to.

Take a chapter on saving water. It argues that small habits will help, but it attaches no figure to a leaking tap, so the claim cannot be checked. That record is critical reading.

questions.question: Design an interactive oral discourse on any one: (a) Seeking information about availability of tickets at ticket counter of movie hall, (b) Telephonic conversation to invite friend to birthday party.
questions.answer:
(a) At the ticket counter of a movie hall

Roles: the customer and the clerk. Aim: to buy two tickets for an evening show.

Customer: Good evening. Two tickets for the 6 p.m. show, please.
Clerk: Which film, sir?
Customer: The new thriller on Hall 2.
Clerk: Balcony or ordinary? Ordinary is one hundred and twenty rupees; balcony is two hundred.
Customer: Ordinary, please. Are any seats available near the centre?
Clerk: Rows F and G are almost full. Row E has a few.
Customer: Then two in row E. Is the show uncut?
Clerk: Yes, the complete version.
Customer: Here is the money. Thank you.
Clerk: Thank you. Please be seated by 5.50.

The exchange is interactive because it has a real purpose, a small negotiation over choice and price, and a polite closing.

(b) Inviting a friend to a birthday party on the telephone

Roles: the host and the invited friend.

Host: Hello, is that Ritu? Meera speaking. How are you?
Ritu: Fine, Meera. And you?
Host: Fine, thank you. I am ringing about my birthday on Sunday. Can you come?
Ritu: Oh, happy birthday! What time should I come?
Host: By four in the afternoon. We are having cake-cutting at half past four in the college auditorium.
Ritu: I would love to. Will you need any help?
Host: You could bring the fruit juice, if you do not mind.
Ritu: Not at all. I will get two bottles. Anything else?
Host: No, that is everything. See you on Sunday, then.
Ritu: See you, Meera. Bye.

Both are rehearsed first and then performed, and in the telephone version the pair sits back to back, so listening and clarification are genuinely exercised.

questions.question: Explain importance of English as a global language.
questions.answer:
English is the most widely learned second language in history, and its importance rests on three things rather than on its size alone.

First, it is the working language of the world. It carries the proceedings of the United Nations, most scientific publishing, international aviation, the internet and a large share of world entertainment. A researcher in Assam whose work is to be read outside India needs it, not because her science is provincial, but because the journals in that field publish in English.

Second, it is a bridge. Inside India it links Assamese, Bodo, Mising and the other languages to one another; outside India it links India to the world. That is its place under the three-language formula and under NEP 2020 — a link and bridge language, not a replacement for the mother tongue.

Third, it carries economic value: job notices in Guwahati and in Bengaluru both ask for good English.

But there is a catch worth stating. The same global role can do harm if English is allowed to displace the language a child thinks in. As a teacher I would keep both — the home language builds the child, English opens the door outward.

questions.question: Describe various ways that you will adopt to increase vocabulary of your students.
questions.answer:
Vocabulary grows by exposure, context and use, not by being taught as a list of definitions. I would work on it in six ways.

1. Build the environment. A word wall of twenty high-frequency words with pictures, labelled classroom objects, and displays of the children's own writing, so that words are met all day and not in one period.
2. Pre-teach before the need arises. Five difficult words taught with pictures, objects and gesture before the story, each used three times on the same day.
3. Extend through roots and affixes. A family tree from one root (port to import, export, transport, portable) turns one known word into five. Suffixes too, since they show what kind of word it is.
4. Teach in blocks and in company: topic banks such as clothes or farming with pictures, and collocations — make a decision, make an effort, make friends.
5. Use the English around the school: signboards, bus tickets, medicine labels, weather forecasts.
6. Give the language a purpose. A class newspaper, a market survey and role play at the canteen make words something children need in order to finish a task.

I would also keep a record of which words each child has actually used, since recognised vocabulary always outruns used vocabulary.

questions.question: Explain briefly why is English used as a global language.
questions.answer:
Several conditions came together to make English global, and none alone would have been enough.

- History. English spread with traders and settlers across several continents, and later through a colonial empire that gave it administration, law and schooling in much of the world. It was left behind on the ground when that empire went.
- Numbers and economics. It has the largest mother-tongue population of any language after Chinese, and the economic weight of the United States and of international business reinforced it well after the colonial period.
- It is comparatively easy to learn. English has little inflection, no tone of meaning and a small set of verb forms, and it is regular in spelling more often than most languages.
- Science and the internet. Scientific publishing settled in English for practical reasons, and the internet inherited that settlement.
- Adoption by others. It is used by African, South-East Asian and South American speakers who had no colonial stake in it at all and who chose it for their own reasons.

These advantages are practical, not moral. Nothing about them makes the home language dispensable.

questions.question: Write a news report on celebration of Sports week in your institute.
questions.answer:
SPORTS WEEK ENDS ON A HIGH NOTE

Guwahati, 12 March: The annual Sports Week of the institute, held from 6 to 12 March, closed on Saturday with a colour of the field procession and the presentation of trophies.

The week opened on Monday with the flag hoisting and an oath taken by nearly four hundred students and teacher-trainees. Events on the following days included the 100-metre sprint, long jump, shot put, tug-of-war, a football tournament and a relay race. Students of the Assamese, English and Hindi departments entered in six teams each.

The football final drew the largest crowd. The Assamese department beat the English department by two goals to one, the winner coming in the last four minutes. The tug-of-war was drawn at first and had to be repeated.

Presenting the trophies, the principal, Dr R. K. Das, said that sport and study are not rivals, and that a student who has learnt to work in a team has learnt something a textbook cannot give. Individual champions received medals and the winning team was handed a rolling trophy.

Staff, parents and former students attended. The institute will hold its inter-college meet next year.

questions.question: Imagine you are cultural secretary of your institute, draft a notice for a fancy dress competition.
questions.answer:

Sd/-

questions.question: Design one activity to improve the vocabulary of students studying at elementary stage.
questions.answer:
Activity: The Five Word Day

Aim: children learn five new words properly and use each of them at least three times in the same day.

Material: five word cards, a chart ruled into five columns, picture cut-outs from old magazines, coloured pencils.

Procedure:
1. Before the lesson, I choose five words from the story to be read that day. I say each word aloud, show the picture and act it out where the word allows it, and let the class repeat. No definition is given; the word is attached to its situation.
2. I write the five words vertically on the chart and place the pictures beside them.
3. During the day, every time a child uses one of the words in speech or writing, that column is ticked. Children may tick their own.
4. At the end of the day each child picks one word from the chart and draws it.

Follow-up: the chart stays on the wall and the same five words are met again on the next two days. Three encounters in real contexts, rather than thirty in a list, is what makes a word stick.

The teacher's record of which words each child actually used is more useful than any test, because it shows productive vocabulary, not merely recognised vocabulary.

questions.question: Design an oral discourse on any one: (a) Seeking information about availability of seats at ISBT, (b) Telephonic conversation to order food.
questions.answer:
(a) At the ISBT counter

Roles: a passenger and the enquiry clerk. Aim: to find whether a bus is available and to book a seat.

Passenger: Excuse me, could you tell me whether a bus to Dibrugarh leaves in the evening?
Clerk: Yes. There is one at 5.30 p.m. from Bayanagar.
Passenger: Are seats available?
Clerk: About twenty, but the last ten are window seats only.
Passenger: Could I get two window seats?
Clerk: Certainly. I will enter them on the 5.30 service.
Passenger: What is the fare?
Clerk: Three hundred and forty rupees each. The journey takes nine hours.
Passenger: Here is the money. Where should I board?
Clerk: Platform 4. Please report by 5.00 p.m. with a photo identity card.

The learner handles a polite opening, a noun request, a modal question and a confirmation — the whole range of counter discourse in seven turns.

(b) Ordering food on the telephone

Roles: a customer and the staff of a restaurant.

Caller: Good evening. Is that the Green Leaf Restaurant?
Staff: Yes, speaking. What can I do for you?
Caller: I would like to order two vegetable cutlets and a bowl of chicken soup for delivery.
Staff: Certainly. Anything to drink?
Caller: Two bottles of lemon soda, please, and one mineral water.
Staff: Let me repeat that back: two cutlets, one soup, two lemon sodas and one mineral water.
Caller: That is correct.
Staff: The total is four hundred and twenty rupees. It will take about thirty minutes.
Caller: Send it to Flat 3B, Sunrise Apartments, near the petrol pump, please.
Staff: Noted. Pay the delivery boy on arrival.
Caller: On arrival, then. And make one of the cutlets extra spicy.
Staff: I have marked it. Thank you for calling.

questions.question: First language facilitates the learning of second language in the Indian context. Discuss.
questions.answer:
In the Indian classroom the first language does not obstruct English; it carries it. This is why NCF 2005 and NEP 2020 keep the mother tongue as the medium at least till Grade 5, preferably till Grade 8, and make English a link and bridge language.

Three reasons explain the facilitation.

- Thinking comes first in the first language. A child who has no word for compare in the language she thinks in cannot easily hold two objects side by side and judge between them. New concepts attach to words the child already owns.
- Skills transfer. Reading strategy, spelling, sentence order and the habit of holding a pencil are learned in the mother tongue and can be practised in English. Only the vocabulary and the sound system have to be learned afresh.
- Learning becomes possible. A child who understands the question can answer, guess, risk a wrong word and be corrected. Rejecting a correct answer given in Assamese teaches the child that the language in which she thinks is worthless.

There is a gain as well: an English word taught from an Assamese or Bodo base carries a reference the learner already owns. The policy word for all this is additive multilingualism — more languages, not fewer.

questions.question: Elucidate some measures to organise a language rich classroom.
questions.answer:
Language richness is not the amount of English the teacher speaks; it is the density of meaningful language children hear, use and think in across the day. I would organise it in six ways.

1. Print in the environment. An English word wall of twenty high-frequency words with pictures, labelled classroom objects, and displays of the children's own writing.
2. Talk in every subject. Before a child may hold up an object, I require an explanation in words; before every written answer, a think-pair-share.
3. Dialogue, not recitation. A question box in the corner, assigned roles, and four question stems taught as sentence frames on the table.
4. Language for real purposes. A class newspaper, a lost-and-found announcement, a request letter to the head teacher, a survey of the vegetable market.
5. Explicit vocabulary work. Five words pre-taught with pictures and gesture before a story, each used three times the same day.
6. Every language honoured. Children may explain first in their home language and then in English, and displays are labelled in both.

The test is simple: is there something the children want to say today, and does using English help them say it?

questions.question: Elucidate the differences between mother-tongue and the second language.
questions.answer:
The difference lies in the place the language holds in a child's life, not in its worth.

Aspect | Mother tongue (L1) | Second language (L2)
Where acquired | At home, before school | In the classroom, from books and media
Domain of use | Home, worship, market, inner speech | School, shop, office, news, further study
Level of skill | Fluent and automatic | Effortful; correctness is worked for
Learner's attitude | Unselfconscious | Valued, but treated as a subject rather than a resource
Typical errors | Very few | Sound substitution from the first system; over-generalised grammar
Teacher's stance | Respect and use; never punished as a wrong medium | A bridge, taught with support in the first language

The two systems also interact. A learner who meets very, zoo, ship and measure is hearing sounds Assamese does not contrast, and the substitution is a strategy rather than carelessness. The mother tongue does not disappear either; it remains the language in which the child plans. What the school adds is a second language, and the child who leaves with both has gained, not lost.

questions.question: Describe how language serves as a means of communication and thought.
questions.answer:
Language does two jobs at once, and a teacher has to know both.

As a means of communication, it lets one person share an idea or a feeling with another. Without it, teaching falls back on demonstration and imitation; the child can copy a gesture but cannot be told why.

As a means of thinking, it is far more powerful, because it lets a person work inside an idea at all. A child with no word for compare cannot easily hold two objects side by side and judge between them; a child with no word for because cannot hold a cause and its effect together. Concepts are held in words, and so is reasoning itself.

The consequence for education is large. Education is limited by the conceptual apparatus of the language in which it is done, which is why the medium of instruction is a policy question and not only an administrative one. A Class III group speaking Assamese, Mising and Bodo cannot be taught well in a language none of them thinks in.

This is why I hold to additive multilingualism: the child thinks in Assamese and adds English, rather than trading one for the other.

questions.question: Define monophthongs. Provide examples. [4 Marks]
questions.answer:
A monophthong is a pure vowel sound — a vowel phoneme produced with a single, fixed mouth position, without any glide away from it. The word itself means "one sound" (mono = one, phthong = sound), and it marks the difference between the two kinds of vowel English has: the twelve pure vowels on one side, and the eight gliding vowels or diphthongs on the other. A diphthong such as /eɪ/ in face or /aʊ/ in house moves from one vowel quality to another inside a single syllable; a monophthong stays put. English has 44 phonemes in all — 24 consonants and 20 vowels — and 12 of those vowels are monophthongs.

The twelve, with a model word for each:
- Close vowels: /iː/ sheep, /ɪ/ ship, /uː/ food, /ʊ/ full
- Close-mid and open-mid vowels: /e/ bed, /æ/ bad, /ɜː/ girl, /ʌ/ cup, /ɔː/ door
- Open vowels: /ɒ/ cot, /ɑː/ father
- The central vowel: /ə/ as in about, banana, teacher

These twelve are arranged on a quadrilateral chart by two dimensions — height (close to open) and backness (front to back) — and this is how they are written in the International Phonetic Alphabet. Two of them, /æ/ and /ɑː/, are peculiar to English: no other language in the world has them, and an Assamese-medium child meets both of them for the first time in "cat" and "father".

The practical reason for teaching them as a set is contrast, because a phoneme is defined not by its sound but by the difference it makes. Monophthongs are therefore best learned through minimal pairs: ship–sheep tests vowel length, bad–bed tests vowel frontness, cot–caught tests lip-rounding. A child who can hold those distinctions apart will read words accurately; a child who has merely learned "a letter for the vowel" will guess from the shape of the print and be wrong whenever the guess fails.

questions.question: A blood donation camp is being organised in your institute. Write a notice inviting students and teachers to donate blood, mentioning the date, time and venue of the camp. [4 Marks]
questions.answer:
A model notice would run like this.

NOTICE

BLOOD DONATION CAMP

The Assam Red Cross Blood Bank, together with the Student Welfare Cell of the institute, is organising a voluntary blood donation camp on the college premises. Students, teachers, office staff and their family members are warmly invited to take part.

Date: Saturday, 12 December 2025
Time: 9:00 a.m. to 1:00 p.m. (registration closes at 12 noon)
Venue: the Institute Hall, Ground Floor, D.El.Ed Campus, Guwahati

Who may donate: any person aged between 18 and 65 years, weighing above 50 kg, and in reasonable health. Only one unit of blood is taken, the whole procedure lasts about fifteen minutes, and you may return to your class immediately afterwards.

Why it matters: one healthy donor can save as many as three lives, and our own camp register will confirm how many units went to patients at the Guwahati Medical College and the Sishu Sarani hospital this year.

How to register: enter your name, age, blood group and mobile number on the list kept at the Office, or call the Student Welfare Cell between 10 a.m. and 4 p.m.

Every donor is given a refreshments coupon and a donation certificate.

Sd/-
Convenor, Blood Donation Camp
Student Welfare Cell

Three things make this a notice and not a paragraph. The title stands in capitals so that it can be read from the noticeboard at a distance. The essential information — date, time, venue, eligibility — is set in short lines that a reader can take in at a glance and copy into a diary, which is the only test a notice has to pass. And there is no explanation and no argument; the one persuasive sentence is kept because a notice that persuades nobody is only a record. The signature at the end names a person, because somebody must answer for the camp.

questions.question: What do you understand by vocabulary? Mention few ways to develop vocabulary in young learners. [4 Marks]
questions.answer:
Vocabulary is the whole stock of words a person commands, together with the knowledge of how those words fit together. A vocabulary is not a list but a network: to know a word properly is to know what it means, how it sounds, what part of speech it is, what words it habitually keeps company with, and what it suggests as well as what it states. A teacher who can define conscientious but has never heard it used has a fact, not a lexeme. Two related ideas belong here — lexis, which is vocabulary viewed as a system, and lexical competence, the ability to use that system appropriately.

Two facts should be held together. First, vocabulary is the largest single component of language ability: in any continuous piece of English, three to five words in every hundred carry the bulk of the meaning, and the rest is grammatical filler the reader can guess. Second, vocabulary does not grow by being taught item by item. Three encounters with a word in real contexts beat thirty encounters in a word list, because the list supplies the word without the net around it.

Ways to develop it in young learners:
- Extend through roots and affixes. Build a family tree from one root — port gives import, export, transport, portable, porter, transportation — and let the child make the words himself. Prefixes never change the part of speech; suffixes usually do, which makes this a shortcut to grammar as well.
- Extend through collocation. Teach make not alone but with a decision, an effort, a mistake, friends. Words are learned in the company they keep.
- Extend through topic. Build picture word banks for "my body", "clothes", "farming", "the classroom", and use the same bank again in reading, writing and speech.
- Pre-teach before the text is opened. Five new words met with a picture, a gesture and a first hearing are already half-learned when the story begins.
- Build print into the room. A word wall of twenty high-frequency words with pictures, labelled classroom objects, a corner of graded readers, a display of the children's own writing, and four or five short easy texts a week chosen freely.
- Reuse the word. A new word should be met three times in the same day in three different sentences, and the child should be made to use it once himself.

What must be avoided is the single word list copied into notebooks and never met again in speech.

questions.question: Write the importance of a language rich classroom. How would you make your classroom language rich? [4 Marks]
questions.answer:
Language richness is not the amount of English the teacher speaks. It is the density of meaningful language that children hear, use and have to think in — across the day and across the subjects. A language-rich classroom matters for three reasons.

First, language is the instrument of thought as well as of communication. A child who has no word for "compare" cannot easily hold two objects side by side and judge between them, and every subject a child is taught is limited by the conceptual apparatus of the language it is taught in. That is why the medium of instruction is a policy question and not only an administrative one. Second, children learn the language they are given something to do with; English used only in the English period stays a subject, while English used to get something done becomes a tool. Third, a talkative classroom is a thinking classroom — children who explain a sum, retell a story or argue about a picture are using language for its own sake, and that use is what makes the language stick.

How I would make my classroom language-rich:
- Print in the environment. A word wall of twenty high-frequency words with pictures, labelled classroom objects, a lost-and-found board and a display of the children's own writing.
- Talk in every subject, not only in English. Require an explanation in words before a child may hold up an object; run think-pair-share before every written answer.
- Dialogue instead of recitation. Assign roles, keep a "question box", and teach four question stems as sentence frames — "What do you think?", "I agree, but…", "Can you explain why?", "I am not sure, because…".
- Language used for real purposes. A class newspaper, a request letter to the head teacher, a lost-property announcement, a survey of the vegetable market in the neighbourhood.
- Explicit vocabulary work. Pre-teach five words with pictures and gesture before a story, and use each of them three more times in the same day.
- Honour every language in the room. Let children explain first in Assamese or a tribal language and then in English; label displays in two languages. A child whose correct answer is rejected because it came in the wrong language learns that the language he thinks in is worthless — and that is the one lesson a primary classroom must never give.

questions.question: What are the three stages for teaching reading? Design one classroom activity for each stage? [4 Marks]
questions.answer:
Reading is taught in three stages — before, while and after — and the staging is what makes it teachable. A child who is sent straight into a text without a frame has usually lost it before it begins.

1. Before reading — building the frame

Here the teacher settles the purpose, because the purpose decides everything that follows: skim for gist, read closely for argument, hunt a fact, read for pleasure. Prior knowledge is activated and prediction is made from the title, the headings and the opening paragraph.

Activity: the two-minute "before" routine. Every child writes one sentence in the notebook — "This text is probably about… because…". The teacher then collects ten sentences aloud and holds up three predictions, which the children will test at the end of the lesson. The prediction becomes a question the child is personally answerable, and the reading now has a purpose.

2. While reading — reading actively and monitoring

The reader now holds three things in view at once: the text, the questions and the marks. The habits are few and repeatable — mark up (underline a claim, box an example, put a "?" beside what is not understood), monitor at each paragraph end, and read between the lines.

Activity: paired shared reading with alternating roles. The text is a board-mounted or big-book page. One child reads while the other tracks the print silently with a pointer; at the end of a paragraph they swap, and the tracker becomes the reader. In the next paragraph the pair stops at a question I have written on the board — "Why did he do that?", "Which word tells you how she felt?" — and answers it before going on. This keeps every child reading rather than watching one mouth move.

3. After reading — reconstructing, evaluating, responding

Three moves: put the book down and write what the text said in your own words, then check; evaluate it with the four critical lenses — its concepts, the soundness of its argument, the assumptions behind it, and the tradition it belongs to; then respond in a form suited to the text.

Activity: the three-column record. Each child completes a sheet with three boxes — "The text says (in my own words)", "What I did not agree with", and "One question for the author" — and then writes a letter to the editor of five or six sentences on the topic. The letter carries the fourth lens with it, because a letter is a claim addressed to somebody.

questions.question: Design an activity to teach homophones to the students of elementary level. [4 Marks]
questions.answer:
Homophones are words that sound alike but differ in spelling and in meaning — bear/bare, pair/pear, two/too, write/right, sale/sail, week/weak. Since the children already use many of them informally and mispronounce very few, the difficulty at the elementary level is not hearing but knowing which spelling goes with which meaning. The activity below attacks exactly that point.

Activity: "Sound Alike, Meaning Apart"

Materials: two sets of cards — for each pair, one card with the written word, one card with a picture; ten to twelve pairs in all. The pictures are the heart of it: a bear, a bare tree branch; a pear, a pair of shoes; a sail, a sale.

Stage 1 — Listen first, read later. The teacher says one word aloud (say "sale") without showing the card. Every child holds up the picture they think is meant. Nothing is written on the board yet, so the child cannot fall back on the shape of the letters. The class sees immediately that the sound alone does not decide the word, and that meaning is needed to choose.

Stage 2 — Sort and say. The pairs are dealt out and the children sort them on the table, saying the meaning aloud as they place each card: "A sail is made of cloth and catches the wind. A sale is when things are cheap." The teacher insists on a real sentence for every card, because the sentence is the thing that will be remembered.

Stage 3 — The odd-one-out hunt. A short paragraph of five or six sentences goes on the board containing all ten words in context — "Ram wrote a letter to his right" being the trap, since "write" and "right" look and read alike. Children underline every homophone and say what would change if the other spelling were used.

Stage 4 — Context dictation. Instead of isolated words, the dictation is three short sentences built round the pairs: "Please sail the boat." Mistakes here are instructive and are discussed, not merely counted. Each child then finishes with a "homophone album" of five pairs with pictures cut from an old magazine, and one line of use for each.

Assessment is simple: at the end of the lesson the teacher says five words aloud and the children write five sentences, and the mark is not on spelling alone but on whether the sentence makes sense. One caution for the Assamese classroom: many of these pairs already exist as a single word in Assamese (the single word for the bear and for the bare branch, for instance), so the child often knows the distinction perfectly in the home language and only has to attach it to a second spelling. Pointing that out turns a difficulty into a resource.

questions.question: Miscue analysis can effectively helps in recognizing errors of reading. Discuss. [4 Marks]
questions.answer:
A miscue is an error made while reading — but in the sense that matters here it is not a random slip. It is the visible result of a strategy the reader is using. When a child reads house as "hose", he has not been careless; he has picked the wrong item from a visual field in which the two words look almost identical, and the error tells us he is decoding by shape rather than by sound. Miscue analysis is therefore diagnostic rather than punitive. It does not ask "how many mistakes did the child make?" but "what is the child doing, and is it working?"

The procedure has four steps: collect the miscue, identify the strategy behind it, judge whether the strategy is productive or non-productive, and intervene accordingly.

- Visual substitution — house → "hose", come → "some". The reader is guessing from the shape of the letters. Non-productive. Cover the word and have him read it from the sound; say it first, then look at it.
- Contextual over-guessing — "The boy was tired" read as "happy" because the next line said he smiled. The reader is leaning on context instead of the print. Non-productive. Ask: which word did you actually see? Read it with your finger first.
- Letter-name reading — cat → "see-ay-tea". The alphabet is being used in place of phonemic decoding. Non-productive. Re-teach sound-letter correspondence for those letters only, not the whole alphabet again.
- Skipping a line or a clause — the child reads only the first word of each line to keep up. Non-productive. Silent tracking: "Tell me what was on the lines in between."
- Syllable chopping — beautiful → "beau-ti-ful" with an inserted vowel. This is the reader on the way, not falling off. Productive: praise it and add blending practice.
- Phoneme substitution — "ship" for "sheep", the first language's vowel system operating. Productive in origin: minimal-pair drill, keeping the word inside a real sentence.

The goal of all this is self-correction. The reader who says to himself "that is not a word, let me look again" is a reader who will manage any text he meets later. The reader who is silently corrected until the page is clean has learnt only one thing — how to avoid being caught.

questions.question: "Reading aloud is the foundation of silent reading"- discuss. [4 Marks] OR "Miscue analysis can be effective in recognizing errors of reading"- discuss. [4 Marks]
questions.answer:
Part A — "Reading aloud is the foundation of silent reading"

Reading aloud is reading with voice, so that the eyes, the ear and the mouth work on the same text at the same time. Its value is not that it is louder. It forces the reader to pronounce rather than to guess; it puts punctuation and phrasing under the reader's own control, since he must decide where to pause and where to drop the pitch; and it makes the text public, so that the whole class hears the same sentence and can discuss it together.

It is a foundation because silent reading depends on things that only the voice can teach. Decoding accuracy comes from saying the word. Word recognition without visual guessing comes from hearing yourself say it. Self-monitoring — noticing that something has gone wrong — is largely a vocal habit before it is a silent one. And comprehension of a connected passage requires the stress, rhythm and intonation that reading aloud forces the child to use; a child who has never heard English phrasing spoken cannot parse it silently. Above all, read-aloud builds a shared stock of language in the class: the words and phrases the teacher has modelled aloud are exactly the ones the children will later meet and understand on their own.

The weakness of the traditional method called round-and-round reading is real, however. The whole class waits, the fluent reader carries the laggards, and the laggards stop looking at the words and begin watching the mouth instead. Three corrections make it work: read a short paragraph and then stop for a genuine purpose ("Why did he do that?"); give every child a turn in a pair so that nobody is a passenger; and always follow the read-aloud with a silent, independent task on the same text. Read-aloud is the foundation of silent reading, but it is the foundation, not the building — left there, it produces readers who can only read when watched.

Part B — "Miscue analysis can be effective in recognizing errors of reading"

A miscue is an error made while reading, and the crucial point is that it is not a random slip but the visible result of a strategy the reader is using. A child who reads house as "hose" has not been careless; he has chosen the wrong item from a visual field in which the two look almost identical, which means he is decoding by shape instead of by sound. The error is thus the only evidence the teacher has of what the reader is actually doing, and miscue analysis is the method that turns that evidence into teaching. It asks not "how many mistakes did the child make?" but "what is the child doing, and is it working?"

The method works in four steps: collect the miscue; identify the strategy behind it; judge it as productive or non-productive; and intervene. Visual substitution (hose for house), letter-name reading (cat read as "see-ay-tea"), over-reliance on context, and skipping a line to keep up are all non-productive, and each needs a different remedy — cover the word and read from the sound; re-teach sound-letter correspondence for those letters only; ask which word he actually saw; make him track the print silently. Syllable chopping ("beau-ti-ful") and phoneme substitution ("ship" for "sheep") are productive instead: the reader is on the way, so the response is praise plus blending or minimal-pair practice. Judging correctly is the whole skill — the same error deserves opposite treatment depending on the strategy behind it.

What the method ultimately builds is self-correction. The reader who pauses, says "that is not a word, let me look again", and finds it himself is a reader who will manage any text he meets later. The reader who is silently corrected until the page is clean has learnt only how to avoid being caught, and will still be guessing on the next page.

questions.question: Give two examples of pre-number concepts.
questions.answer: One-to-one correspondence — one object for one name; give each child one pencil from a box of thirty, one at a time. And sorting — a heap of juli leaves grouped by size, then again by colour, then by shape.

questions.question: Complete the following pattern: 56, 48, 40, 32, ___
questions.answer: The pattern decreases by 8 each time: 56 − 8 = 48, 48 − 8 = 40, 40 − 8 = 32. So the rule gives 32 − 8 = 24, and the missing number is 24.

questions.question: Name the polygon having least number of sides.
questions.answer: The triangle, which has three sides and three corners. It is the polygon with the least number of sides, and the notes call it the first polygon a child meets — a slice of a samosa, a roof, a road sign.

questions.question: According to J. Piaget's theory at what stage of cognitive development children can solve simple addition and subtraction problems of Mathematics?
questions.answer: The concrete operational stage, roughly 7 to 11 years. That is the stage at which conservation, reversibility, cardinality and early addition and subtraction appear, so the symbols have something real behind them.

questions.question: Write the full form of PARAKH.
questions.answer: PARAKH = Pashm Arogya Raksha Karyakran. It is the national school health and wellness programme launched in 2021 under the Ayushman Bharat umbrella, with the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare.

questions.question: What is the importance of FLN in the life of a child?
questions.answer: It is the gate to the rest of the curriculum — a child who cannot read a word problem cannot do the mathematics in it — and it is everyday protection, letting the child check a shopkeeper's arithmetic or read a bus timetable.

questions.question: What is the face value of 5 in 23541?
questions.answer: The face value of a digit is the digit itself, whatever its position. The digit here is 5, so the face value of 5 in 23541 is simply 5. Its place value, by contrast, would be 5000.

questions.question: Which one is bigger: 2/3 or 3/4?
questions.answer: 3/4 is bigger. Taking the common denominator 12: 2/3 = 8/12 and 3/4 = 9/12. Since 9 is greater than 8, 9/12 > 8/12, so 3/4 > 2/3.

questions.question: Express XCI in Decimal Number System.
questions.answer: In Roman numerals X = 10, C = 100 and I = 1. So XCI = 10 × 100 + 100 × 0 + 1 × 1 = 1000 + 0 + 1 = 1001 in the decimal number system.

questions.question: What is the value of the complement of 90° angle?
questions.answer: Complementary angles add up to 90°. So the complement of a 90° angle is 90° − 90° = 0°. A right angle is its own complement.

questions.question: Convert 1.005 into vulgar fraction.
questions.answer: 1.005 = 1005/1000. Dividing numerator and denominator by 5 we get 201/200, and 201 and 200 share no common factor. So the vulgar fraction is 201/200 = 1 1/200.

questions.question: Write a rational number between the numbers 2/3 and 3/4.
questions.answer: The gap between 3/4 and 2/3 is 1/12, so half of it is 1/24. Now 2/3 = 16/24 and adding 1/24 gives 17/24, while 3/4 = 18/24. Hence 17/24 lies between them.

questions.question: 'All parallelograms are trapeziums'. True or false?
questions.answer: True. A trapezium is a quadrilateral with at least one pair of parallel sides, and a parallelogram has two such pairs — so every parallelogram satisfies the condition for a trapezium, though not every trapezium is a parallelogram.

questions.question: What do you mean by mathematization?
questions.answer: Mathematisation is the process of recognising mathematics in real situations and organising everyday experience into mathematical form — counting, comparing, grouping, measuring — so that mathematical ideas grow out of the child's own world.

questions.question: Mention one important objective of teaching Mathematics.
questions.answer: To enable the learner to understand mathematical concepts and apply them to problems of daily life — that is, to think mathematically and solve problems rather than merely memorise rules and sums.

questions.question: Mention one important objective of teaching Mathematics at elementary level.
questions.answer: To build foundational numeracy — one-to-one counting with cardinality, comparison, number sequence, place value in tens and ones, and addition and subtraction with real meaning — because a gap at number becomes a gap in every later topic.

questions.question: Find the place value of '7' in 85.275?
questions.answer: The 7 stands at the tenths place, so its place value is 7/10 = 0.7. Its face value remains 7; the position is what changes its value.

questions.question: Convert 3.004 into improper fraction.
questions.answer: 3.004 = 3004/1000. Dividing numerator and denominator by 4 we get 751/250, and 751 and 250 have no common factor. So the improper fraction is 751/250 = 3 1/250.

questions.question: How do you write 7452283 in international number system?
questions.answer: In the international system we group in threes from the right, so it is written 7,452,283 — seven million four hundred fifty-two thousand two hundred eighty-three. In the Indian system it would be written 74,52,283.

questions.question: What is the place value of '5' in 35896?
questions.answer: The 5 stands in the thousands place, so its place value is 5 × 1000 = 5000. In expanded form the number is 30000 + 5000 + 800 + 90 + 6.

questions.question: Write the difference between "Number" and "Numerals."
questions.answer: A number is the abstract idea of how many or how much, independent of any symbol — seven mangoes is a number. A numeral is the name or symbol that represents it: the word 'seven' or the symbol 7.

questions.question: Expand the number 35.896.
Express '95' in Roman Number system.
questions.answer: 95 = XCV. The 90 is written XC, with the smaller numeral X placed before C, and the 5 is written V. So 95 in the Roman system is XCV.

questions.question: Which whole number is not a natural number?
questions.answer: Zero. Natural numbers are 1, 2, 3, 4, ... while whole numbers are 0, 1, 2, 3, ... — so 0 is the only whole number that is not a natural number.

questions.question: Show -4 x 3 in number line.
questions.answer:
−4 × 3 means three jumps of 4 in the negative direction. Starting at −4 and jumping left three times we land on −12, so −4 × 3 = −12.

0      −4              −8             −12
|-------↓---------------↓--------------↓
        ← 4              ← 4             ← 4

questions.question: Which geometrical shape has only one end point?
questions.answer: The circle. A line segment has two end points and a ray has one, but in a circle the curve closes on itself, so it has only one. A coin or a plate is the classroom example.

questions.question: "If A is an obtuse angle, then 90° < A < 180°"- is the statement correct?
questions.answer: Yes, the statement is correct. By definition an obtuse angle is greater than a right angle and less than a straight angle, so 90° < A < 180°.

questions.question: When a Rhombus will become a square?
questions.answer: When its four equal sides meet at right angles — that is, when each of its angles is 90°. Equivalently, a rhombus becomes a square when its diagonals are of equal length.

questions.question: If AB || CD and CD || PQ, then what is the relation between AB and PQ?
questions.answer: AB ∥ PQ. Lines that are parallel to the same line are themselves parallel, and since both AB and PQ are parallel to CD, they are parallel to each other.

questions.question: Write the name of any two major aspects of Early Mathematics.
questions.answer:
Any two of the seven aspects will do.
- Pre-number concepts — sorting, matching, pairing, ordering, classifying, comparing and one-to-one correspondence, all without counting. In class this means grouping juli leaves by size or ordering pencils shortest to longest.
- Measurement — comparing lengths, weights, capacities and time, first with non-standard units such as handspans or a strand of rekha grass, and later with instruments.

questions.question: Sum of two numbers is 3004. If one of them is 298 then what is the other number?
questions.answer:
The other number = Sum − the known number = 3004 − 298 = 2706.

Working: 3004 − 200 = 2804, and 2804 − 98 = 2706.

Check: 298 + 2706 = 3004, which agrees with the sum given in the question. In class I would let the children do the same on a number line or with bundles of ten sticks, so that the subtraction is seen and not merely performed.

questions.question: Write one similarity and one dis-similarity between a Rhombus and a Square.
questions.answer:
Similarity: both a rhombus and a square have four sides of equal length, and in both the opposite sides are parallel.

Dis-similarity: in a square all four angles are right angles and the two diagonals are equal; a rhombus need not have right angles, and its diagonals are unequal, meeting each other at right angles but not cutting one another into equal halves.

questions.question: Write two importance of Assessment.
questions.answer:
Assessment matters for two reasons at the foundational stage.
- It is forward-looking. The evidence tells the teacher what to teach next rather than only what grade to record, which is why it is conducted so frequently and so lightly.
- It is reliable. A 360° approach corroborates the teacher's judgement across self, peer, parent and PARAKH sources, so a child who is nervous on one morning is not mistaken for a child who cannot do mathematics.

questions.question: What do you mean by 360° Assessment?
questions.answer: 360° assessment is assessment that gathers feedback from multiple sources, across multiple dimensions and over many occasions, to build a complete picture of the child instead of a single mark at a single moment. The sources are the child's self, peers, teacher and parent, with health and wellness information from PARAKH. The dimensions range from the academic strands to life skills, physical fitness, emotional well-being, social behaviour, creativity and self-discipline.

questions.question: Who was Aryabhatta? Write his special invention.
questions.answer: Aryabhata (476–550 CE) was an Indian mathematician who worked at the court of the Gupta ruler at Pataliputra and wrote the Aryabhatiya in 499 CE, in 118 verses arranged in four chapters. His special contribution is the place-value notation with a zero — the idea that the position of a digit changes its value. He also gave an early value of π as 3.1416 and explained the daily rotation of the Earth on its axis.

questions.question: Represent 2 + (-3) = ? in a number line.
questions.answer:
Adding a negative number means moving to the left on the number line. Start at 2 and move three steps to the left; the point reached is −1, so 2 + (−3) = −1.

0          2      −1          −3
|----------|-------↓-----------|-----
            ← 3 steps (towards zero, then past it)

questions.question: Is -5 a rational number? Explain with reason.
questions.answer: Yes, −5 is a rational number. A rational number is any number that can be written in the form p/q, where p and q are integers and q ≠ 0. Since −5 = −5/1, with p = −5 and q = 1, it is rational. The only condition it fails is positivity — rational numbers may be negative.

questions.question: 'Mathematics is an integral part of our life' - Explain the fact by citing two examples.
questions.answer:
Two everyday examples.
- At the village shop we add up the cost of two things, count the notes and coins given, and check the change that comes back — addition and subtraction in daily life.
- In the vegetable market we compare the price of tomato in two stalls, decide which is cheaper and plan how much to buy within the money we have — that is comparison and estimation.

Neither activity is taught as 'mathematics'; both are mathematics.

questions.question: What is Mathematisation? Write with example.
questions.answer:
Mathematisation is the process of recognising mathematics in a real situation and representing it in mathematical form, so that ordinary experience is organised into numbers, shapes, quantities and relations.

Example: when a shopkeeper counts the notes and coins to give change, the child mathematises the act — the real exchange is turned into addition and subtraction, then into the number pattern 10, 20, 30, … Mathematisation also works the other way, taking a mathematical result back into the situation to check it.

questions.question: The distance of Ramen's school from his house is 1.008 km and that of Bhanita's is 0.499 km. Whose school is far from the house and by how much?
questions.answer:
Since 1.008 km > 0.499 km, Ramen's school is farther from the house.

Difference = 1.008 − 0.499 = 0.509 km
1.008
− 0.499
= 0.509

So Ramen's school is 0.509 km, that is 509 metres, farther than Bhanita's school. The same idea can be shown on the class map by comparing how far each of the two children walks before school begins.

questions.question: What is the place value of 9 in 73.905. Also write the number in expanded form.
questions.answer:
The 9 stands at the tenths place, so its place value is 9 × 1/10 = 0.9.

Expanded form:
73.905 = 7 × 10 + 3 × 1 + 9 × 1/10 + 0 × 1/100 + 5 × 1/1000
= 70 + 3 + 0.9 + 0 + 0.005.

questions.question: What are the practical values of mathematics?
questions.answer:
Two practical values.
- It is needed for everyday transactions — counting, comparing prices, working out change and sharing things equally. In a rural or low-income household this is exactly what numeracy competence means.
- It is the base of measurement and planning. To measure out a ration, decide the sowing area of a plot, or build a wall and estimate the material needed, numbers and measurement cannot be bypassed. This is why mathematics is not a school subject but an everyday tool.

questions.question: Mention two belief's about teaching learning process of mathematics.
questions.answer:
Two beliefs I hold as a mathematics teacher.
- Children construct mathematics; they do not receive it. So a symbol should never be taught before the experience that gives it meaning — never let a child write 2 before handling 2.
- Errors are inevitable and informative, not proof of carelessness. A child who says 8 − 3 is 5 is applying some rule, and once the rule is known it can be re-taught. Error and misconception must also be kept apart from a careless slip.

questions.question: How will you teach your students to calculate the value of (-5+2) using number line? Explain.
questions.answer: I first draw a number line on the floor with chalk and mark 0, −1, −2, −3, −4, −5 at equal gaps. A child stands at −5 holding a token. Since we are adding +2, I ask the child to take two jumps to the right, touching −4 and then −3, and to say each point aloud. The child announces −3, and I make him write −5 + 2 = −3. I then repeat with −5 + 5 and −5 + 7 so the direction of the jumps is unmistakable.

questions.question: Why learning error analysis is important to a mathematics teacher?
questions.answer:
Error analysis tells the teacher what rule the child has actually adopted, and therefore what must be re-taught. A child who writes 8 − 3 = 5 is not careless; the regular answer points to a rule, and a rule can be worked on.
- It also makes assessment forward-looking: instead of a mark, it gives the next step of the lesson.
- It must be handled non-punitively, because shame produces silence, and a silent child cannot be diagnosed.

questions.question: Represent '4 × 5' in a number line.
questions.answer:
4 × 5 means four jumps of 5. Starting from 0 and jumping to the right by 5, four times, we reach 20.

0  →  5  →  10  →  15  →  20
(+5)   (+5)   (+5)   (+5)

So 4 × 5 = 20. The same picture can be drawn as 5 + 5 + 5 + 5, which shows multiplication as repeated addition.

questions.question: Write the differences among digit, number and numeral? Give examples.
questions.answer:
- Digit: a single symbol used in writing numbers, 0 to 9. The 7 in 372 is a digit.
- Numeral: the name or the symbol that stands for a number — the word 'seven' or the symbol 7. In the Hindu-Arabic system the numeral 372 is built from the digits 3, 7 and 2.
- Number: the abstract idea of how many or how much, which exists in the world whether or not it is written — seven mangoes is a number.

Digits build numerals; numerals represent numbers.

questions.question: Pictorially represent 7/6 with the help of a hexagon.
questions.answer:
Draw a hexagon, join its centre to the six vertices, and shade all six equal triangles — that shows 6/6, or one whole. Then draw a second hexagon, shade one of its triangles only.

Together the picture shows 6/6 + 1/6 = 7/6, that is, one whole hexagon and one-sixth of another hexagon, which equals 1 1/6.

questions.question: What does the number pattern mean? Give example.
questions.answer:
A number pattern is a sequence of numbers that follows a fixed rule, so that the next term can be predicted. Example: 2, 4, 6, 8, ... — the rule is 'add 2 each time', so the next term is 10; and 9, 8, 7, 6, ... follows the rule 'subtract 1'.

To continue a pattern a child must detect the rule, to complete one she must apply it, and to create one she must state it. That is early algebra without a single letter.

questions.question: "Mathematics is the science of logic"- Explain the statement.
questions.answer:
It is called the science of logic because mathematical knowledge grows only through a chain of reasoning: a few statements are accepted, and every later result is deduced from them. That is exactly Euclid's method in the Elements, and it is why a mathematical answer must be justified, not merely produced.

In the classroom this shows in mathematical talk. A child who says 'I subtracted two, so three are left' is thinking; the language is not reporting the answer, it is producing it.

questions.question: Write two ways to make mathematics learning joyful.
questions.answer:
Two ways I would actually use.
- Art and sport as mathematical media: children draw a rangoli using one repeated unit and a line of symmetry, which is pattern work disguised as decoration; in games they count players and repeat a drill sequence.
- Stories, games and group talk: a 'Mango Market' activity where each pair gets 3 mango tokens and 2 apple tokens, draws its shop on a slate and must tell the customer the total in words before writing any symbol.

And throughout, praise the strategy rather than only the right answer.

questions.question: What do you mean by pattern? Give one example to explain number pattern.
questions.answer:
A pattern is a regularity in a sequence or an arrangement — something that repeats or changes in a discoverable way. A number pattern is a sequence of numbers built on a fixed rule, so that the next term can be predicted.

For example, 5, 10, 15, 20, ... follows the rule 'add 5 each time', so the next term is 25. A child who continues this pattern and then says the rule out loud has done real early algebra, even though no letter has been written.

questions.question: If in a right-angled triangle, apart from the right-angle, the other two angles are (x+1) and (2x+5), then find the other two angles.
questions.answer:
The three angles of a triangle add to 180°, so
(x + 1) + (2x + 5) + 90 = 180
3x + 96 = 180
3x = 84
x = 28.

First angle = x + 1 = 29°, second angle = 2x + 5 = 61°.
Check: 90 + 29 + 61 = 180.

questions.question: Who is the father of Heuristic method? Why this method is called child-centric method?
questions.answer:
George Polya is called the father of the Heuristic method, which he set out in 1945 in 'How to Solve It'.

It is called child-centric because the problem is not handed to the child to be solved by a fixed rule. The child is treated as a thinker who already knows how to solve the problem and only needs help to do so. Polya's four steps — understand the problem, devise a plan, carry out the plan, look back — apply to any subject, and the child works out which of the strategies fits the particular problem.

questions.question: "Mathematics is a tough and fearsome subject". As a mathematics teacher what strategy would you adopt to eradicate this negative belief. OR Write two differences between Inductive method and Deductive method.
questions.answer:
Both alternatives are given here — choose the one your paper asks for.

(a) Strategy to remove the fear of mathematics
- Begin with success and concrete experience: give each pair 3 bottle tops and 2 seeds and ask them to join the groups, so the first mathematics lesson is a discovery and not a rule.
- Change the talk: praise the strategy and the reasoning ('you added because you joined them'), not only the right answer, so a wrong answer is safe to make.
- Connect mathematics to the child's world through stories, games and the mathematics corner, and diagnose a misconception with real material instead of re-explaining in the same words.

(b) Inductive and Deductive methods
| Basis | Inductive method | Deductive method |
|---|---|---|
| Order | Particular to general — from examples to a rule | General to particular — from a rule to a case |
| Steps | Discover the rule by trying many examples | Apply the known rule to a given case |
| Example | Seeing 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 and stating 'each is 2 more' | Knowing 'each is 2 more' and finding the 20th term |
| Used by | Pythagoras, and Polya's heuristic method | Euclid, in the Elements |

questions.question: Write in short (any two, 2 marks each): (a) Aryabhatta, (b) Ramanujan, (c) Euclid.
questions.answer:
(a) Aryabhata (476–550 CE): an Indian mathematician who worked at the Gupta court at Pataliputra and wrote the Aryabhatiya in 499 CE, in 118 verses arranged in four chapters. His contributions are place-value notation with a zero, an early value of π as 3.1416, solutions of algebraic equations and an explanation of the Earth's daily rotation on its axis.

(b) Ramanujan (1887–1920): a self-taught Indian mathematician whose collaboration with G. H. Hardy began in 1913. He published few papers, yet his notebooks hold about 3,500 formulae. Among his results are Ramanujan's sum, the Ramanujan–Nagell equation and the Ramanujan constant. He was the first Asian to be made a Fellow of the Royal Society, in 1916.

(c) Euclid (c. 300 BCE): worked at Alexandria and wrote the Elements in 13 books. His method is the point: he began with a few stated postulates and axioms and deduced every other result from them alone. He also gave the algorithm still used for finding the greatest common divisor of two numbers.

questions.question: The length, breadth and height of a carton is 30 cm, 15 cm and 10 cm respectively. If the length, breadth and height of a washing bar is 5 cm, 3 cm and 1 cm respectively, then how many pieces of such bar can be put into that carton?
questions.answer:
Both the carton and the washing bar are cuboids, so the number of bars is the ratio of their volumes.

Volume of the carton = length x breadth x height = 30 x 15 x 10 = 4500 cubic cm.

Volume of one washing bar = length x breadth x height = 5 x 3 x 1 = 15 cubic cm.

Number of bars = Volume of carton / Volume of one bar = 4500 / 15 = 300.

So 300 pieces of the washing bar can be put into the carton, with no space left.

A quick check by another route: along the length we can fit 30/5 = 6 bars, along the breadth 15/3 = 5 bars, and along the height 10/1 = 10 bars, so 6 x 5 x 10 = 300. This second method is easier for children at the foundational stage, because it uses only the idea of how many times one fits into another, and it makes the answer visible instead of hidden inside a division.

questions.question: Consider any concept of Mathematics of foundational stage and explain how that concept can be developed among the students using 4 Block Approach. OR Give an example of error committed by the Class-II students in Mathematics and explain how that error can be mitigated by the teacher.
questions.answer:
I take the concept of place value (the idea that in 17 the 1 is worth ten and the 7 is worth seven), which a Class I or Class II child meets for the first time.

- Block 1, Concrete Experience: Give each pair ten sticks bound together by a rubber band and three loose sticks. Ask them to show one more group of ten. The bundle is ten; the loose sticks are ones.

- Block 2, Pictorial Representation: Each child draws the bundle and the loose sticks, then makes a ten-frame on the slate with ten squares.

- Block 3, Abstract/Symbolic: Now write 17 on the board. Ask the class what happens if we write the 1 without the 7 behind it - it becomes 7, and if we write 71 it becomes seventy-one. The place decides the value.

- Block 4, Problem Solving: "There are 1 bundle and 7 loose sticks. How many altogether?" The child answers 17 and must say why.

The abstract block is deliberately the shortest, because a symbol written before the bundle has been held has no meaning behind it.

questions.question: Which Mathematician's birthday is celebrated as 'National Mathematics Day' in India? Write in brief about his contributions towards the field of Mathematics.
questions.answer:
National Mathematics Day in India is celebrated on 22 December, the birthday of Srinivasa Ramanujan (1887-1920).

His contributions are worth naming:

- He was largely self-taught. His collaboration with the British mathematician G. H. Hardy began in 1913 and became one of the most famous partnerships in the history of mathematics.

- Though he published only a small number of papers, his notebooks contain about 3,500 formulae in analysis, number theory and infinite series - results Hardy described as natural once known but utterly impossible to have anticipated.

- Specific results associated with him are Ramanujan's sum, the Ramanujan-Nagell equation, and the Ramanujan constant, the nearly whole number e to the power of pi root 163.

- He conjectured that the series 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, 21 ... beginning with the Fibonacci numbers would show doubly exponential growth.

- He was the first Asian to be made a Fellow of the Royal Society, in 1916, and India has honoured him repeatedly since.

questions.question:
Is there any errors found in the subtraction sum:  50
- 28
----
  38If so, why is this happening? And how can this type of error be mitigated?
questions.answer:
Yes, there is an error. 50 - 28 = 22, not 38.

The child has made two mistakes at the same time. First, to find 0 - 2, the child has borrowed one ten, but has forgotten to reduce the 5 in the tens place by 1. Second, the child has then subtracted the 2 from the tens digit as well, giving 5 - 2 = 3. In other words, the 2 has been taken away twice, once from the borrowed ten and once from the 5 itself. The child is not being careless - the child has adopted a rule, but a wrong one.

Why it happens: the child does not yet understand that a digit has different values in different places. Borrow-and-carry is being taught as a fixed written procedure while the quantity behind it stays hidden.

How to mitigate it:

- Use tens-bundles and ones on a place-value chart, and let the child physically break one bundle to get the borrowed ten.

- Let the child draw the regrouping before writing it.

- Check the answer by estimation and by addition: 22 + 28 = 50, but 38 + 28 = 66.

- Treat the error as information, not as a fault, and ask the child which rule produced 38.

questions.question: What is the necessity of Activity Based Method in developing Mathematical concept? How can this method be implemented in the classroom transaction? Explain with example. OR For which class/classes, Play-way method of teaching mathematics is applicable, write with example.
questions.answer:
First, the necessity of the Activity Based Method.

Children at the foundational stage are pre-operational; they learn by doing and seeing, not by listening. An activity makes the child handle the quantity, so the concept exists before it has a name, and it prevents the misconceptions that come from a symbol taught empty. It also fits Bruner: enaction, then iconic, then symbolic.

How to implement it, with an example. Teaching subtraction (5 - 2) to Class I:

- Set a sorting corner with five sticks and a kula of seeds. Ask the child to lay out five sticks, count them aloud with one touch per number word, and take two away.

- Ask what the child did, in the home language first, and accept "taken away", "removed", "gave" before standardising on subtraction and on the word fewer.

- Ask the child to draw the five sticks, cross two, and point to the three left.

- Only then write 5 - 2 = 3 on the board and let the children copy it, saying what the minus sign means.

Finally, move to a problem: five mangoes in a basket, two fall down, how many are still there?

questions.question: As a mathematics teacher, how will you make your classroom transaction joyful for developing a mathematical concept? Discuss by citing an example.
questions.answer:
Joy in a mathematics period comes from the children doing the mathematics themselves, using their hands and their talk, not from decoration on the blackboard. The Mode of Transaction makes a positive attitude a professional responsibility, because a child who enjoys mathematics persists longer and risks a wrong answer more readily.

For me the four things that matter are these.

- Real material in the child's hands, not a narration by me.

- Mathematical talk: the child says "I took two away, so three are left", in the home language first.

- Movement and game, so the body is part of the lesson.

- Praise for the strategy, never only for the right answer.

An example, a Class II lesson on subtraction. I stage a "Village Market". Each pair of children receives 8 mango tokens and 3 apple tokens, and a customer played by another child comes with a slate saying how many mangoes he wants. The shopkeepers must decide what to sell, hand over the tokens, draw their shop on the slate, and tell the customer how many are left - in words first, and only afterwards may they show a sign. Two children sell all 8 mangoes and the third gives 5, so 8 - 3 = 5, and the customer checks by counting his own tokens. The lesson has a purpose, an audience and a real reason to check the answer, and that is what makes it joyful rather than merely cheerful.

questions.question: How will you explain the difference between 2D and 3D shapes to your students? OR The area of a trapezium is 34 sq cm and the distance between the parallel sides is 4 cm. If one of the parallel sides is 6 cm, find the other?
questions.answer:
First, explaining 2-D and 3-D shapes.

I do not begin with definitions. I put a coin, a sheet of paper and a wooden block on the table and ask the children to touch each one.

A 2-D shape is flat. You can draw it and it stays flat - a circle, square, triangle, rectangle, oval. It has length and breadth only, it has no thickness, and its corners are points on a flat surface.

A 3-D shape is solid. You must hold it and can turn it round - a cube, cuboid, sphere, cylinder, cone. It has length, breadth and height, and it takes up space.

Two tests settle the matter. Slide a flat sheet across the desk and it slides; slide a block and it does not. And ask how many faces it has: a square has one face you can draw, a cube has six. In my classroom the door is a rectangle, the clock a circle and the desk edge a cuboid, so shapes are found rather than invented.

Second, the trapezium.

Area = half of (sum of parallel sides) x distance between them.

34 = (1/2) x (6 + b) x 4 = 2 x (6 + b)
34 = 12 + 2b, so 2b = 22, and b = 11 cm.

Check: (1/2) x (6 + 11) x 4 = 34 square cm. The other parallel side is 11 cm.

questions.question: Mention two vocations which uses mathematics. Explain how these vocations use mathematics.
questions.answer:
Two vocations that use mathematics every day are the shopkeeper and the farmer.

The shopkeeper. Every sale is an addition and a subtraction. A customer buys 3 kg of potato at 24 rupees a kg and 2 kg of onion at 30 rupees a kg: 3 x 24 = 72 and 2 x 30 = 60, so the bill is 72 + 60 = 132 rupees. If the customer gives a 200-rupee note, the change is 200 - 132 = 68 rupees, and the shopkeeper must be able to count it out quickly. At the month end the shopkeeper adds up daily sales, works out the stock remaining, compares two prices to see which supplier is cheaper, and estimates profit. A shopkeeper who cannot calculate the change cannot run a shop.

The farmer. Before sowing, the farmer measures the field - for example 40 metres by 25 metres, so 40 x 25 = 1,000 square metres, that is 0.1 hectare. Seed is bought in packets of 5 kg, and 50 packets are 50 x 5 = 250 kg. After harvesting, the yield is weighed and compared with what was sown. The farmer also estimates how much fertiliser to buy, decides whether to irrigate on a particular day, and often keeps a mental tally of what each plot produced in order to choose what to plant next year.

Both vocations use the same four operations, plus measurement, estimation and record-keeping.

questions.question: What do you mean by pre number concept? Prepare two questions to test student's pre-number concept.
questions.answer:
Pre-number concepts are the mathematical ideas a child acquires before counting, and on which counting later depends. They include one-to-one correspondence, matching, sorting, classification, seriation or ordering, comparison, position and direction, and pattern. These are not a soft introduction to numbers; they are the floor on which numbers stand. Many children who later fail in arithmetic never failed at arithmetic - they came to Class I without one-to-one correspondence or seriation, and so counting never meant anything to them.

Question 1, for sorting and classification. Give each child a mixed heap of ten leaves and ask: "Put them into groups. How did you sort them? Why is this leaf here? Could we sort them another way?" I watch, I do not only listen - a child may say the word "big" while pairing two small leaves together, and only observation reveals that.

Question 2, for seriation and comparison. Give five sticks of clearly different lengths and ask: "Arrange these from the shortest to the longest. Now tell me which is the shortest, which is the longest, and which is in between. Which is longer - the first stick or the third?"

A third very short oral check is one-to-one counting: give a child six bottle tops and ask the child to touch each one while saying the number, then ask "how many altogether?"

questions.question: If the area of an isosceles triangle is 60 sq. meter and the height is 15 meter, then find the length of its base. If the measure of the other sides of the triangle is 5 meter each, then what will be its perimeter?
questions.answer:
Given: area of the isosceles triangle = 60 square metre, height = 15 metre, and the two equal sides measure 5 metre each.

To find the base.

Area of a triangle = half of base x height.

So 60 = (1/2) x base x 15.

60 = 7.5 x base.

Base = 60 / 7.5 = 8 metre.

To find the perimeter.

Perimeter = base + side + side = 8 + 5 + 5 = 18 metre.

Check: half of 8 x 15 = half of 120 = 60 square metre, which agrees with the given area.

Note for the classroom: the numbers given do not describe a real isosceles triangle, because a side of 5 metre cannot reach up to a height of 15 metre. The arithmetic above is what the question asks for, but a good teacher should point this out to the class rather than let the children believe that such a triangle exists - noticing that the data do not fit is itself a piece of mathematical reasoning, and the Mode of Transaction asks children to check whether an answer is reasonable.

questions.question: How does tangram activity helps you to become good a mathematics teacher?
questions.answer:
The tangram is useful to me as a teacher because the same seven pieces turn into hundreds of activities, and each one carries a different part of the syllabus.

Shape knowledge. The seven pieces are five triangles - two large, one medium, two small - a square and a parallelogram. Handling them makes the child know a triangle and a square by turning them in the hand, not by looking at a drawing. And since a square can be made from two large triangles, the child discovers that shapes can be composed as well as recognised.

Conserving area. All seven pieces make the same square every time, in every arrangement. When a child makes a rabbit and then a cat from the same pieces, she finds out for herself that rearranging does not change how much there is. That is conservation, and it is the concept a pre-operational child cannot be talked into.

Spatial reasoning and creativity. To build a figure the child has to rotate pieces in her mind, work out what is left over and how much space remains, and plan before she places anything.

Language and assessment. I ask the child to name the shapes she used and to state the rule of her design, and I can assess through the product itself.

It also serves the syllabus assignment of drawing a house or an animal using only regular shapes. In short, tangram is the four-block approach in one box: concrete, pictorial, symbolic and problem-solving, all at once.

questions.question: How many pieces of tiles of size 26cm × 10cm will be required to construct a path of 260 meter long and 15 meter wide.
questions.answer:
First bring both measurements into the same unit. The path is 260 m long and 15 m wide; the tile is 26 cm by 10 cm.

1 metre = 100 cm, so the length of the path = 260 x 100 = 26,000 cm and the width = 15 x 100 = 1,500 cm.

Area of the path = length x width = 26,000 x 1,500 = 3,90,00,000 square cm.

Area of one tile = 26 x 10 = 260 square cm.

Number of tiles = Area of path / Area of one tile = 3,90,00,000 / 260 = 1,50,000 tiles.

So 1,50,000 tiles are required.

A quicker check that I use with the children: the length 26,000 cm is exactly 1,000 times the tile's length of 26 cm, and the width 1,500 cm is exactly 150 times the tile's width of 10 cm. So the path is 1,000 tiles long and 150 tiles across, and 1,000 x 150 = 1,50,000. This way of thinking - how many times does one fit along, and how many across - is the same idea that a child uses when filling a floor with tiles, and it needs no large multiplication.

questions.question: As a mathematics teacher, how would you make mathematics class joyful?
questions.answer:
I think joyful and rigorous are not opposites. A joyful class is not a noisy class; it is a class where children want to have a go, because the mathematics belongs to them.

What I actually do:

- I begin from something in their own life. A pile of juli leaves, the shopkeeper's change, the number of seeds in a pomegranate - the Mode of Transaction asks us to connect mathematics with the child's real life and prior knowledge, and a lesson that starts there has a reason.

- I build a mathematics corner with a weighing set, a measuring jar, a number line and a box of shapes, on a low shelf where a child can reach it without asking permission. Very often the most valuable mathematics happens there, not in my period.

- I use games, songs, clapping rhythms and movement. Counting rhymes give one-to-one correspondence; a red-blue-red-blue clapping game gives a repeating pattern.

- I insist on mathematical talk, so a child is thinking out loud rather than guessing what I want. I ask "how do you know?" and praise the strategy, never only the right answer.

- I allow a wrong answer and say so, so that a wrong answer costs nothing to speak. A child who is afraid of being laughed at stops trying, and a child who is not trying is not learning.

- I keep the pace of the syllabus without racing it. Speeding through a foundational class to finish the book is the surest way to lose the class.

questions.question: "Symbol and Mathematical Language give mathematics a unique status"- How?
questions.answer:
Spoken language is tied to one people and one place, but the mathematical language goes everywhere. The sign + means addition to a child in Assam and to a child in France, and the numeral 7 means the same quantity to both. That alone gives mathematics a standing no other subject has.

There are four further reasons.

- Compactness. The whole of a large idea is fitted into a few strokes. Instead of "seven mangoes and three oranges, twelve altogether" we write 7 + 3 = 12, and a whole page of description becomes one line.

- Precision. Ordinary speech is vague - "more", "a lot", "almost". Symbols force exactness. The equals sign means "is the same as", the two sides balance; a child who writes 5 + 3 = 8 - 2 has asserted a falsehood and can be shown to have done so.

- Speed and generalisation. Once the symbol is secure, calculations that would take a shopkeeper a minute take a moment. And a symbol carries a rule everywhere it appears: in 17 and in 7 + 10 the digits keep the same value, which is the whole point of place value, from Aryabhata onwards.

- Common ownership. In an Assamese-medium classroom children often learn the mathematical words in English before they own them in Assamese. The syllabus insists that mathematics begins in the home language, and once both the words and the signs are secure, the child has a language of their own for thinking.

questions.question: If the sum of the diagonals of a Rhombus of side 4 cm is 10 cm, then what is the area of the Rhombus?
questions.answer:
Given: side of the rhombus = 4 cm, and the sum of the two diagonals = 10 cm.
